vce-chem12-atomic-structure-and-isotopes: chem12a1-ast-1
How many neutrons are in one atom of chlorine-37 (³⁷₁₇Cl)?
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20. 17 is the number of protons, and 37 is the total number of nucleons.
chem12a1-ast-2
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 have the same chemical properties because they have the same
mass number.
number of neutrons.
number of nucleons.
number and arrangement of electrons.

Isotopes have the same number of protons and therefore, as neutral atoms, the same electron configuration. Chemical behaviour depends on the electrons. Their neutron numbers and mass numbers are different.
chem12a1-ast-3
The ion ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ contains
26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons.
26 protons, 30 neutrons and 29 electrons.
23 protons, 33 neutrons and 26 electrons.
26 protons, 56 neutrons and 23 electrons.
Fe has atomic number 26, so it has 26 protons. Neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30. A 3+ charge means 3 electrons have been lost: 26 − 3 = 23. Gaining 3 electrons (29) would give a 3− ion.
chem12a1-ast-4
A sample of copper contains 69.2% copper-63 and 30.8% copper-65 (take the isotopic masses as 63.0 and 65.0). The relative atomic mass of copper in this sample is closest to
Ar = (63.0 × 0.692) + (65.0 × 0.308) = 43.6 + 20.0 = 63.6. 64.0 is the simple average, which ignores that copper-63 is more abundant.
chem12a1-ast-5
In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but a very small number were deflected back. This showed that
electrons occupy fixed energy levels.
atoms are solid, indivisible spheres.
an atom is mostly empty space with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
negative charges are spread evenly through a positive sphere.

Most particles passing through shows the atom is mostly empty space. Strong deflection of a few shows a tiny, dense, positive centre. Fixed energy levels come from Bohr's model, and the evenly spread charge describes Thomson's model, which this result disproved.
chem12a1-ast-6
Define the term isotopes and explain why ¹²C and ¹⁴C react identically with oxygen. (2 marks)

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons/atomic number) with different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers); both isotopes have 6 electrons with the same configuration (2,4), and chemical reactions depend on electrons, so they react identically.
chem12a1-ast-7
Naturally occurring boron is 19.9% ¹⁰B (isotopic mass 10.0) and 80.1% ¹¹B (isotopic mass 11.0). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron to three significant figures. Show your working. (2 marks)
chem12a1-ast-8
A particle contains 16 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. Identify the particle and write its full symbol, including mass number and charge. Explain how you determined the charge. (3 marks)
16 protons means the element is sulfur; mass number = 16 + 18 = 34, symbol ³⁴S²⁻ (³⁴₁₆S²⁻); there are 2 more electrons than protons, so the charge is 2−.
chem12a1-ast-9
The atomic number of an element is the number of
neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
protons in the nucleus of an atom.
protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
electrons in the outer shell of an atom.
The atomic number is the number of protons, and it defines the element. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, so that option describes the wrong quantity.
chem12a1-ast-10
Which statement best describes the mass number of an atom?
The total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.
The number of protons in its nucleus.
The mass of one atom in grams.
The weighted average mass of all its isotopes.
Mass number = protons + neutrons, always a whole number for a particular isotope. The weighted average mass of the isotopes is the relative atomic mass, which is usually not a whole number.
chem12a1-ast-11
Chlorine consists of 75.8% ³⁵Cl (isotopic mass 35.0) and 24.2% ³⁷Cl (isotopic mass 37.0). The relative atomic mass of chlorine is closest to
Ar = (35.0 × 0.758) + (37.0 × 0.242) = 26.5 + 9.0 = 35.5. 36.0 is the simple average, which ignores that ³⁵Cl is about three times as abundant as ³⁷Cl.
chem12a1-ast-12
How many electrons are in one ²⁴Mg²⁺ ion?
Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral atom has 12 electrons. A 2+ charge means two electrons have been lost, leaving 10. 12 is the number of protons, which does not change when the ion forms.
chem12a1-ast-13
The electron configuration of a calcium atom (atomic number 20) is

Shells fill 2, 8, 8 and the remaining two electrons go in the fourth shell, giving 2,8,8,2. 2,8,10 is wrong because the third shell is filled with 8 electrons before the fourth shell begins, in this model for the first 20 elements.
chem12a1-ast-14
In a mass spectrometer, positive ions are separated according to their
mass-to-charge ratio.
number of neutrons only.
electronegativity.
number of occupied electron shells.

Ions are deflected by a magnetic field by an amount that depends on their mass-to-charge ratio, so isotopes of an element are separated. Neutron number matters only because it contributes to the mass.
chem12a1-ast-15
Which subatomic particle has a relative mass of approximately 1 and no electrical charge?
Electron
Proton
Neutron
Nucleus
The neutron has about the same mass as a proton but is uncharged. The proton has similar mass but a positive charge, and the electron is negatively charged with almost no mass.
chem12a1-ast-16
Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N
¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O
⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca
²³₁₁Na and ²³₁₁Na
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, as in ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O. ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N have the same mass number but different atomic numbers, so they are different elements.
chem12a1-ast-17
A species contains 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. It is
³⁵Cl⁺
³⁵Ar⁻
³⁵Cl⁻
³⁵S²⁻
17 protons identifies chlorine and 17 + 18 = 35 is the mass number. One more electron than protons gives a 1− charge, so it is ³⁵Cl⁻. A 1+ charge would need fewer electrons than protons.
chem12a1-ast-18
An atom has the electron configuration 2,8,5. It is located in
Group 5, period 2.
Group 13, period 3.
Group 15, period 5.
Group 15, period 3.

Three occupied shells means period 3. Five outer electrons means Group 15 (the group number is 10 + number of valence electrons for main groups 13 to 18). Group 5 does not apply to main-group elements.
chem12a1-ast-19
The relative atomic mass of most elements is not a whole number because it is
affected by fractions of protons in the nucleus.
a weighted average of the masses of the naturally occurring isotopes.
increased by the mass of the electrons.
calculated from the mass of the most abundant isotope only.

Ar is a weighted average of isotopic masses using their relative abundances, so it is rarely whole. Electrons contribute almost no mass, and using only the most abundant isotope would give a whole number.
chem12a1-ast-20
Magnesium has three isotopes: ²⁴Mg (79.0%), ²⁵Mg (10.0%) and ²⁶Mg (11.0%). Taking isotopic masses as 24.0, 25.0 and 26.0, the relative atomic mass of magnesium is closest to
Ar = (24.0 × 0.790) + (25.0 × 0.100) + (26.0 × 0.110) = 18.96 + 2.50 + 2.86 = 24.3. 25.0 is the simple average of the three masses, which ignores the abundances.
chem12a1-ast-21
How many valence electrons does a sulfur atom (atomic number 16) have?
Sulfur's configuration is 2,8,6, so the outer (valence) shell holds 6 electrons. 8 is the number in the second shell, and 16 is the total number of electrons.
chem12a1-ast-22
An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Its symbol is
⁸₆C
¹⁴₈O
¹⁴₇N
¹⁴₆C
6 protons means carbon, and the mass number is 6 + 8 = 14, so the symbol is ¹⁴₆C. ⁸₆C would result from using the neutron number as the mass number.
chem12a1-ast-23
Element X has two isotopes, ⁷⁹X and ⁸¹X, and a relative atomic mass of 79.9. It can be concluded that
⁸¹X is the more abundant isotope.
⁷⁹X is the more abundant isotope.
the two isotopes are equally abundant.
no conclusion about abundance can be made.
A 50:50 mixture would give an Ar of 80.0. Because 79.9 is closer to 79, ⁷⁹X must be slightly more abundant.
chem12a1-ast-24
Describe how the nuclear model of the atom proposed by Rutherford differed from Thomson's plum pudding model. (3 marks)

Thomson's model had positive charge spread evenly through the whole atom with electrons embedded in it [1]; Rutherford's model placed all the positive charge and almost all the mass in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre [1]; the electrons are outside the nucleus, so the atom is mostly empty space [1].
chem12a1-ast-25

Naturally occurring neon consists of 90.5% ²⁰Ne, 0.3% ²¹Ne and 9.2% ²²Ne. Taking isotopic masses as 20.0, 21.0 and 22.0, calculate the relative atomic mass of neon to three significant figures. (2 marks)
chem12a1-ast-26
Write the electron configuration of an aluminium atom (atomic number 13) and of an Al³⁺ ion, and explain the difference. (3 marks)
Al atom: 2,8,3 [1]; Al³⁺ ion: 2,8 [1]; the atom loses its three outer-shell electrons to form the 3+ ion, so the third shell is no longer occupied [1].
chem12a1-ast-27
State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in one ⁶⁵Zn²⁺ ion (zinc has atomic number 30). (3 marks)
Protons = 30 [1]; neutrons = 65 − 30 = 35 [1]; electrons = 30 − 2 = 28 because the 2+ charge means two electrons have been lost [1].
chem12a1-ast-28
Lithium has two stable isotopes, ⁶Li (isotopic mass 6.0) and ⁷Li (isotopic mass 7.0). The relative atomic mass of lithium is 6.94. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. (3 marks)
Let the fraction of ⁷Li be x: 7.0x + 6.0(1 − x) = 6.94 [1]; x = 0.94, so ⁷Li is 94% [1]; ⁶Li is therefore 6% [1].
chem12a1-ast-29
Describe what a mass spectrum of an element shows and explain how it is used to determine the relative atomic mass of the element. (3 marks)

The horizontal axis shows mass-to-charge ratio (mass of each isotope for singly charged ions) and each peak represents one isotope [1]; the height of each peak gives the relative abundance of that isotope [1]; the relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotopic masses using these abundances [1].
chem12a1-ast-30
Describe two ways in which Bohr's model of the atom improved on Rutherford's nuclear model. (2 marks)

Electrons are in fixed shells (energy levels) at set distances from the nucleus, each with a specific energy [1]; electrons can move between energy levels only by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy [1].
chem12a1-ast-31

Atom X has 12 protons and 12 neutrons, atom Y has 12 protons and 14 neutrons, and atom Z has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Identify which two atoms are isotopes of the same element and write the symbol for each of them. (3 marks)
X and Y are isotopes because they have the same number of protons (12) but different numbers of neutrons [1]; the element is magnesium, so X is ²⁴Mg [1] and Y is ²⁶Mg [1].
chem12a1-ast-32
A ⁴⁰Ca atom forms a Ca²⁺ ion. State the number of electrons in the ion, write its electron configuration, and name the noble gas atom with the same configuration. (3 marks)
The ion has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons [1]; configuration 2,8,8 [1]; the same configuration as argon [1].
chem12a1-ast-33
How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in one ³¹P³⁻ ion? (P has atomic number 15)
15 protons, 16 neutrons, 18 electrons
15 protons, 16 neutrons, 12 electrons
15 protons, 31 neutrons, 18 electrons
16 protons, 15 neutrons, 15 electrons
The atomic number gives 15 protons, 31 − 15 = 16 neutrons, and the 3− charge means 15 + 3 = 18 electrons. Subtracting the charge (12 electrons) is a common error.
vce-chem12-as-c1
Which pair of atoms contains the same number of neutrons?
¹²C and ¹⁴N
¹⁴C and ¹⁶O
³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl
¹H and ²H
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. Isotopes of one element have different neutron numbers.
vce-chem12-electron-configuration-and-su: Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of a potassium atom?
K has 19 electrons. The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so the 19th electron goes into 4s. A p subshell can hold at most 6 electrons, so 3p⁷ is impossible.
The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a d subshell is
A d subshell has 5 orbitals, and each orbital holds 2 electrons, giving 10. An s subshell holds 2, a p subshell 6 and an f subshell 14.
The ground-state electron configuration of copper is an exception to the usual filling order. It is
Copper adopts 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ because a full d subshell is more stable. 3d⁹ 4s² is the configuration predicted by the simple filling order, but it is not the observed ground state.
The electron configuration of the Fe³⁺ ion is

Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are removed first, then the 3d electrons. Removing 2 electrons from 4s and 1 from 3d leaves [Ar] 3d⁵. [Ar] 3d³ 4s² would mean the 3d electrons were removed first.
The outermost subshell of an element's ground-state atom is 4p³. The element is in
The 4p subshell places the element in period 4 and the p-block. The configuration ends 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p³, so there are 5 valence electrons (4s² 4p³), which puts it in group 15. The element is arsenic.
Write the full subshell electron configuration for a sulfur atom and for the sulfide ion, S²⁻. (2 marks)
S: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴; S²⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (two electrons added to 3p, same configuration as argon).
Using the Schrödinger (subshell) model, explain why the 19th electron of calcium enters the 4s subshell rather than the 3d subshell, and state how many electrons a single orbital can hold. (2 marks)
Subshells fill in order of increasing energy, and the 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first; each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, which have opposite spins.

When a sample of a lithium salt is placed in a flame, a crimson colour is seen. Through a spectroscope this light appears as a series of distinct coloured lines. Explain how these lines arise and why each element gives a unique pattern. (3 marks)

Heat energy promotes (excites) electrons to higher energy levels; when the electrons return to lower energy levels they release the energy difference as light (photons) of specific energies/wavelengths, giving discrete lines; each element has a unique set of energy levels (different nuclear charge and electron arrangement), so the energy differences, and therefore the line pattern, are unique to that element.
How many orbitals are there in a p subshell?
A p subshell contains 3 orbitals, each holding up to 2 electrons. The number 6 is the maximum number of electrons in the subshell, not the number of orbitals.
Which subshells are found in the third shell (n = 3)?
The third shell contains three subshells: s, p and d. An f subshell does not appear until the fourth shell, and every shell contains an s subshell.
What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the third shell (n = 3)?
The third shell has 3s (2), 3p (6) and 3d (10) subshells, giving 18 electrons. A value of 8 would only count the 3s and 3p subshells.
The ground-state electron configuration of chromium is
Chromium has 24 electrons and adopts a half-filled 3d subshell with one electron in 4s. The configuration [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² follows the simple filling order but is not observed.
The electron configuration of the magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, is
A magnesium atom (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²) loses its two 3s electrons to form Mg²⁺. Keeping the 3s² electrons would describe the neutral atom.
The electron configuration of the Zn²⁺ ion is
Zinc is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s². Both 4s electrons are removed to form Zn²⁺, leaving a full 3d subshell. [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² is the neutral atom.
Which subshell is filled immediately after the 4s subshell in the ground-state filling order?
The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so 3d fills next, followed by 4p. The 3p subshell has already been filled before 4s.
How many unpaired electrons are in a ground-state nitrogen atom?
Nitrogen is 1s² 2s² 2p³. By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving 3 unpaired electrons. Pairing two of them would raise the energy.
Which ion has the same electron configuration as an argon atom?
Ca has 20 electrons, so Ca²⁺ has 18, the same as Ar. Mg²⁺ and Na⁺ each have 10 electrons (like neon) and O²⁻ also has 10.
The outer subshell configuration of the atoms of a group 16 element is
Group 16 elements have 6 valence electrons, arranged as ns² np⁴. The configuration ns² np⁶ belongs to the noble gases (group 18).
An atom has the ground-state configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹. The element is
The configuration contains 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 13 electrons, so the atomic number is 13, which is aluminium. Boron has a similar valence pattern (2s² 2p¹) but only 5 electrons.
Which list shows the subshells in order of increasing energy?
The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, and 3d is lower than 4p. Placing 3d before 4s ignores the energy overlap between the third and fourth shells.
The electron configuration of the Cu⁺ ion is
Copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Removing the single 4s electron gives [Ar] 3d¹⁰. Removing a 3d electron instead would give [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s¹, which is incorrect since 4s electrons are lost first.
How many electrons are in the 2p subshell of a ground-state oxygen atom?
Oxygen has 8 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. The 2p subshell therefore holds 4 electrons, not 6, because it is not yet full.
According to the Pauli exclusion principle, two electrons in the same orbital must
have the same energy only if unpaired
An orbital holds at most two electrons and they must have opposite spins. Having the same spin in one orbital is not permitted.
The electron configuration of the Ni²⁺ ion is
Nickel is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². The two 4s electrons are removed first, leaving [Ar] 3d⁸. [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² would imply the 3d electrons were removed first.
Write the full subshell electron configurations for an aluminium atom and an aluminium ion, Al³⁺, and state which noble gas atom the ion has the same configuration as. (3 marks)
Al: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹ [1]. Al³⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ [1]. Al³⁺ has the same configuration as neon [1].
Define the terms subshell and orbital, and state the number of orbitals in a d subshell. (3 marks)

A subshell is a group of orbitals of the same type (s, p, d, f) within a shell, with the same energy [1]. An orbital is a region of space where an electron is likely to be found, holding a maximum of two electrons [1]. A d subshell contains 5 orbitals [1].
Write the electron configurations of a vanadium atom and a V³⁺ ion using noble gas shorthand. (2 marks)
V: [Ar] 3d³ 4s² [1]. V³⁺: [Ar] 3d² (the 4s electrons are removed first, then one 3d electron) [1].
Explain why scandium is classified as a d-block element while calcium is classified as an s-block element. (2 marks)
Calcium (1s² … 4s²) has its last electron enter the 4s subshell, so it is an s-block element [1]. Scandium ([Ar] 3d¹ 4s²) has its last electron enter the 3d subshell, so it is a d-block element [1].
Write the electron configuration of a cobalt(II) ion, Co²⁺, using noble gas shorthand, state the number of unpaired electrons, and explain which electrons are removed when the ion forms. (3 marks)

Co²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁷ [1]. There are 3 unpaired electrons (3d⁷ gives two paired and three unpaired in five orbitals) [1]. Cobalt is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; the two 4s electrons are removed first when the ion forms [1].
How many unpaired electrons are there in a ground-state Mn²⁺ ion? (Mn has atomic number 25)
Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s², and the 4s electrons are lost first, so Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵ with one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals. Seven would count the 4s electrons wrongly as unpaired 3d electrons.
An atom has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p². The element is
Argon has 18 electrons, so the total is 18 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 32, which is germanium. Silicon also has two p electrons but its outer shell is n = 3, not n = 4.
Write the full subshell electron configuration of a bromine atom (atomic number 35) and of a bromide ion, Br⁻, and name the noble gas with the same configuration as Br⁻. (3 marks)
Br: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ [1]; Br⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶ [1]; Br⁻ has the same configuration as krypton [1].
The electron configuration of the Fe³⁺ ion (Fe: Z = 26) is:
Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first, then a 3d electron: 3d⁵.
vce-chem12-periodic-table-trends: chem12a1-pt-1
Moving from sodium to chlorine across period 3, atomic radius decreases. The best explanation is that
the number of occupied shells decreases.
core charge increases while the number of occupied shells stays the same.
the number of neutrons increases, pulling electrons closer.
electronegativity decreases across the period.

All period 3 atoms have three occupied shells. Core charge rises from +1 to +7, so the valence electrons are pulled more strongly towards the nucleus. The number of shells does not decrease, and neutrons have no effect on electron attraction.
chem12a1-pt-2
Which period 3 element has the highest first ionisation energy?
Sodium
Magnesium
Chlorine
Argon

First ionisation energy generally increases across a period as core charge increases and atomic radius decreases. Argon, with a core charge of +8, holds its valence electrons most strongly. Sodium has the lowest value in the period.
chem12a1-pt-3
The core charge experienced by the valence electrons of a sulfur atom is
Core charge = number of protons − number of inner-shell electrons = 16 − 10 = +6. +16 is the full nuclear charge, which ignores shielding by the 10 inner electrons.
chem12a1-pt-4
Potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium does. This is mainly because, in potassium,
the valence electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.
the core charge is greater.
there are more valence electrons.
the atom has a smaller atomic radius.

Both atoms have a core charge of +1. Potassium has an extra occupied shell, so its valence electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted. It therefore has a lower ionisation energy and is lost more readily in reactions.
chem12a1-pt-5
Element X has a core charge of +7 and three occupied electron shells. Compared with fluorine, X would be expected to
have a higher electronegativity.
have a smaller atomic radius.
be less reactive and have a lower electronegativity.
lose electrons more readily to form positive ions.

X is chlorine (2,8,7). It has the same core charge as fluorine, but its valence shell is further from the nucleus, so it attracts electrons less strongly. This makes it less electronegative and less reactive as an oxidising agent. Its radius is larger, and as a non-metal it tends to gain electrons, not lose them.
chem12a1-pt-6
The ions Na⁺ and F⁻ both have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Explain why Na⁺ has a smaller radius than F⁻. (2 marks)

Both ions have the same number of electrons in the same shells (isoelectronic); Na⁺ has 11 protons compared with 9 in F⁻, so its greater nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer, giving a smaller radius.
chem12a1-pt-7
Describe and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down group 1 from lithium to caesium. (3 marks)

First ionisation energy decreases down the group; core charge stays constant at +1, but the number of occupied shells increases, so the valence electron is further from the nucleus; the weaker attraction (with more shielding) means less energy is needed to remove it.
chem12a1-pt-8
The electronegativities of four period 3 elements are: Na 0.9, Mg 1.3, P 2.2, Cl 3.2. Describe the trend shown and explain it in terms of atomic structure. (2 marks)
Electronegativity increases across period 3 from Na to Cl; core charge increases and atomic radius decreases with the same number of shells, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons more strongly.
chem12a1-pt-9
The core charge experienced by the valence electrons of a magnesium atom is
Core charge = 12 protons − 10 inner-shell electrons = +2. +12 is the full nuclear charge and ignores shielding by the inner electrons.
chem12a1-pt-10
Which of the following atoms has the largest atomic radius?
Lithium
Beryllium
Sodium
Magnesium

Sodium and magnesium have three occupied shells, so they are larger than lithium and beryllium. Of these two, sodium has the lower core charge (+1 compared with +2), so its valence electron is held less tightly and its radius is largest.
chem12a1-pt-11
Which statement correctly describes electronegativity down group 17 from fluorine to iodine?
It increases because the number of protons increases.
It decreases because the valence shell is further from the nucleus.
It stays constant because every halogen has a core charge of +7.
It decreases because the core charge decreases.

Core charge is +7 for all halogens, but the number of occupied shells increases, so bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and attracted less. More protons does not increase attraction because inner electrons shield them.
chem12a1-pt-12
Which element has the highest electronegativity?
Caesium
Chlorine
Oxygen
Fluorine

Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so it is greatest at the top right of the table (excluding noble gases). Fluorine has a high core charge and the smallest radius of these, so it attracts bonding electrons most strongly.
chem12a1-pt-13
Which of the following lists the halogens in order of decreasing reactivity?
F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂
I₂ > Br₂ > Cl₂ > F₂
Cl₂ > F₂ > Br₂ > I₂
F₂ = Cl₂ = Br₂ = I₂

Halogens react by gaining an electron, and this is easiest when the attracting nucleus is closest to the incoming electron. Reactivity therefore decreases down the group. The reverse order is the trend for group 1 metals, not halogens.
chem12a1-pt-14
In period 3, which element has a lower first ionisation energy than the element immediately before it?
Magnesium
Silicon
Aluminium
Phosphorus

The outermost electron of aluminium is in a 3p subshell, which is slightly higher in energy and further out than the 3s electrons of magnesium, so it is easier to remove. This is a small exception to the general increase across the period.
chem12a1-pt-15
Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties mainly because they have
the same number of occupied shells.
the same number of valence electrons.
the same atomic radius.
the same number of protons.
The number of valence electrons determines how an atom bonds and reacts, and it is the same for all members of a group. Atoms in a group have different numbers of shells, radii and protons.
chem12a1-pt-16
Which of the following period 3 elements is the most metallic?
Aluminium
Silicon
Sulfur
Magnesium

Metallic character decreases across a period as core charge rises and valence electrons are held more tightly. Magnesium is furthest to the left of these, so it loses electrons most readily. Sulfur is a non-metal.
chem12a1-pt-17
A magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, has a smaller radius than a magnesium atom because
the ion has more protons than the atom.
the ion has lost its entire third shell, so it has fewer occupied shells.
the ion has a lower core charge than the atom.
the ion has gained electrons in the second shell.
Mg (2,8,2) loses its two valence electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2,8), which has only two occupied shells. The number of protons does not change when an ion forms, and electrons are lost, not gained.
chem12a1-pt-18
The chloride ion, Cl⁻, has a larger radius than the chlorine atom because
the ion has an extra occupied shell.
the ion has more protons in its nucleus.
the same nuclear charge attracts more electrons, and the greater repulsion between electrons expands the electron cloud.
the ion has a higher core charge.

Chlorine gains an electron into the same valence shell. The nuclear charge is unchanged, but there are more electrons to attract and they repel one another more, so the radius increases. No new shell is added and the number of protons stays at 17.
chem12a1-pt-19
An element in group 15 and period 3 has a core charge of
The atom is phosphorus, with 15 protons and 10 inner-shell electrons, so core charge = 15 − 10 = +5. +15 is the full nuclear charge and ignores shielding.
chem12a1-pt-20
Which of the following has the larger atomic radius, and why?
Carbon, because it has a lower core charge than fluorine.
Fluorine, because it has more protons than carbon.
Fluorine, because it has more valence electrons than carbon.
Carbon, because it has more occupied shells than fluorine.

Carbon and fluorine both have two occupied shells, but carbon's core charge is +4 compared with +7 for fluorine, so its valence electrons are attracted less strongly. More protons in fluorine increases attraction, giving a smaller radius.
chem12a1-pt-21
Which of the following elements has the highest first ionisation energy?
Lithium
Beryllium
Nitrogen
Boron

All four are in period 2, where first ionisation energy generally increases with core charge. Nitrogen has the greatest core charge (+5) of the four and the smallest radius, so its valence electrons are held most strongly.
chem12a1-pt-22
Compared with sodium, rubidium has
a lower first ionisation energy and a larger atomic radius.
a higher first ionisation energy and a larger atomic radius.
a lower first ionisation energy and a smaller atomic radius.
the same first ionisation energy because both are in group 1.

Both have a core charge of +1, but rubidium has five occupied shells compared with three. Its valence electron is therefore further out and more easily removed. Being in the same group means similar, not identical, values.
chem12a1-pt-23
Neon has a higher first ionisation energy than argon. This is because neon's valence electrons are
in a shell with fewer occupied shells beneath it, so they are closer to the nucleus and held more strongly.
fewer in number than those of argon.
experiencing a lower core charge than those of argon.
in a half-filled subshell.

Both have a full valence shell and the same core charge of +8, but neon has only two shells, so its electrons are closer to the nucleus and harder to remove. Both have eight valence electrons and neither has a lower core charge.
chem12a1-pt-24
Define the term core charge and calculate the core charge of an aluminium atom. (2 marks)

Core charge is the net positive charge experienced by valence electrons: number of protons minus number of inner-shell (non-valence) electrons [1]; aluminium has 13 protons and 10 inner-shell electrons, so core charge = +3 [1].
chem12a1-pt-25
Calcium reacts more vigorously with water than magnesium does. Explain this difference in terms of atomic structure. (3 marks)

Both atoms have a core charge of +2 and two valence electrons [1]; calcium has four occupied shells compared with three for magnesium, so its valence electrons are further from the nucleus [1]; they are less strongly attracted, so they are lost more easily, making calcium more reactive [1].
chem12a1-pt-26
The atomic radii of four period 3 elements are: Na 186 pm, Mg 160 pm, Al 143 pm and Si 117 pm. Describe the trend and explain it. (3 marks)

Atomic radius decreases from sodium to silicon across the period [1]; the number of occupied shells stays the same (three) while core charge increases from +1 to +4 [1]; the increasing attraction pulls the valence electrons closer to the nucleus [1].
chem12a1-pt-27
Which group 2 element has the lowest first ionisation energy?
beryllium
magnesium
calcium
barium
Down a group the valence electrons are in shells further from the nucleus and are shielded by more inner shells, so they are removed more easily. Beryllium has the highest value, not the lowest.
chem12a1-pt-28
Which of the following species has the largest radius?
O²⁻
F⁻
Na⁺
Mg²⁺
All four are isoelectronic (2,8), so the radius depends on nuclear charge. O²⁻ has the fewest protons (8), so it attracts its electrons least strongly and is largest.
chem12a1-pt-29
The first five ionisation energies of an element, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 738, 1451, 7733, 10 543 and 13 630. The element is in group

There is a very large jump between the second and third ionisation energies, so the atom has two valence electrons and the third is removed from an inner shell. Group 1 would show the large jump after the first.
chem12a1-pt-30
The first four ionisation energies of an element in period 3 are 577, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. State the group of the element, justify your answer and identify the element. (3 marks)

The very large increase between the third and fourth ionisation energies shows that the fourth electron is removed from an inner shell [1]; so the atom has three valence electrons and is in group 13 [1]; in period 3 this is aluminium [1].
chem12a1-pt-31
Compare the first ionisation energy of sodium with that of chlorine and explain the difference. (2 marks)
Chlorine has the higher first ionisation energy [1]; both have three occupied shells but chlorine's core charge is +7 compared with +1, so its valence electrons are held much more strongly [1].
vce-chem12-pt-c1
Across period 3 from Na to Cl, atomic radius decreases mainly because:
Core charge increases while the number of occupied shells stays the same
More shells are added across the period, pulling electrons closer
Electronegativity decreases across the period, so the atoms shrink
The atoms gain more neutrons, which pull the electrons inwards
Each step adds a proton and an outer-shell electron. The outer electrons feel a greater core charge and are pulled closer.
vce-chem12-metallic-bonding-and-properti: chem12a1-mb-1
In the metallic bonding model, a metal consists of
a lattice of positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
a lattice of alternating positive and negative ions.
discrete molecules held together by dispersion forces.
atoms that share localised electron pairs with neighbours.

Metal atoms give up their valence electrons, which are delocalised throughout a lattice of cations. Bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons. Alternating positive and negative ions describes an ionic lattice.
chem12a1-mb-2
Metals are malleable because
the ions are held in fixed positions by directional bonds.
the delocalised electrons evaporate when the metal is struck.
layers of cations can slide over each other without breaking the non-directional metallic bonding.
metals contain weak intermolecular forces between layers.

Metallic bonding is non-directional. When layers of cations shift, the delocalised electrons still hold them together, so the metal bends instead of shattering. Fixed, directional bonding would make the metal brittle.
chem12a1-mb-3
Which property of metals is NOT well explained by the simple metallic bonding model?
Electrical conductivity
Ductility
Thermal conductivity
The magnetic behaviour of iron, cobalt and nickel

The sea-of-electrons model explains conductivity (mobile electrons) and ductility (non-directional bonding). It cannot explain why only some metals, such as Fe, Co and Ni, are magnetic. This is a known limitation of the model.
chem12a1-mb-4
A piece of steel is heated until red hot and then allowed to cool slowly in air. This treatment, called annealing, produces steel that is
harder and more brittle, with very small crystals.
softer and more ductile, with larger crystals.
harder because carbon atoms leave the lattice.
unchanged in properties.

Slow cooling allows larger crystals (grains) to grow, so there are fewer grain boundaries and the metal is softer and more workable. Rapid cooling (quenching) produces small crystals and a hard, brittle metal.
chem12a1-mb-5
Metals conduct electricity in the solid state because
the cations move towards the negative electrode.
the delocalised electrons can move through the lattice when a potential difference is applied.
metal atoms ionise only when a voltage is applied.
the metal contains free negative ions.
The delocalised valence electrons are free to move and carry charge through the lattice. The cations stay in fixed positions in the solid, and metals do not contain free negative ions.
chem12a1-mb-6
Magnesium melts at 650 °C, whereas sodium melts at 98 °C. Use the metallic bonding model to explain this difference. (2 marks)

Magnesium contributes two delocalised electrons per atom and forms Mg²⁺ ions, while sodium contributes one and forms Na⁺; the higher cation charge and greater density of delocalised electrons give stronger electrostatic attraction in magnesium, so more energy is needed to disrupt the lattice.
chem12a1-mb-7
Steel is an interstitial alloy of iron containing small amounts of carbon. Explain why steel is harder than pure iron. (2 marks)

The small carbon atoms occupy spaces (interstices) between the iron ions in the lattice; this distorts the lattice and makes it harder for layers of iron ions to slide past each other, so the alloy is harder and less malleable.
chem12a1-mb-8
A blacksmith quenches a hot steel blade in cold water and then tempers it. Describe how each treatment changes the crystal structure and properties of the steel. (3 marks)

Quenching (rapid cooling) produces very small crystals, giving a hard but brittle metal; tempering involves reheating the quenched metal to a moderate temperature and cooling it, which allows partial rearrangement of the crystals; tempered steel keeps much of its hardness but is tougher and less brittle.
chem12a1-mb-9
Metals are typically lustrous (shiny) because
delocalised electrons at the surface absorb and re-emit light of most visible wavelengths.
the cations in the lattice emit light of their own.
the metal atoms form shiny covalent bonds on the surface.
the lattice contains trapped photons.
Mobile delocalised electrons can absorb and re-emit visible light, giving the characteristic metallic sheen. Cations do not emit light of their own in this way.
chem12a1-mb-10
Metals are good conductors of heat mainly because
the lattice of cations is a perfect insulator that traps heat.
delocalised electrons move rapidly and transfer kinetic energy through the lattice.
covalent bonds between atoms carry heat along the metal.
the cations migrate through the metal carrying thermal energy.
Energetic delocalised electrons pass kinetic energy to other electrons and cations as they move. The cations only vibrate about fixed positions and do not migrate through the solid.
chem12a1-mb-11
Which statement best explains why a copper rod can be drawn into a wire without breaking?
Copper cations are held in fixed positions by covalent bonds.
Copper contains weak intermolecular forces that are easily broken.
Metallic bonding is non-directional, so cations can shift position while remaining attracted to the delocalised electrons.
The delocalised electrons are removed as the wire is drawn.
Because the bonding is non-directional, the cations can move past one another and the electron sea keeps holding them together. Removal of electrons would destroy the bonding, not allow ductility.
chem12a1-mb-12
Which of the following lists sodium, magnesium and aluminium in order of increasing melting point?
Al < Mg < Na
Mg < Na < Al
Na < Al < Mg
Na < Mg < Al

Na, Mg and Al contribute 1, 2 and 3 delocalised electrons per atom and form Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺. Higher cation charge and electron density give stronger metallic bonding, so melting points rise across the period.
chem12a1-mb-13
Melting points of the Group 1 metals decrease down the group (Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C). The best explanation is that
larger cations mean the delocalised electrons are further from the nuclei, so the electrostatic attraction is weaker.
the number of delocalised electrons per atom decreases down the group.
the cations become more highly charged down the group.
covalent bonding replaces metallic bonding in the heavier metals.
Each Group 1 atom donates one electron, so the charge does not change. The cations get larger down the group, weakening the attraction to the electron sea. A change in charge is not the cause.
chem12a1-mb-14
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which have similar atomic radii. Brass is best classified as
an interstitial alloy, with zinc atoms fitting between copper atoms.
a substitutional alloy, with zinc atoms replacing some copper atoms in the lattice.
a compound with ionic bonds between copper and zinc.
a molecular substance of Cu–Zn pairs.
Atoms of similar size can substitute for each other in the lattice, giving a substitutional alloy. Interstitial alloys need much smaller atoms, such as carbon, to fit in the gaps.
chem12a1-mb-15
Brass is harder than pure copper mainly because
zinc forms covalent bonds with copper that hold the layers rigidly.
zinc removes the delocalised electrons from the lattice.
the zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms, which disrupts the regular layers and makes it harder for them to slide.
zinc atoms are smaller and fill the gaps between copper atoms.
Different-sized atoms distort the regular lattice and hinder movement of layers. Zinc is similar in size to copper, so it does not sit in the gaps, and it does not remove delocalised electrons.
chem12a1-mb-16
A copper sheet is repeatedly hammered at room temperature. Compared with the original sheet, it becomes
softer and more ductile, as the crystals grow larger.
unchanged, because metallic bonding is non-directional.
a better conductor because more cations are exposed.
harder and more brittle, as the crystals are deformed and broken into smaller ones.
Cold working distorts and fragments the crystal structure, giving harder, more brittle metal. Larger crystals and a softer metal come from annealing, not from hammering.
chem12a1-mb-17
Compared with the pure metals, alloys generally have
lower electrical conductivity, because the irregular lattice scatters the moving delocalised electrons.
higher electrical conductivity, because they contain more electrons.
the same conductivity, because the delocalised electrons are unaffected.
no electrical conductivity, because the bonding becomes covalent.
Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice, impeding electron flow. Alloys still contain delocalised electrons, so they still conduct.
chem12a1-mb-18
How many delocalised electrons are present in 0.50 mol of magnesium metal? (N_{A} = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
Each Mg atom forms Mg²⁺ and releases two electrons, so 0.50 mol Mg gives 1.00 mol electrons = 6.02 × 10²³. Using one electron per atom would give 3.01 × 10²³.
chem12a1-mb-19
What mass of aluminium (M = 27.0 g mol⁻¹) contains 1.00 mol of delocalised electrons?
Each Al atom contributes three electrons, so 1.00 mol electrons comes from 1.00 / 3 mol Al, which is 9.00 g. 27.0 g would contain 3.00 mol of electrons.
chem12a1-mb-20
Solid magnesium conducts electricity but solid magnesium oxide does not. This is because in solid magnesium oxide
there are no charged particles at all.
the electrons are delocalised but too strongly held to move.
the ions are free to move but are not attracted to the electrodes.
the ions are held in fixed positions and there are no mobile charge carriers.

In an ionic solid the Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions are locked in the lattice, so nothing can carry charge. Metals conduct because of mobile delocalised electrons; the ions in a solid ionic compound are not free to move.
chem12a1-mb-21
When a sheet of metal is struck, it deforms, but when a crystal of sodium chloride is struck, it shatters. The key reason is that
shifting NaCl layers brings ions of like charge together so they repel, whereas shifting metal layers keeps the cations surrounded by the electron sea.
NaCl has weaker bonds than any metal.
metals contain covalent bonds that allow flexing.
NaCl layers are held together by delocalised electrons.
In ionic lattices a shift of one layer lines up like charges, causing repulsion and fracture. Metallic bonding is non-directional, and strength is not the reason; NaCl has no delocalised electrons.
chem12a1-mb-22
Bronze, used in statues and bearings, is an alloy of
copper and zinc.
copper and tin.
iron and carbon.
aluminium and magnesium.
Bronze is mainly copper with tin. Copper and zinc make brass, and iron with carbon makes steel.
chem12a1-mb-23
A block of solid sodium has no overall electric charge. This is because
sodium atoms do not lose any electrons in the metal.
the delocalised electrons are neutral particles.
the total positive charge of the Na⁺ ions equals the total negative charge of the delocalised electrons.
the Na⁺ ions are balanced by Cl⁻ ions in the lattice.
Each Na atom loses one electron, so there is one delocalised electron for every Na⁺ ion and the charges cancel. Sodium metal contains no chloride ions.
chem12a1-mb-24
Copper is used in electrical wiring because it is a good conductor and can be drawn into thin wires. These two properties are explained by
fixed cations, and strong directional covalent bonds, respectively.
free negative ions, and weak intermolecular forces, respectively.
mobile cations, and delocalised electrons that are fixed in place, respectively.
mobile delocalised electrons, and non-directional bonding that lets layers of cations slide, respectively.
Conductivity comes from electrons free to move, and ductility from non-directional bonding. Cations are fixed in the solid and do not carry charge.
chem12a1-mb-25
Calculate the number of delocalised electrons in 2.70 g of aluminium. (M(Al) = 27.0 g mol⁻¹; N_{A} = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
n(Al) = 2.70 / 27.0 = 0.100 mol [1]; each Al atom contributes 3 delocalised electrons, so n(e⁻) = 0.300 mol [1]; number = 0.300 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.81 × 10²³ electrons [1].
chem12a1-mb-26
Calcium has a higher melting point than potassium mainly because calcium atoms
are heavier, so more energy is needed to vibrate them
form covalent bonds with each other
have more neutrons in the nucleus
each release two delocalised electrons and the ions are smaller, giving stronger metallic bonding

Ca contributes two delocalised electrons per atom (K only one) and Ca²⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is stronger. Mass and neutron number do not determine bond strength.
chem12a1-mb-27
Stainless steel contains iron, chromium and nickel. Compared with pure iron, stainless steel is
more resistant to corrosion
a better conductor of electricity
softer and more malleable
less dense than any of its component metals
The added metals form a surface layer that protects the alloy from rusting. Alloying generally lowers electrical conductivity, so it is not a better conductor.
chem12a1-mb-28
Which of the following is an interstitial alloy?
brass
sterling silver (silver and copper)
steel
pewter (tin and copper)
In steel the small carbon atoms sit in the gaps between larger iron atoms. In brass, sterling silver and pewter the metal atoms are of similar size and replace one another in the lattice.
chem12a1-mb-29
Mercury is a liquid at room temperature, whereas most metals are solid. This suggests that, compared with most metals, the metallic bonding in mercury is
stronger
absent
covalent in nature
weaker

A low melting point means little energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the cations and delocalised electrons, so the bonding is relatively weak. Mercury still conducts electricity, so metallic bonding is still present.
chem12a1-mb-30
Describe the metallic bonding model. (2 marks)

A metal is a lattice of positive ions (cations) surrounded by a sea of delocalised valence electrons [1]; the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons [1].
chem12a1-mb-31
Pure gold is soft, so jewellery is often made from 18-carat gold, an alloy of gold with copper and silver. Explain why the alloy is harder than pure gold. (2 marks)

The copper and silver atoms differ in size from gold atoms and disrupt the regular arrangement of the lattice [1]; this makes it harder for layers of atoms to slide over each other, so the alloy is harder [1].
vce-chem12-mb-c1
Magnesium melts at a much higher temperature than sodium. The best explanation is that magnesium:
Has covalent bonds between its atoms as well as metallic bonding
Has a larger atomic radius, so its atoms pack together more tightly
Has fewer protons than sodium, so its electrons are held less strongly
Has 2+ cations and two delocalised electrons per atom, giving stronger attraction
Metallic bonding strength depends on the charge of the cations and the number of delocalised electrons.
vce-chem12-ionic-bonding-and-ionic-compo: chem12a1-ib-1
The correct formula for aluminium sulfate is
AlSO₄
Al₃(SO₄)₂
Al₂(SO₄)₃
Al₂SO₄
Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine in the ratio 2 : 3 to give zero overall charge: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Brackets are needed around the polyatomic ion.
chem12a1-ib-2
Ionic crystals shatter when struck with a hammer because
the delocalised electrons are knocked out of the lattice.
the blow shifts layers so that ions of like charge align and repel.
the covalent bonds within the ions break.
the intermolecular forces between ions are weak.

A shift of one ion layer brings cations next to cations and anions next to anions. The resulting repulsion splits the crystal. Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons, and the bonding between ions is ionic, not intermolecular.
chem12a1-ib-3
Which of the following compounds would be expected to have the highest melting point?
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Potassium bromide, KBr
Caesium iodide, CsI
Magnesium oxide, MgO
MgO consists of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, which have doubled charges and small radii. This gives much stronger electrostatic attraction than in the 1+/1− compounds, and its melting point is about 2850 °C.
chem12a1-ib-4
When magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, each magnesium atom
shares two electrons with an oxygen atom.
transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
gains two electrons from an oxygen atom.
transfers one electron to each of two oxygen atoms.
Mg (2,8,2) loses its two valence electrons to form Mg²⁺. O (2,6) gains them to form O²⁻, and both ions then have stable noble gas configurations. Sharing electrons would be covalent bonding.
chem12a1-ib-5
Solid potassium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten potassium chloride does. This is because, in the molten state,
electrons become delocalised.
the ions are free to move and carry charge.
covalent bonds break to form atoms.
K⁺ ions gain electrons to become atoms.
In the solid, the ions are fixed in the lattice. Melting frees the ions so they can move towards the electrodes and carry charge. Ionic compounds do not have delocalised electrons.
chem12a1-ib-6
Calcium reacts with nitrogen to form calcium nitride. Write the formula of calcium nitride and explain its formation in terms of electron transfer. (3 marks)

Formula Ca₃N₂; each Ca atom loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺ and each N atom gains 3 electrons to form N³⁻; three Ca atoms transfer a total of 6 electrons to two N atoms, so the charges balance (3 × +2 = 2 × 3).
chem12a1-ib-7
Name each of the following ionic compounds: (a) Fe₂O₃ (b) NH₄NO₃ (c) K₂Cr₂O₇. (3 marks)
(a) iron(III) oxide; (b) ammonium nitrate; (c) potassium dichromate.
chem12a1-ib-8

A student finds that an unknown white solid has a high melting point, does not conduct electricity as a solid but conducts when dissolved in water, and shatters when struck. Identify the type of bonding present and explain how any two of these observations support your answer. (3 marks)

Ionic bonding; high melting point: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice needs a lot of energy to overcome; conductivity: ions are fixed in the solid but free to move in solution, so only the solution conducts; brittleness: displacing layers aligns like charges, which repel (any two explanations).
chem12a1-ib-9
The correct formula for calcium phosphate is
CaPO₄
Ca₃(PO₄)₂
Ca₂(PO₄)₃
Ca₃PO₄₂
Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ combine in the ratio 3 : 2 so that 3(+2) + 2(−3) = 0. Ca₂(PO₄)₃ is wrong because it swaps the subscripts and gives a net charge.
chem12a1-ib-10
Which of the following ions has the same electron configuration as a neon atom?
Cl⁻
K⁺
Mg²⁺
S²⁻
Mg loses two electrons to leave 2,8, the same as Ne. Cl⁻, K⁺ and S²⁻ all have 2,8,8, the configuration of argon.
chem12a1-ib-11
The correct name for Cu(NO₃)₂ is
copper(II) nitrate
copper(I) nitrate
copper nitride
copper(II) nitrite
Two NO₃⁻ ions require a 2+ charge on copper, so it is copper(II). Nitrate is NO₃⁻, whereas nitrite is NO₂⁻.
chem12a1-ib-12
Sodium chloride dissolves readily in water mainly because
water molecules form covalent bonds with the ions.
water molecules are attracted to the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and these attractions can overcome the forces holding the ions in the lattice.
the ions react with water to form hydrogen and chlorine gases.
sodium chloride molecules separate from one another.
Polar water molecules surround each ion and the ion–water attractions release enough energy to separate the ions. NaCl contains ions, not molecules, and no new covalent bonds form.
chem12a1-ib-13
In a crystal of sodium chloride, each sodium ion is surrounded by how many nearest chloride ions?
The NaCl lattice is arranged so that each ion has six nearest neighbours of opposite charge. The 1 : 1 formula does not mean one-to-one pairing.
chem12a1-ib-14
How many ions are there in one formula unit of iron(III) sulfate, Fe₂(SO₄)₃?
One formula unit has 2 Fe³⁺ ions and 3 SO₄²⁻ ions, giving 5 ions. The sulfate ion is a single polyatomic ion, so its atoms are not counted separately.
chem12a1-ib-15
The formula of an ionic compound is an empirical formula because it
shows the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in the lattice.
gives the number of ions in each molecule.
shows the number of atoms in a single ion pair.
is determined by the melting point of the compound.
An ionic lattice is a continuous array, so the formula only gives the ratio of cations to anions. Ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules.
chem12a1-ib-16
Which equation correctly represents the formation of an oxide ion from an oxygen atom?
O → O²⁻ + 2e⁻
O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻
O₂ + 2e⁻ → O²⁻
O + 2e⁻ → O₂²⁻
Oxygen gains two electrons to fill its valence shell. The equation with electrons on the right shows loss of electrons, which would give a cation, and O₂ must be balanced to give two O²⁻.
chem12a1-ib-17
Sodium chloride has a higher melting point than potassium chloride because
Na⁺ has a larger charge than K⁺.
sodium chloride has covalent bonds as well.
Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so the electrostatic attraction to Cl⁻ is stronger.
Na⁺ is larger than K⁺, so it packs more tightly.
Both ions carry 1+, but the smaller Na⁺ sits closer to Cl⁻ and attracts it more strongly. The charges are equal, and a larger cation would weaken the attraction.
chem12a1-ib-18
The correct formula for ammonium phosphate is
NH₄PO₄
(NH₄)₃PO₄
(NH₄)₂PO₄
NH₄(PO₄)₃
NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻ combine in a 3 : 1 ratio to balance charge, and brackets are needed around the polyatomic ammonium ion. NH₄PO₄ has a net charge of 2−.
chem12a1-ib-19
Element X is in group 13 and element Y is in group 16. The formula of the ionic compound they form is most likely
XY
X₃Y₂
X₂Y₃
X₂Y
X forms X³⁺ and Y forms Y²⁻, so the ratio for zero charge is 2 : 3. X₃Y₂ reverses the ratio.
chem12a1-ib-20
How many electrons are in a sulfide ion, S²⁻? (S has atomic number 16)
A sulfur atom has 16 electrons and gains two to form S²⁻, giving 18. The 14 results from subtracting instead of adding.
chem12a1-ib-21
Write the formula of each of the following ionic compounds: (a) sodium sulfide (b) magnesium nitrate (c) iron(III) hydroxide (d) ammonium carbonate. (4 marks)
(a) Na₂S [1]; (b) Mg(NO₃)₂ [1]; (c) Fe(OH)₃ [1]; (d) (NH₄)₂CO₃ [1].
chem12a1-ib-22
Explain why sodium chloride dissolves in water. (3 marks)

Water is a polar molecule with partial positive and partial negative ends [1]; the partial negative oxygen ends are attracted to Na⁺ and the partial positive hydrogen ends are attracted to Cl⁻ [1]; the energy released by these ion–water attractions is enough to overcome the ionic bonds in the lattice, so the ions separate and become surrounded by water molecules [1].
chem12a1-ib-23
Write the electron configurations of an aluminium atom and an aluminium ion, and explain why aluminium forms a 3+ ion. (3 marks)
Al atom: 2,8,3 [1]; Al³⁺ ion: 2,8 [1]; Al loses its three valence electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration (same as neon), leaving 13 protons and 10 electrons, so the charge is 3+ [1].
chem12a1-ib-24
Describe the structure of an ionic lattice such as sodium chloride. (2 marks)

A continuous three-dimensional array of alternating positive and negative ions [1]; held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (no discrete molecules) [1].
chem12a1-ib-25
Describe, in terms of electron arrangements, how magnesium and chlorine atoms form magnesium chloride. (3 marks)

Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2,8) [1]; each Cl atom (2,8,7) gains one electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8), so two Cl atoms are needed [1]; the oppositely charged ions attract by electrostatic forces to form a lattice with formula MgCl₂ [1].
chem12a1-ib-26
The correct formula for chromium(III) hydroxide is
Cr(OH)₃
CrOH₃
Cr₃(OH)
Cr₃OH
Cr³⁺ needs three OH⁻ ions for charge balance, and brackets are required around the polyatomic ion when more than one is present. CrOH₃ incorrectly implies three separate hydrogen atoms.
chem12a1-ib-27
In a crystal of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, the ratio of aluminium ions to oxide ions is
The formula shows two Al³⁺ ions (+6) balancing three O²⁻ ions (−6). The ratio 3 : 2 reverses the subscripts.
chem12a1-ib-28
The correct name for Fe(OH)₂ is
iron(III) hydroxide
iron dihydroxide
iron(II) hydroxide
iron(II) hydroxy oxide
Two OH⁻ ions require the iron ion to be Fe²⁺, so the Roman numeral is II. Ionic compounds are not named using prefixes such as di-.
chem12a1-ib-29
Which of the following substances will conduct electricity when dissolved in water?
glucose
ethanol
sucrose
potassium nitrate
Potassium nitrate dissociates into K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions that are free to move and carry charge. Glucose, ethanol and sucrose dissolve as neutral molecules.
chem12a1-ib-30
Element Z has the electron configuration 2,8,2 and element T has the configuration 2,8,7. The compound they form is most likely to have the formula
ZT₂
Z₂T
ZT
Z₂T₇
Z loses two electrons to form Z²⁺ and each T gains one to form T⁻, so one Z²⁺ combines with two T⁻. Z₂T would require Z to form a 1+ ion.
chem12a1-ib-31
Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. (3 marks)

MgO contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, whereas NaCl contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions [1]; the ions in MgO have greater charges and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is stronger [1]; more energy is therefore needed to break the lattice [1].
chem12a1-ib-32
Calculate the total number of ions in 5.30 g of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃. (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹; N_{A} = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
n(Na₂CO₃) = 5.30 ÷ 106.0 = 0.0500 mol [1]; each formula unit has three ions (2Na⁺ + CO₃²⁻), so n(ions) = 0.150 mol [1]; number of ions = 0.150 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²² [1].
chem12a1-ib-33
Calcium and sulfur react to form an ionic compound. Write its formula, give the electron configuration of each ion and state what the two ions have in common. (3 marks)
CaS [1]; Ca²⁺ and S²⁻ both have the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ [1]; they are isoelectronic with each other and with the noble gas argon [1].
vce-chem12-ib-c1
The formula of chromium(III) sulfate is:
Cr₃(SO₄)₂
CrSO₄
Cr(SO₄)₃
Cr₂(SO₄)₃
Cr³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: the lowest common multiple of the charges is 6, so 2 Cr³⁺ and 3 SO₄²⁻. Brackets show more than one polyatomic ion.
vce-chem12-nanomaterials-and-reactivity-: Nanoparticles are generally defined as particles with at least one dimension in the range
The nanoscale is about 1–100 nm (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m). 0.01–0.1 nm is about the size of a single atom, and the µm range describes much larger particles, such as cells.
A 1.0 cm cube of a metal is cut into 1000 identical cubes, each 1.0 mm along each side. Compared with the original cube, the total surface area of the small cubes is

Original: 6 × (1.0 cm)² = 6.0 cm². Each small cube: 6 × (0.10 cm)² = 0.060 cm². Total: 1000 × 0.060 cm² = 60 cm², which is 10 times larger. Dividing particles further increases the surface area to volume ratio, which is why nanoparticles are so reactive.
Which metal reacts vigorously with cold water, producing hydrogen gas?
Potassium is a highly reactive group 1 metal: 2K(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H₂(g). Iron reacts only very slowly (rusting needs both oxygen and water), and copper and silver do not react with water.
Zinc granules are added to dilute hydrochloric acid. The products of the reaction are
A reactive metal and a dilute acid produce a salt and hydrogen: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Chlorine is not produced, and the metal oxide or hydroxide does not form in acid.
A colloidal solution of gold nanoparticles appears deep red, while bulk gold appears yellow. The best explanation is that
the gold has been oxidised to Au³⁺ ions.
nanoparticles contain a different isotope of gold.
materials at the nanoscale can show different properties from the same material in bulk.
water reacts with gold to form a red compound.

At the nanoscale, particle size affects how a material interacts with light, along with its other properties, so gold nanoparticles look red. The gold is still metallic gold, not ions or a new compound, and isotopes have no effect on colour.
Write balanced equations, including states, for (a) the reaction of calcium with water and (b) the reaction of magnesium with oxygen. (2 marks)

Pieces of three metals, A, B and C, of equal size were placed in separate test tubes of 1.0 M hydrochloric acid. A produced bubbles rapidly, B produced bubbles slowly, and C showed no reaction. Rank the metals in order of reactivity and suggest a possible identity for each from magnesium, iron and copper. (3 marks)
Order of reactivity: A > B > C; A could be magnesium (reacts rapidly with dilute acid); B could be iron (reacts slowly), and C could be copper (does not react with dilute HCl).

Silver nanoparticles are added to some wound dressings because of their antibacterial action. Explain why nanoparticles are more effective than the same mass of bulk silver, and state one possible concern about their use. (3 marks)

Nanoparticles have a much larger surface area to volume ratio, so a larger proportion of silver atoms are exposed at the surface; this allows more contact with and greater release of silver ions to bacteria, so a small mass is very effective; concern: nanoparticles may penetrate cells or tissue, accumulate in the body or the environment, or harm beneficial organisms, and their long-term health effects are not fully known.
The prefix nano means 10⁻⁹, so 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. 10⁻⁶ m is one micrometre and 10⁻³ m is one millimetre.
A cube of side length 2.0 cm has a surface area to volume ratio of
Surface area = 6 × (2.0 cm)² = 24 cm² and volume = (2.0 cm)³ = 8.0 cm³, so the ratio is 3.0 cm⁻¹. 6.0 cm⁻¹ is the ratio for a 1.0 cm cube, not a 2.0 cm cube.
Sodium is added to water containing a few drops of universal indicator. The final solution is most likely
neutral, because only hydrogen gas forms.
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, so the solution is alkaline even though hydrogen gas is also released.
Which of the following metals will NOT produce hydrogen gas when added to dilute sulfuric acid?
Silver is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not displace it from dilute acid. Zinc, magnesium and iron are all more reactive than hydrogen and release H₂.
A student places a piece of zinc in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is expected?
A reddish-brown deposit forms on the zinc and the blue colour fades.
A grey deposit forms on the zinc and the blue colour deepens.
Bubbles of hydrogen form and the solution stays blue.
No change occurs because zinc is less reactive than copper.
Zinc is more reactive than copper, so Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Copper metal is deposited and the Cu²⁺ ions that make the solution blue are used up.
Which list shows the metals in order of decreasing reactivity?
From most to least reactive, the order is Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. The other lists place at least one pair of metals in the wrong order.
A gas is collected from the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid. A lit splint is held at the mouth of the test tube. The gas is confirmed as hydrogen if
Hydrogen burns explosively with oxygen in air, giving a squeaky pop. An extinguished splint suggests carbon dioxide or nitrogen, and a relighting glowing splint indicates oxygen.
Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in some sunscreens. A main reason they are preferred to larger particles is that they
are more reactive with sodium ions in sweat.
have a lower melting point than larger particles.
are made of a different element from bulk titanium dioxide.
absorb ultraviolet light but are small enough to appear transparent on the skin.

Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, so they do not scatter it and the sunscreen looks clear while still absorbing UV. Their composition does not change; only their size does.
Nanoparticles of platinum are often more effective catalysts than the same mass of platinum foil mainly because they
have a larger surface area, so more atoms are exposed to reactants.
have more protons in each atom.
are chemically different from bulk platinum.
A greater surface area to volume ratio exposes more platinum atoms where reactants can adsorb and react. The atoms themselves are identical in nanoparticle and bulk form.
In the reaction Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which statement is correct?
Magnesium atoms gain electrons and copper ions lose electrons.
Magnesium and copper ions both lose electrons.
Magnesium atoms lose electrons and copper ions gain electrons.
Electrons are not transferred in this reaction.
Magnesium is oxidised, losing two electrons per atom, and the Cu²⁺ ions are reduced by gaining those electrons to form copper atoms. Electron transfer is what drives all metal displacement reactions.
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but reacts quickly with steam. The products of the reaction with steam are
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g). Hydrogen, not oxygen, is the gas given off, as the metal displaces hydrogen from water.
Aluminium is above zinc in the reactivity series, yet aluminium pots are used for cooking. This is because aluminium
does not form any oxide when exposed to air.
is coated by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that protects the metal beneath.
Aluminium reacts rapidly with oxygen to form a tightly bonded Al₂O₃ layer that prevents further reaction. It is the oxide coating, not low reactivity, that protects it.
Iron nails are placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The balanced equation for the reaction is
Iron reacts with dilute acid to form iron(II) chloride and hydrogen. The Fe³⁺ product is not formed under these conditions, and chlorine is not produced because Cl⁻ is not oxidised.
Magnesium powder reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid much faster than a magnesium ribbon of the same mass. This is best explained by the powder having
a higher reactivity as an element.
a lower mass of magnesium atoms.
a different number of electrons per atom.
a greater surface area exposed to the acid.
More surface atoms are in contact with the acid, so collisions are more frequent. The metal's intrinsic reactivity as an element is the same for powder and ribbon.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with side length 10 nm and compare it with that of a cube with side length 1.0 cm. Give your answers in nm⁻¹. (3 marks)

Ratio for a cube = 6 ÷ side length, so for 10 nm: 6 ÷ 10 = 0.60 nm⁻¹ [1]; 1.0 cm = 1.0 × 10⁷ nm, so ratio = 6 ÷ (1.0 × 10⁷) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ nm⁻¹ [1]; the 10 nm cube's ratio is 10⁶ (one million) times larger [1].
A cube of side length 40 nm is compared with a cube of side length 20 nm of the same material. The surface area to volume ratio of the larger cube is
twice that of the smaller cube
half that of the smaller cube
the same as the smaller cube
four times that of the smaller cube
The ratio for a cube is 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side halves the ratio (0.15 nm⁻¹ compared with 0.30 nm⁻¹). Smaller particles have the greater ratio, not the larger.
Which of the following reactions will occur?
Magnesium is above iron in the reactivity series, so it displaces Fe²⁺ from solution. In the other mixtures the solid metal is less reactive than the metal ion present.
A concern about the use of nanoparticles in consumer products such as cosmetics is that they
may cross cell membranes, and their long-term health effects are not yet well understood
have a smaller surface area to volume ratio than bulk material
cannot be detected by any instrument
Because of their tiny size, nanoparticles may enter cells and tissues, and their long-term effects are still being studied. Nanoparticles have a larger, not smaller, surface area to volume ratio.
What mass of zinc (M = 65.4 g mol⁻¹) must react with excess hydrochloric acid to produce 0.100 mol of hydrogen gas?
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, so n(Zn) = n(H₂) = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 65.4 = 6.54 g. Using a 2 : 1 ratio would wrongly give 13.1 g.
Metal P reacts rapidly with cold water, metal Q reacts only with dilute acid, and metal R does not react with dilute acid. The order of decreasing reactivity is
More reactive metals react under milder conditions, so P (cold water) is most reactive, then Q (acid), then R (no reaction with acid). The order R > Q > P is reversed.
An iron nail is placed in a blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Describe two observations and write the net ionic equation for the reaction. (3 marks)
A reddish-brown deposit (copper) forms on the nail [1]; the blue colour of the solution fades (towards pale green) [1]; Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) [1].
Silver nanoparticles are used in some sports clothing. Describe one benefit and one potential risk of this use. (2 marks)

Benefit: the nanoparticles are antibacterial, which reduces odour (or the growth of bacteria) in the fabric [1]; risk: nanoparticles washed out of the clothing may enter waterways and harm aquatic organisms (or may be absorbed through skin with unknown effects) [1].
A 1 cm cube of metal is cut into 1 mm cubes. By what factor does the total surface area increase?
One 1 cm cube has 6 cm². 1000 cubes of 0.1 cm each have 6 × 0.01 = 0.06 cm², giving 60 cm²: ten times more. This is why nanoparticles are so reactive.
vce-chem12-lewis-structures-and-covalent: chem12a1-lc-1
How many non-bonding (lone) pairs of electrons are on the nitrogen atom in an ammonia molecule, NH₃?
N has 5 valence electrons. Three are used in N–H bonds, and the remaining two form one lone pair, which completes an octet around N.
chem12a1-lc-2
Which of the following molecules contains a triple covalent bond?
O₂
H₂O
N₂
CH₄
Each N atom has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more, so the two atoms share three pairs (N≡N). O₂ contains a double bond, and H₂O and CH₄ contain only single bonds.
chem12a1-lc-3
In the Lewis structure of carbon dioxide, CO₂, the total number of lone pairs is
The structure is O=C=O. Carbon has no lone pairs, and each O has two lone pairs, giving 4 in total. 16 valence electrons − 8 bonding electrons = 8 electrons = 4 lone pairs.
chem12a1-lc-4
An ethene molecule, C₂H₄, contains a total of how many shared (bonding) pairs of electrons?
Ethene has four C–H single bonds (4 pairs) and one C=C double bond (2 pairs), giving 6 bonding pairs. The 12 valence electrons are all used in bonding, so there are no lone pairs.
chem12a1-lc-5
A covalent bond is best described as
the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
the attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalised electrons.
the attraction between neighbouring molecules.
the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.

In a covalent bond, two atoms (usually non-metals) share a pair of electrons, and both nuclei are attracted to it. The other options describe ionic bonding, metallic bonding and intermolecular forces.
chem12a1-lc-6
Describe the Lewis structure of methanal, CH₂O, stating the central atom, the type of each bond and the number of lone pairs on each atom. (3 marks)
Carbon is the central atom; C forms a double bond to O and single bonds to each of the two H atoms; O has two lone pairs while C and H have none (C and O have octets, H has 2 electrons).
chem12a1-lc-7
For phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃, state the total number of valence electrons, the number of bonding pairs and the total number of lone pairs in the molecule. (3 marks)
Valence electrons: 5 + 3 × 7 = 26; 3 bonding pairs (three P–Cl single bonds); lone pairs: 1 on P + 3 on each Cl = 10 lone pairs (26 − 6 = 20 electrons).
chem12a1-lc-8
Explain why covalent molecular substances such as iodine, I₂, have low melting points and do not conduct electricity. (2 marks)

Melting only requires overcoming weak intermolecular (dispersion) forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds within them, so little energy is needed; the molecules are neutral and all electrons are localised in bonds or lone pairs, so there are no free charged particles to carry a current.
chem12a1-lc-9
What is the total number of valence electrons that must be shown in the Lewis structure of sulfur dioxide, SO₂?
S has 6 valence electrons and each O has 6, so 6 + 2 × 6 = 18. The value 12 counts only the two O atoms' electrons and leaves out S.
chem12a1-lc-10
Which of the following molecules has a central atom that does NOT have a complete octet in its Lewis structure?
NH₃
BF₃
H₂O
CF₄
B has only 3 valence electrons, so in BF₃ it forms three single bonds and has just 6 electrons around it. N in NH₃, O in H₂O and C in CF₄ all reach 8 electrons.
chem12a1-lc-11
How many lone pairs of electrons are present in total in the Lewis structure of tetrachloromethane, CCl₄?
Each Cl forms one bond to C and has 3 lone pairs, so 4 × 3 = 12 lone pairs. Carbon has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so 4 is not the total.
chem12a1-lc-12
Hydrazine, N₂H₄, contains one N–N single bond and four N–H single bonds. How many lone pairs of electrons are in the molecule?
There are 2 × 5 + 4 = 14 valence electrons, and the 5 bonds use 10 of them. The remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, one on each N atom.
chem12a1-lc-13
In stable covalent molecules such as CH₄ and CCl₄, how many covalent bonds does a carbon atom usually form?
Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete an octet, so it forms four covalent bonds. Three bonds would leave carbon without an octet.
chem12a1-lc-14
Ethyne (acetylene), C₂H₂, has the structure H–C≡C–H. How many electrons are shared in the molecule in total?

There are two C–H single bonds (2 pairs) and one C≡C triple bond (3 pairs), giving 5 shared pairs or 10 shared electrons. The value 6 counts only the three pairs in the triple bond and ignores the two C–H bonds.
chem12a1-lc-15
Why is a hydrogen atom never the central atom in a Lewis structure?
Hydrogen is a metal and does not form covalent bonds.
Hydrogen has no valence electrons.
Hydrogen needs eight electrons to be stable.
Hydrogen can form only one covalent bond because it needs just two electrons to fill its valence shell.
H has one valence electron and is stable with 2 electrons, so one shared pair is enough. A central atom must bond to at least two others, which H cannot do.
chem12a1-lc-16
How many lone pairs of electrons are on the chlorine atom in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?
Cl has 7 valence electrons and uses one in the H–Cl bond, leaving 6 electrons as 3 lone pairs. Cl would have only 1 lone pair if it had formed three bonds, which is not the case.
chem12a1-lc-17
Methanol, CH₃OH, has a carbon atom bonded to three H atoms and to an O atom, and the O atom is also bonded to one H atom. How many bonding pairs of electrons are in the molecule?
The bonds are 3 C–H, 1 C–O and 1 O–H, all single, giving 5 bonding pairs. The oxygen's remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, which are not counted as bonding pairs.
chem12a1-lc-18
Which of the following carbon–carbon bonds is the shortest?
C–C in ethane, C₂H₆
C=C in ethene, C₂H₄
C≡C in ethyne, C₂H₂
All are the same length.
More shared pairs pull the two nuclei closer together, so the triple bond is shortest (and strongest). The lengths differ because the number of shared pairs differs.
chem12a1-lc-19
How many electrons are shared between two atoms in a double covalent bond?
A double bond consists of two shared pairs, which is 4 electrons. Two electrons is the number shared in a single bond.
chem12a1-lc-20
In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, one of the four N–H bonds can be described as a coordinate (dative) covalent bond. This is because
both electrons in that bond were supplied by the nitrogen atom.
the hydrogen atom has donated two electrons.
that bond is an ionic bond.
the bond is a double bond.
The N atom in NH₃ donates its lone pair to an H⁺ ion, which has no electrons, so both electrons in the new bond come from N. Once formed, the bond is identical to the other N–H bonds.
chem12a1-lc-21
What is the total number of lone pairs in the Lewis structure of hydrogen cyanide, HCN?
The structure is H–C≡N. H and C have no lone pairs, and N has 5 − 3 = 2 non-bonding electrons, which is one lone pair. The total of 10 valence electrons is shared as 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair.
chem12a1-lc-22
Hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, has the structure H–O–O–H. How many lone pairs of electrons are in the molecule?
There are 14 valence electrons and 3 bonds use 6, leaving 8 electrons or 4 lone pairs (2 on each O). Counting only 2 lone pairs would leave each O without an octet.
chem12a1-lc-23
What is the total number of valence electrons shown in the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
4 + 3 × 6 = 22, and the 2− charge adds 2 extra electrons, giving 24. Using 22 forgets to add the electrons that give the ion its negative charge.
chem12a1-lc-24
Oxygen difluoride, OF₂, has an oxygen atom single-bonded to two fluorine atoms. What is the total number of lone pairs in the molecule?
There are 6 + 2 × 7 = 20 valence electrons and 2 bonds use 4, leaving 16 electrons or 8 lone pairs (2 on O and 3 on each F). Using 6 would count only the lone pairs on the fluorine atoms.
chem12a1-lc-25
Distinguish between a bonding pair and a lone pair of electrons in a Lewis structure. (2 marks)

A bonding pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, forming a covalent bond [1]. A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom only and is not involved in bonding [1].
chem12a1-lc-26
Nitrogen, N₂, has a bond energy of 945 kJ mol⁻¹, whereas oxygen, O₂, has a bond energy of 498 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference in terms of the covalent bonds present. (3 marks)

N₂ contains a triple bond (three shared pairs) whereas O₂ contains a double bond (two shared pairs) [1]. More shared pairs mean a greater electrostatic attraction between the shared electrons and the two nuclei [1]. This makes the N≡N bond shorter and stronger, so more energy is needed to break it [1].
chem12a1-lc-27
Draw or describe the Lewis structure of carbon disulfide, CS₂, including the total number of valence electrons. (3 marks)

Total valence electrons = 4 + 2 × 6 = 16 [1]. Carbon is the central atom and forms a double bond to each sulfur atom (S=C=S) [1]. Each S atom has two lone pairs and C has none, so all atoms have an octet [1].
chem12a1-lc-28
Explain how the atoms in a water molecule, H₂O, achieve stable electron configurations by forming covalent bonds. (2 marks)
