Oxygen (6 valence electrons) shares one electron with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two single bonds, and has two lone pairs, giving it 8 electrons (an octet) [1]. Each hydrogen shares one pair, giving it 2 electrons in its valence shell, the same as helium [1].
chem12a1-lc-29
Explain why covalent bonds typically form between atoms of non-metals rather than between a metal and a non-metal. (2 marks)

Non-metal atoms have high and similar attractions for electrons, so neither atom can remove electrons completely from the other [1]. Instead they share electrons, so that each atom attains a stable noble-gas electron configuration [1].
chem12a1-lc-30
Compare the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom in methane, CH₄, ammonia, NH₃, and water, H₂O. (3 marks)

In CH₄, the central C has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs [1]. In NH₃, the central N has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair [1]. In H₂O, the central O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, so the central atom has an octet (4 pairs in total) in each molecule [1].
chem12a1-lc-31

Ethanol has the molecular formula C₂H₆O, with the atoms joined as CH₃–CH₂–OH. Determine the total number of valence electrons and describe the Lewis structure, including the number of bonding pairs and any lone pairs. (4 marks)

Total valence electrons = 2 × 4 + 6 × 1 + 6 = 20 [1]. All bonds are single bonds: C–C, C–O, O–H and five C–H bonds [1]. This gives 8 bonding pairs (16 electrons) [1]. The remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, both on the oxygen atom, and no other atom has lone pairs [1].
vce-chem12-ls-c1
In the Lewis structure of hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N, the numbers of bonding pairs and lone pairs are:
3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs
2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair
One C–H pair plus three pairs in C≡N make 4 bonding pairs; nitrogen has one lone pair. Total valence electrons: 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 = 5 pairs.
vce-chem12-vsepr-and-molecular-shape: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of an ammonia molecule, NH₃, is

N has four electron pairs around it (3 bonding and 1 lone pair), arranged roughly tetrahedrally. Molecular shape describes only the positions of the atoms, so NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal. Trigonal planar would require three bonding pairs and no lone pairs.

In CO₂, carbon has two double bonds (two regions of electron density) and no lone pairs, so the two regions are 180° apart. H₂O and H₂S have lone pairs on the central atom and are V-shaped, and SO₂ is also bent.
The H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule is approximately
Water has four electron pairs around O (2 bonding, 2 lone). Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so the angle is squeezed from the tetrahedral 109.5° to about 104.5°.
Which of the following molecules is tetrahedral in shape?
Si has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the four H atoms sit at the corners of a tetrahedron. PH₃ is pyramidal, H₂S is V-shaped and HCN is linear.
The central carbon atom in methanal, CH₂O, has three regions of electron density and no lone pairs. The shape of the molecule and its approximate bond angle are
A double bond counts as one region of electron density. Three regions with no lone pairs spread out in a flat triangle at about 120°. A pyramidal shape would need a lone pair on C.
Use VSEPR theory to explain why the water molecule is V-shaped rather than linear. (2 marks)

The O atom has four electron pairs (two bonding, two lone pairs) which repel each other and arrange themselves tetrahedrally to be as far apart as possible; the shape is described by the atoms only, so the two H atoms and O form a V (bent) shape with an angle of about 104.5°.
Predict the shape and approximate bond angle for (a) hydrogen cyanide, HCN, and (b) tetrachlorosilane, SiCl₄. (2 marks)
(a) HCN: linear, 180° (two regions of electron density around C, no lone pairs); (b) SiCl₄: tetrahedral, 109.5° (four bonding pairs, no lone pairs on Si).
The H–N–H bond angle in ammonia is about 107°, whereas the H–C–H angle in methane is 109.5°. Explain this difference. (2 marks)

Both central atoms have four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally; N in ammonia has one lone pair, which repels more strongly than bonding pairs, pushing the N–H bonds closer together and reducing the angle, while methane has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
Boron trifluoride, BF₃, has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs around the central atom. Its shape is
Three regions of electron density with no lone pairs spread out in one plane at 120°. Trigonal pyramidal would need a lone pair on B.
Which of the following molecules has a trigonal pyramidal shape?
N in NCl₃ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so the atoms form a pyramid. BF₃ is trigonal planar, CCl₄ is tetrahedral and OF₂ is V-shaped.
How many lone pairs of electrons are on the central atom of an OF₂ molecule?
O has six valence electrons and uses two in bonding to the two F atoms, leaving four electrons, which form two lone pairs. This gives a V-shaped molecule.
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂, has two bonding regions and one lone pair on S. Its shape and approximate bond angle are

Three regions of electron density are arranged in a triangle, but only the two atoms are counted in the shape, so SO₂ is V-shaped. The lone pair squeezes the angle slightly below 120°. SO₂ is not linear like CO₂.
Beryllium chloride, BeCl₂, has two bonding pairs and no lone pairs around Be. The Cl–Be–Cl bond angle is
Two regions of electron density are furthest apart when 180° from each other, so the molecule is linear. 120° would need three regions.
The ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, has a shape that is
All four electron pairs around N are bonding pairs, so the H atoms sit at the corners of a tetrahedron. Unlike NH₃, there is no lone pair to make the shape pyramidal.
The shape of the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺, is
O has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so the three H atoms form a pyramid with O at the apex. It is isoelectronic with NH₃ and has the same shape.
In ethene, C₂H₄, each carbon atom has three regions of electron density. The shape around each carbon atom and the H–C–H angle are
The C=C double bond counts as one region, plus two C–H bonds, giving three regions and no lone pairs. These spread into a flat triangle at about 120°.
Ethyne, C₂H₂, has the structure H–C≡C–H. The shape around each carbon atom is
Each C has two regions of electron density (one C–H bond and one triple bond) and no lone pairs, so the arrangement is linear with a 180° angle.
The shape of a dichloromethane molecule, CH₂Cl₂, is
C has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the four atoms are at the corners of a tetrahedron. Having different atoms attached does not change the basic shape.
Which of the following has the smallest bond angle?
The angles are 109.5° for CH₄, about 107° for NH₃, 104.5° for H₂O and 180° for CO₂. Water has two lone pairs, which repel the strongest and squeeze the bonding pairs closest.
The correct order of repulsion between electron pairs, from strongest to weakest, is
bonding pair–bonding pair > lone pair–bonding pair > lone pair–lone pair.
lone pair–bonding pair > lone pair–lone pair > bonding pair–bonding pair.
bonding pair–bonding pair > lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair.
lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair.
Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only and occupy more space, so lone pair repulsions are strongest. Bonding pairs are held between two nuclei, so they repel least.
In a hydrogen sulfide molecule, H₂S, the arrangement of electron pairs around S and the shape of the molecule are respectively
S has four electron pairs (two bonding, two lone), arranged tetrahedrally. Only the atoms are used to name the shape, which is V-shaped.
Which pair of molecules has the same shape?
Both NH₃ and PCl₃ have three bonding pairs and one lone pair on the central atom, so both are trigonal pyramidal. CH₄ is tetrahedral and BF₃ is trigonal planar.
Lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other because a lone pair
has fewer electrons than a bonding pair.
is found further from the central atom.
is attracted to only one nucleus and so occupies more space.
A lone pair is held by only the central atom's nucleus, so it spreads out more and repels neighbouring pairs more strongly. A bonding pair is shared by two nuclei and is more confined.
Carbon dioxide is linear but sulfur dioxide is V-shaped. Explain this difference using VSEPR theory. (3 marks)

In CO₂ the carbon atom has two regions of electron density and no lone pairs [1]; these are furthest apart at 180°, so the molecule is linear [1]; in SO₂ the sulfur atom has three regions including one lone pair, so the two bonded atoms are not opposite each other and the shape is V-shaped [1].
The H–O–H angle in water is 104.5°, while the H–N–H angle in ammonia is about 107°. Explain why the angle in water is smaller. (3 marks)

Both central atoms have four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally [1]; water has two lone pairs but ammonia has only one [1]; the extra lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly, squeezing the angle further below 109.5° in water [1].
Distinguish between the arrangement of electron pairs and the shape of a molecule, using ammonia as an example. (2 marks)

The arrangement of electron pairs includes both bonding and lone pairs; in NH₃ the four pairs are arranged tetrahedrally [1]; the shape describes only the positions of the atoms, so with one lone pair the NH₃ molecule is trigonal pyramidal [1].
Which of the following species is NOT tetrahedral in shape?
NH₃ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so its atoms form a trigonal pyramid. SiF₄, CF₄ and NH₄⁺ each have four bonding pairs and no lone pairs on the central atom, so all are tetrahedral.
Sulfur trioxide, SO₃, has the central S atom bonded to three O atoms, one of them through a double bond. Its shape is
A double bond counts as one region of electron density, so S has three regions and no lone pairs, giving a trigonal planar shape. Trigonal pyramidal would need a lone pair on the central atom.
Which statement about VSEPR theory is correct?
A double bond is treated as two regions of electron density.
Lone pairs repel other electron pairs less strongly than bonding pairs do.
A double bond is treated as one region of electron density.
The shape of a molecule includes the positions of its lone pairs.

Each multiple bond is counted as a single region of electron density when predicting the arrangement of electron regions. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, and the molecular shape describes only the positions of the atoms.
The oxygen atom in ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, is bonded to one carbon atom and one hydrogen atom. The C–O–H grouping is V-shaped because the oxygen atom has
two bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
three bonding pairs and one lone pair.
four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
two bonding pairs and two lone pairs.

Oxygen has six valence electrons. Two are used in single bonds, leaving two lone pairs, so four electron pairs surround O and the three atoms form a V-shape. With no lone pairs, the C–O–H grouping would be linear.

Boron trifluoride, BF₃, and nitrogen trifluoride, NF₃, both have three fluorine atoms bonded to a central atom, yet their shapes differ. Name the shape of each molecule and explain the difference. (3 marks)

BF₃ is trigonal planar, with three bonding pairs and no lone pairs around B [1]; NF₃ is trigonal pyramidal, as N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so four electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally [1]; the lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly, pushing the F atoms closer together so the F–N–F angle is less than 109.5° [1].
Which pair of particles has the same shape?
NH₄⁺ and CH₄ both have four bonding pairs and no lone pairs: tetrahedral. NH₃ is pyramidal, H₂O bent and CO₂ linear.
vce-chem12-electronegativity-and-polarit: Which bond is the most polar?
Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the H–F bond has the largest electronegativity difference (about 1.8). C–H is almost non-polar, with a difference of about 0.4.
Which molecule contains polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
CO₂ is linear, so the two equal C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. NH₃ and H₂O are polar because their asymmetrical shapes leave a net dipole, and HCl has only one polar bond.
A charged plastic rod is held next to thin streams of four liquids. Which stream would be deflected most noticeably?
Water molecules are polar, so they orient in the electric field and are attracted towards the rod. Hexane and cyclohexane are non-polar hydrocarbons, and CCl₄ is symmetrical with cancelling dipoles.
The bond between which pair of elements would have the greatest ionic character?

Caesium has one of the lowest electronegativities and fluorine the highest, giving the largest electronegativity difference and therefore the greatest ionic character. Sodium iodide is also ionic, but with a smaller difference.
the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons in a covalent bond.
the charge on an ion formed by an atom.
the number of valence electrons in an atom.
Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons towards itself. The first option defines first ionisation energy, which follows a related but different trend.
Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, contains four polar C–Cl bonds yet is a non-polar molecule. Explain. (2 marks)
Cl is more electronegative than C, so each C–Cl bond is polar (Cδ+–Clδ−); the molecule is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the four equal bond dipoles cancel and there is no overall dipole.
Explain why a water molecule is polar. In your answer, identify which atoms carry partial positive and partial negative charges. (3 marks)

O is more electronegative than H, so the shared electrons in each O–H bond are pulled towards O, making each bond polar; O carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and each H a partial positive charge (δ+); the molecule is V-shaped (asymmetrical), so the bond dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole.
Rank the bonds H–F, H–Cl and H–Br in order of increasing polarity and explain the trend using atomic structure. (2 marks)

H–Br < H–Cl < H–F; electronegativity decreases down group 17 because the valence shell is further from the nucleus (more shells, same core charge), so the halogen's attraction for the shared electrons, and therefore the electronegativity difference with H, decreases from F to Br.
Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?

Oxygen is small and has a high effective nuclear charge, so it is more electronegative than nitrogen, sulfur and chlorine. Chlorine is tempting because it is a halogen, but its larger atomic radius makes it less electronegative than oxygen.
Which list shows the elements in order of increasing electronegativity?
Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period, so the order across period 3 is Si < P < S < Cl. The reverse order lists the elements by decreasing electronegativity.
Both atoms in Cl–Cl are identical, so they attract the shared electrons equally and the bond is non-polar. C–O and N–H join different elements with different electronegativities, so each is polar.
In an N–H bond, which description of the partial charges is correct?
Both atoms are neutral because the electrons are shared

Nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons are drawn towards N, giving it a partial negative charge. Sharing the electrons does not make them equally shared unless the atoms are identical.
In CH₃Cl the C–Cl bond is much more polar than the C–H bonds, so the dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole. CH₄, CCl₄ and CO₂ are all symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel.
BF₃ is trigonal planar, so its three equal B–F dipoles cancel. NH₃ and PCl₃ are trigonal pyramidal and H₂S is bent, so their dipoles do not cancel.
Which bond is the least polar?
Carbon and hydrogen have very similar electronegativities, so the C–H bond has the smallest electronegativity difference. F–H has the largest difference of these four.
Whether a molecule is polar depends on
both the polarity of its bonds and its shape.
only the polarity of its bonds.
only the number of atoms in the molecule.
only the mass of the molecule.
A molecule is polar only if it has polar bonds whose dipoles do not cancel because of its shape. Polar bonds alone are not enough, as shown by CO₂ and CCl₄.
Electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period because
the number of electron shells increases.
nuclear charge increases while the valence electrons stay in the same shell.
Across a period the number of protons rises but the valence shell stays the same, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons more strongly. Atoms get smaller, not larger, across a period.
In a diagram of a polar bond, the arrow used to show a bond dipole points
towards the atom with more electrons in total.
The dipole arrow points towards the end of the bond that carries the partial negative charge, which is the more electronegative atom. Pointing it to the δ+ atom is a common reversal.
HCN is a linear molecule, yet it is polar. This is because
the two bond dipoles are equal and cancel.
hydrogen is the most electronegative atom in the molecule.
the C–H and C≡N bond dipoles are different and do not cancel.
For a linear molecule to be non-polar the two end bonds must be identical, as in CO₂. In HCN the two bonds differ, so their dipoles are unequal and leave a net dipole.
CO₂ and SO₂ both contain two polar double bonds, but only SO₂ is polar. This is because SO₂
is bent, so its bond dipoles do not cancel.
is linear, so its bond dipoles do not cancel.
has less polar bonds than CO₂.
has a greater number of valence electrons around the central atom.
SO₂ has a lone pair on sulfur that makes the molecule bent, so the dipoles add to give a net dipole. CO₂ is linear and its dipoles cancel.
As the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms increases, the bond changes from
ionic to polar covalent to non-polar covalent.
polar covalent to ionic to non-polar covalent.
non-polar covalent to polar covalent to ionic.
metallic to polar covalent to ionic.
A difference of zero gives a non-polar bond, a moderate difference a polar covalent bond, and a very large difference approaches ionic bonding. The reverse order describes decreasing difference.
In an S–Cl bond, which atom carries the partial positive charge?
Chlorine, because it is larger than sulfur
Sulfur, because it is less electronegative than chlorine
Sulfur, because it has more valence electrons than chlorine
Chlorine is more electronegative than sulfur, so it draws the shared electrons and sulfur becomes δ+. The bond is between different elements, so it is polar.
Explain why ammonia, NH₃, is a polar molecule. (3 marks)

N is more electronegative than H, so each N–H bond is polar with Nδ− and Hδ+ [1]; the molecule is trigonal pyramidal because of the lone pair on N, so it is asymmetrical [1]; the bond dipoles therefore do not cancel and the molecule has a net dipole [1].
Trichloromethane, CHCl₃, has a tetrahedral shape like CCl₄, but CHCl₃ is polar. Explain. (3 marks)

The three C–Cl bonds are strongly polar, whereas the C–H bond is almost non-polar [1]; the four bonds are not identical, so the molecule is not symmetrical in its charge distribution [1]; the bond dipoles do not cancel, so there is a net dipole [1].
Electronegativity values are Na 0.9, H 2.2 and Cl 3.2. Calculate the electronegativity difference for Na–Cl, H–Cl and Cl–Cl and classify each bond. (3 marks)
Na–Cl: 3.2 − 0.9 = 2.3, ionic [1]; H–Cl: 3.2 − 2.2 = 1.0, polar covalent [1]; Cl–Cl: 0, non-polar covalent [1].
Electronegativity values are H 2.2 and S 2.6. Predict whether hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, is polar, giving reasons. (3 marks)

S is slightly more electronegative than H, so each S–H bond is slightly polar with Sδ− and Hδ+ [1]; H₂S is bent because of the two lone pairs on S, so it is asymmetrical [1]; the bond dipoles do not cancel, so H₂S is weakly polar [1].
A student claims that any molecule with polar bonds must be polar. Explain why this is wrong, and why a diatomic molecule with a polar bond is always polar. (3 marks)

Polarity depends on the shape as well as the bonds, and in a symmetrical molecule such as CO₂ the equal bond dipoles cancel [1]; a diatomic molecule has only one bond, so there is nothing to cancel its dipole [1]; hence a diatomic molecule such as HCl with a polar bond has a net dipole and is polar [1].
Electronegativity decreases down group 17 from fluorine to iodine mainly because
the shared electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded from it.
the nuclear charge decreases down the group.
the atoms have fewer valence electrons down the group.
the atoms become smaller down the group.

Going down the group the atoms have more occupied shells, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons. Nuclear charge actually increases and atomic radius increases, so those options are wrong.
Which molecule is non-polar overall even though it contains polar bonds?

SiF₄ is tetrahedral with four identical Si–F bonds, so the bond dipoles cancel. NF₃ and OF₂ have lone pairs on the central atom, and CH₂F₂ has two different types of bond, so their dipoles do not cancel.
Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, N 3.0, O 3.4, F 4.0. Which bond has the greatest electronegativity difference?
C–F has a difference of 1.4, compared with 1.2 for O–H, 0.8 for N–H and 0.8 for C–O. Oxygen and hydrogen are the most familiar polar pair, but the C–F bond is more polar.
Electronegativity values are H 2.2, C 2.6 and O 3.4. (a) Arrange the bonds C–H, C–O and O–H in order of increasing polarity. (b) Show the partial charges on the C–O bond. (2 marks)

(a) The differences are C–H 0.4, C–O 0.8 and O–H 1.2, so the order of increasing polarity is C–H < C–O < O–H [1]; (b) oxygen is more electronegative, so it carries the partial negative charge and carbon the partial positive charge, Cδ+–Oδ− [1].
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂, is a polar molecule but sulfur trioxide, SO₃, is non-polar. Explain why. (3 marks)

Both molecules contain polar S–O bonds, with S the less electronegative atom [1]; SO₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel and there is no net dipole [1]; SO₂ is V-shaped because S has a lone pair, so the bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule has a net dipole [1].
All have polar or slightly polar bonds, but CCl₄, CO₂ and CH₄ are symmetrical, so their dipoles cancel. In CHCl₃ one H replaces a Cl, so the dipoles do not cancel.
vce-chem12-intermolecular-forces: chem12a1-im-1
The strongest type of intermolecular force between methanol molecules, CH₃OH, is
dispersion forces.
hydrogen bonding.
dipole–dipole attraction without hydrogen bonding.
covalent bonding.

Methanol has an H atom bonded directly to a highly electronegative O atom. This allows hydrogen bonding with lone pairs on neighbouring O atoms, which is stronger than dispersion and other dipole–dipole forces. Covalent bonds act within molecules, not between them.
chem12a1-im-2
The boiling points of the noble gases increase from helium to xenon. The best explanation is that
the atoms become more polar down the group.
hydrogen bonding increases down the group.
the larger number of electrons gives stronger dispersion forces.
covalent bonds form between larger atoms.

Noble gases are non-polar monatomic particles, so only dispersion forces act between them. Larger atoms have more electrons, which form larger, more easily formed temporary dipoles, so the attraction is stronger.
chem12a1-im-3
Which substance CANNOT form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?
Hydrogen fluoride, HF
Ammonia, NH₃
Methanol, CH₃OH
Chloromethane, CH₃Cl
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to N, O or F. In CH₃Cl the H atoms are bonded to C, so it shows only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.
chem12a1-im-4
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane both have the formula C₅H₁₂. Pentane boils at 36 °C, while 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at about 10 °C. This difference is best explained by
pentane forming hydrogen bonds.
the compact shape of 2,2-dimethylpropane reducing contact between molecules, so it has weaker dispersion forces.
2,2-dimethylpropane having fewer electrons.
pentane being a polar molecule.

Both molecules have the same number of electrons and are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act. The long chain of pentane gives a larger contact area between molecules, so its dispersion forces are stronger. Neither substance can hydrogen bond.
chem12a1-im-5
Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C, whereas hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a heavier molecule, boils at −60 °C. The main reason is that
water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
the O–H covalent bond is stronger than the S–H bond.
H₂S has fewer electrons than H₂O.
H₂S is a linear molecule.

Boiling separates molecules, so it depends on intermolecular forces, not bond strength within molecules. Water forms hydrogen bonds because O is small and highly electronegative, whereas S is not electronegative enough. H₂S actually has more electrons than H₂O and is V-shaped.
chem12a1-im-6
Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. (3 marks)

In ice, each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a fixed, open hexagonal lattice; this arrangement holds molecules further apart than in the liquid; when ice melts some hydrogen bonds break and molecules pack more closely, so the same mass occupies a smaller volume in the liquid (ice has a lower density and floats).
chem12a1-im-7

The boiling points of the hydrogen halides are: HF 20 °C, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. Explain (a) why HF has the highest boiling point and (b) why the boiling point rises from HCl to HI. (3 marks)

(a) HF molecules form hydrogen bonds (H bonded to highly electronegative F), which are much stronger than the intermolecular forces in the other hydrogen halides; (b) HCl, HBr and HI cannot hydrogen bond; from HCl to HI the number of electrons increases, so dispersion forces become stronger, outweighing the decrease in dipole–dipole attraction as bond polarity falls.
chem12a1-im-8
Identify all the types of intermolecular forces present between molecules in each of: (a) methane, CH₄ (b) hydrogen chloride, HCl (c) ammonia, NH₃. (3 marks)
(a) CH₄: dispersion forces only (non-polar); (b) HCl: dispersion and dipole–dipole forces; (c) NH₃: dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
chem12a1-im-9
Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
CH₄
SiH₄
GeH₄
SnH₄

All four are non-polar and have only dispersion forces. SnH₄ has the most electrons, so its dispersion forces are strongest. CH₄ has the weakest forces despite its strong C–H bonds, because boiling does not break covalent bonds.
chem12a1-im-10
Which statement correctly describes a hydrogen bond between two ammonia molecules?
An attraction between an H atom bonded to N in one molecule and the lone pair on the N atom of a neighbouring molecule
An attraction between the N atom of one molecule and the N atom of another molecule
A covalent bond formed when an H atom is shared between two N atoms
An attraction between temporary dipoles in neighbouring molecules

A hydrogen bond forms between an H atom covalently bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a highly electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule. Attraction between temporary dipoles describes dispersion forces, not hydrogen bonding.
chem12a1-im-11
The only type of intermolecular force acting between carbon dioxide molecules, CO₂, is
dipole–dipole attraction.
dispersion forces.
hydrogen bonding.
ionic attraction.
CO₂ is linear and symmetrical, so its polar C=O bond dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar. Therefore only dispersion forces act between molecules, even though the bonds themselves are polar.
chem12a1-im-12
Which list shows the types of attraction in order of increasing strength?
Hydrogen bond, dispersion force, covalent bond
Covalent bond, hydrogen bond, dispersion force
Dispersion force, hydrogen bond, covalent bond
Dispersion force, covalent bond, hydrogen bond

Covalent bonds within molecules are much stronger than any intermolecular force. Between molecules, a hydrogen bond is typically stronger than a dispersion force of a similar-sized non-polar molecule.
chem12a1-im-13
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, boils at 78 °C, whereas dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, which has the same molecular formula, boils at −24 °C. The best explanation is that
dimethyl ether has stronger covalent bonds.
dimethyl ether has more electrons than ethanol.
ethanol molecules can form hydrogen bonds with each other.
ethanol is non-polar.

Ethanol has an H atom bonded directly to O, so it forms hydrogen bonds. In dimethyl ether all H atoms are bonded to C, so only weaker dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act. Both have the same number of electrons.
chem12a1-im-14
Which of the following molecules has dipole–dipole forces between its molecules?
CHCl₃
CCl₄
CO₂
BF₃
CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but the C–H and C–Cl bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar. CCl₄, CO₂ and BF₃ are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel and they are non-polar.
chem12a1-im-15
When solid iodine, I₂, sublimes on gentle heating, which interactions are overcome?
Covalent bonds between iodine atoms
Dispersion forces between I₂ molecules
Hydrogen bonds between I₂ molecules
Ionic bonds between iodine atoms
I₂ is a non-polar molecular substance, so only dispersion forces hold the molecules together in the solid. Changing state does not break the I–I covalent bonds, which remain intact in the gas.
chem12a1-im-16
Octane, C₈H₁₈, boils at 126 °C but butane, C₄H₁₀, boils at −1 °C. This is mainly because octane has
hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
a greater dipole moment.
stronger covalent bonds.
more electrons and a larger surface area, giving stronger dispersion forces.

Both are non-polar hydrocarbons, so only dispersion forces act. The longer octane molecule has more electrons and greater contact with its neighbours, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
chem12a1-im-17
Which substance can form the greatest number of hydrogen bonds per molecule?
H₂O
HF
NH₃
CH₃OH

Each water molecule has two H atoms available and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds. HF has one H atom, NH₃ has one lone pair and CH₃OH has only one H atom bonded to O, so each can form fewer.
chem12a1-im-18
When liquid water boils, which of the following occurs?
O–H covalent bonds break to form hydrogen and oxygen gases.
Hydrogen bonds between molecules are overcome, but the molecules remain H₂O.
Ionic bonds between H⁺ and OH⁻ break.
The molecules are converted to H₂O₂.
Boiling is a physical change in which intermolecular forces are overcome and molecules separate. The strong O–H covalent bonds within each molecule are not broken.
chem12a1-im-19
Glycerol, C₃H₅(OH)₃, is much more viscous than ethanol, C₂H₅OH. The best explanation is that glycerol
has weaker dispersion forces.
is non-polar.
has covalent bonds between molecules.
has three –OH groups per molecule, so it forms more hydrogen bonds.
Each glycerol molecule has three O–H groups, allowing extensive hydrogen bonding between molecules, which makes them harder to flow past each other. Ethanol has only one O–H group per molecule.
chem12a1-im-20
Dispersion forces between non-polar molecules arise from
temporary dipoles caused by momentary uneven distribution of electrons.
permanent dipoles caused by differences in electronegativity.
the sharing of electrons between molecules.
hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
The electrons in a molecule are constantly moving, so a temporary dipole can form and induce a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. Permanent dipoles cause dipole–dipole forces instead.
chem12a1-im-21
Hydrogen chloride, HCl, boils at −85 °C and fluorine, F₂, boils at −188 °C, even though both have 18 electrons. The better explanation is that
HCl forms hydrogen bonds.
HCl is polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces as well as dispersion forces.
F₂ has stronger covalent bonds.
F₂ is polar.

With the same number of electrons the dispersion forces are similar. HCl is polar and so has additional dipole–dipole attraction. It cannot hydrogen bond because Cl is not N, O or F, and F₂ is non-polar.
chem12a1-im-22
Which list shows increasing boiling points?
H₂O, HCl, Ne
HCl, H₂O, Ne
Ne, HCl, H₂O
Ne, H₂O, HCl
Ne has only weak dispersion forces, HCl adds dipole–dipole forces, and H₂O forms strong hydrogen bonds, giving the order Ne < HCl < H₂O.
chem12a1-im-23
Define a hydrogen bond and state the conditions needed for one to form. (2 marks)

A hydrogen bond is an attractive intermolecular force between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) in one molecule and a lone pair on a N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule [1]; the molecule must therefore contain H bonded directly to N, O or F and the other atom must have a lone pair [1].
chem12a1-im-24
The boiling points of methane, ethane, propane and butane are −162 °C, −89 °C, −42 °C and −1 °C respectively. Explain this trend. (3 marks)

These are non-polar molecules, so only dispersion forces act between them [1]; the number of electrons and the molecular size increase from methane to butane [1]; stronger dispersion forces mean more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point rises [1].
chem12a1-im-25
Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, boils at 78 °C, while propane, C₃H₈, boils at −42 °C, even though both have 26 electrons. Explain this difference. (3 marks)

Both have similar numbers of electrons, so their dispersion forces are of similar strength [1]; ethanol has an H atom bonded directly to O, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds [1]; hydrogen bonds are stronger than the dispersion forces alone in propane, so more energy is needed to boil ethanol [1].
chem12a1-im-26
Distinguish between intramolecular and intermolecular forces, and state which type is overcome when water boils. (2 marks)

Intramolecular forces (covalent bonds) act within a molecule, whereas intermolecular forces act between separate molecules [1]; when water boils only intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces) are overcome, and the O–H covalent bonds stay intact [1].
chem12a1-im-27
Water boils at 100 °C, hydrogen fluoride at 20 °C and ammonia at −33 °C. All three form hydrogen bonds. Explain why water has the highest boiling point. (3 marks)

Each water molecule has two H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds [1]; HF has only one H atom per molecule and NH₃ has only one lone pair, so each can form fewer hydrogen bonds per molecule [1]; more extensive hydrogen bonding in water requires more energy to overcome, giving the highest boiling point [1].
chem12a1-im-28
At room temperature fluorine, F₂, is a gas but iodine, I₂, is a solid. Explain why. (2 marks)

Both are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between molecules [1]; I₂ has many more electrons and is larger than F₂, so its dispersion forces are much stronger, which holds the molecules in a solid at room temperature [1].
chem12a1-im-29
At the same temperature, which of these liquids has the highest vapour pressure?
Propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH
Butan-1-ol, C₄H₉OH
Pentan-1-ol, C₅H₁₁OH
Ethanol, C₂H₅OH

All four form hydrogen bonds, but ethanol has the fewest electrons, so its dispersion forces are weakest and its molecules escape most easily. The longer-chain alkanols have stronger dispersion forces and lower vapour pressures.
chem12a1-im-30
Which substance can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules but not with other molecules of its own kind?
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
Ammonia, NH₃
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH

Propanone has an O atom with lone pairs to accept a hydrogen bond from water, but no H atom bonded to O or N to donate. Ethanol, ammonia and ethanoic acid all have an H atom bonded to O or N, so they can hydrogen-bond to themselves.
chem12a1-im-31
Describe the forces overcome when (a) solid carbon dioxide sublimes and (b) liquid ethanol evaporates, and state whether any covalent bonds are broken in either process. (3 marks)

(a) Subliming CO₂ overcomes only the weak dispersion forces between molecules [1]; (b) evaporating ethanol overcomes hydrogen bonds (as well as dipole–dipole and dispersion forces) between molecules [1]; no covalent bonds within the molecules are broken in either process [1].
chem12a1-im-32
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃ (M = 58.0 g mol⁻¹), boils at 56 °C, while propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (M = 60.0 g mol⁻¹), boils at 97 °C. Explain this difference. (2 marks)

The two molecules have similar molar masses, so their dispersion forces are of similar strength, but propan-1-ol has an O–H group and forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules whereas propanone has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces [1]; the hydrogen bonds are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules of propan-1-ol, giving it the higher boiling point [1].
vce-chem12-im-c1
Which shows the boiling points of the hydrogen halides from highest to lowest?
HI > HBr > HCl > HF
HF > HCl > HBr > HI
HCl > HBr > HI > HF
HF > HI > HBr > HCl
Dispersion forces increase from HCl to HI, so boiling point rises. HF is highest because it forms hydrogen bonds.
vce-chem12-covalent-lattices-and-carbon-: chem12a1-cl-1
In diamond, each carbon atom is
covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms in flat layers.
covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement.
ionically bonded to four neighbouring carbon ions.
part of a C₆₀ molecule.

Diamond is a three-dimensional covalent network in which every C forms four single covalent bonds arranged tetrahedrally. Bonding to three atoms in flat layers describes graphite, and C₆₀ is a fullerene.
chem12a1-cl-2
Graphite conducts electricity because
each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move along the layers.
it contains free carbon ions.
dispersion forces between layers carry charge.
all of its valence electrons are held in covalent bonds.

Each C in graphite forms three covalent bonds within its layer. The fourth valence electron is delocalised across the layer and can move when a voltage is applied. If all valence electrons were localised in bonds, as in diamond, graphite would not conduct.
chem12a1-cl-3
Which substance has a covalent network lattice structure?
Carbon dioxide, CO₂
Iodine, I₂
Silicon dioxide, SiO₂
Sodium chloride, NaCl
In SiO₂ (quartz), each Si is covalently bonded to four O atoms and each O to two Si atoms in a continuous three-dimensional network. CO₂ and I₂ are covalent molecular substances, and NaCl is ionic.
chem12a1-cl-4
Graphite is used as a dry lubricant because
its covalent bonds are weak.
it has a low melting point.
it reacts with metal surfaces to form a slippery coating.
the weak dispersion forces between its layers allow the layers to slide over each other.

Within each layer the covalent bonds are very strong, but the layers are held together only by weak dispersion forces, so they slide easily. Graphite actually has a very high sublimation point, above 3600 °C.
chem12a1-cl-5
Graphene is
a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons, as in one layer of graphite.
a spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms.
a three-dimensional tetrahedral carbon network.
an alloy of carbon and iron.

Graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of hexagonally bonded carbon. It is extremely strong, conducts electricity well and is nearly transparent. C₆₀ is buckminsterfullerene, and the tetrahedral network is diamond.
chem12a1-cl-6
Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon. Explain why diamond is very hard and does not conduct electricity, whereas graphite is soft and conducts electricity. (3 marks)

In diamond each C is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3D tetrahedral network, so it is very hard, and all valence electrons are localised in bonds so it cannot conduct; in graphite each C bonds to three others in layers held together by weak dispersion forces, so layers slide and it is soft; the fourth electron of each C is delocalised within the layers, so graphite conducts.
chem12a1-cl-7
Silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C, whereas carbon dioxide sublimes at −78 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding. (2 marks)

SiO₂ is a covalent network lattice, so melting requires breaking many strong covalent Si–O bonds throughout the structure; CO₂ consists of discrete non-polar molecules, so only weak dispersion forces between molecules must be overcome.
chem12a1-cl-8
Carbon nanotubes are rolled sheets of graphene. Suggest one use of carbon nanotubes and link it to a specific property and its structural explanation. (2 marks)

Use: e.g. reinforcing lightweight sports equipment or composite materials, or as tiny electrical conductors in electronics; property and explanation: very high tensile strength because of the strong covalent bonds in the continuous hexagonal carbon network, or electrical conductivity because of the delocalised electrons in the graphene structure.
chem12a1-cl-9
Diamond has a very high melting point because
weak dispersion forces between its molecules are very strong.
ionic bonds between carbon ions are broken on melting.
many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice must be broken.
its delocalised electrons hold the carbon atoms together.

Melting a covalent network lattice requires breaking a huge number of strong covalent bonds, which takes a great deal of energy. Diamond contains no discrete molecules, no ions and no delocalised electrons.
chem12a1-cl-10
Within a single layer of graphite, the carbon atoms are arranged
in hexagonal rings, with each carbon covalently bonded to three others.
in a tetrahedral arrangement, with each carbon bonded to four others.
in hexagonal rings, with each carbon bonded to four others.
as separate C₆₀ molecules.
Each carbon in a graphite layer forms three covalent bonds in a flat hexagonal pattern. Four bonds per carbon in a tetrahedral arrangement describes diamond.
chem12a1-cl-11
Allotropes are best defined as
atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
different elements with the same crystal structure.
compounds with the same empirical formula but different properties.
different structural forms of the same element in the same state.
Diamond, graphite and C₆₀ are all pure carbon with different bonding arrangements. Atoms differing in neutron number are isotopes, not allotropes.
chem12a1-cl-12
Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, has a much lower sublimation point than diamond because
each carbon atom in C₆₀ has only one covalent bond.
only weak dispersion forces between C₆₀ molecules need to be overcome.
the covalent bonds within C₆₀ molecules are weaker than those in diamond.
C₆₀ is held together by ionic bonding.
C₆₀ is a discrete covalent molecule, so changing state only overcomes weak dispersion forces between molecules. The covalent bonds within each molecule are not broken.
chem12a1-cl-13
Diamond does not conduct electricity because
it contains positive and negative ions that are fixed in position.
its layers are held together by weak forces.
all four valence electrons of each carbon atom are localised in covalent bonds.
it is a non-metal, and non-metals never conduct.
Every carbon in diamond uses all four valence electrons in covalent bonds, so no charge carriers are free to move. Graphite is also a non-metal yet conducts, so the last option is wrong.
chem12a1-cl-14
In the covalent network lattice of silicon dioxide, each silicon atom is bonded to
four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms.
two oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is bonded to four silicon atoms.
four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is bonded to four silicon atoms.
one oxygen atom by a double bond, forming discrete SiO₂ molecules.
Each Si bonds to four O and each O to two Si, which gives the 1 : 2 ratio in SiO₂. The formula is an empirical ratio, not a molecule.
chem12a1-cl-15
Which of the following is NOT an allotrope of carbon?
Graphene
Carbon nanotube
Buckminsterfullerene
Silicon carbide
Silicon carbide, SiC, is a compound of silicon and carbon, so it cannot be an allotrope. The other three are all forms of pure carbon.
chem12a1-cl-16
How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in a C₆₀ molecule?
Two
Three
Four
Six
Each carbon in C₆₀ is bonded to three other carbons, as in graphite, with the sheet curved into a sphere. The fourth valence electron is delocalised over the molecule.
chem12a1-cl-17
Silicon carbide, SiC, is used as an abrasive on sandpaper and grinding wheels. This use is best explained by it being
a covalent network lattice, so it is very hard.
an ionic lattice, so it is hard but brittle.
a covalent molecular substance with strong dispersion forces.
a metallic lattice with delocalised electrons.
SiC has a three-dimensional network of strong covalent bonds like diamond, making it extremely hard. Covalent molecular substances are soft even when dispersion forces are significant.
chem12a1-cl-18
Which of the following lists the substances in order of increasing melting point?
Diamond, silicon dioxide, carbon dioxide
Silicon dioxide, carbon dioxide, diamond
Carbon dioxide, diamond, silicon dioxide
Carbon dioxide, silicon dioxide, diamond

CO₂ is molecular with only weak dispersion forces, so it has the lowest value. SiO₂ (about 1700 °C) and diamond (above 3500 °C) are both network lattices, with the stronger C–C network of diamond giving the highest.
chem12a1-cl-19
Graphite is soft and slippery, yet it sublimes only above 3600 °C. This is because
its layers are held by strong covalent bonds, but its atoms within layers are not bonded.
strong covalent bonds within layers make melting difficult, but weak dispersion forces between layers allow sliding.
it is a covalent molecular substance with weak forces between molecules.
its delocalised electrons make it metallic and so soft.

Softness relates to the weak forces between layers, while the very high sublimation point relates to the strong covalent bonding within the layers. The atoms within a layer are strongly bonded, so the first option is reversed.
chem12a1-cl-20
A diamond has a mass of 0.50 g. Approximately how many carbon atoms does it contain? (M(C) = 12.0 g mol⁻¹; Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
n(C) = 0.50 ÷ 12.0 = 0.0417 mol, and N = 0.0417 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.5 × 10²². The option 3.6 × 10²⁴ comes from multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing.
chem12a1-cl-21
Graphite conducts electricity well along its layers but very poorly between layers. This is because
delocalised electrons can move within a layer but not easily from one layer to the next.
ions can move within layers but not between them.
covalent bonds between layers are broken by an applied voltage.
the layers are positively charged and repel each other.
The delocalised electrons are spread across each layer, and the layers are separated by relatively large gaps. Graphite contains no ions.
chem12a1-cl-22
A carbon nanotube can be best described as
a sheet of graphene rolled into a cylinder.
a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms.
a tetrahedral network of carbon atoms in a long tube.
a stack of graphene layers held together by covalent bonds.
A nanotube is a graphene sheet rolled up, so each carbon still bonds to three others in hexagons. The hollow sphere is C₆₀, and stacked layers with weak forces between them describe graphite.
chem12a1-cl-23
Compare the structures of diamond and silicon dioxide and state two properties they share as a result. (3 marks)

Both are covalent network lattices, with atoms joined by strong covalent bonds in a continuous three-dimensional arrangement [1]; in diamond each C bonds to four C atoms, while in SiO₂ each Si bonds to four O and each O to two Si [1]; shared properties include very high melting point and hardness, and being non-conductors of electricity [1].
chem12a1-cl-24
Describe the structure of buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, and explain why it is much softer than diamond. (3 marks)

C₆₀ is a discrete spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms arranged in hexagons and pentagons, with each carbon bonded to three others [1]; in the solid, separate C₆₀ molecules are held together only by weak dispersion forces [1]; these are easily overcome, whereas diamond is a rigid network of strong covalent bonds throughout [1].
chem12a1-cl-25
Explain why graphene is able to conduct electricity. (2 marks)

Each carbon atom in graphene forms three covalent bonds with neighbouring carbons, leaving one valence electron that is not used in bonding [1]; this electron is delocalised across the sheet and is free to move when a voltage is applied, carrying charge [1].
chem12a1-cl-26
Diamond is used on drill bits and graphite is used in electrodes. For each use, link the property that makes it suitable to the structure of the allotrope. (4 marks)

Drill bits use hardness of diamond [1]; because each C is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral lattice [1]; electrodes use the electrical conductivity of graphite [1]; because each C bonds to only three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move through the layers [1].
chem12a1-cl-27
A student states that diamond melts at a very high temperature because strong dispersion forces between carbon atoms must be overcome. Identify the error and give the correct explanation. (2 marks)

The error is that diamond is not held together by dispersion forces between molecules, as it contains no discrete molecules [1]; it is a covalent network lattice and melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms [1].
chem12a1-cl-28
In a sheet of graphene, each carbon atom forms
four covalent bonds and has no delocalised electrons.
three covalent bonds and contributes one delocalised electron.
two covalent bonds and contributes two delocalised electrons.
three covalent bonds and has no delocalised electrons.
Each C atom bonds to three neighbours in a hexagonal sheet, leaving one valence electron that is delocalised across the sheet. Forming four bonds with no delocalised electrons describes diamond.
chem12a1-cl-29
Graphite has a lower density than diamond mainly because
graphite contains fewer carbon atoms per mole.
graphite has weaker covalent bonds than diamond.
the layers in graphite are widely spaced and held only by weak dispersion forces.
the carbon atoms in graphite are smaller than those in diamond.
The layers are about 0.34 nm apart, so the atoms are packed less closely than in the compact diamond lattice. The atoms are the same element, so the mass per mole and atom size are identical.
chem12a1-cl-30
A solid is very hard, melts above 2500 °C and does not conduct electricity either as a solid or when molten. It is most likely to be a
metallic lattice.
ionic lattice.
molecular lattice.
covalent network lattice.

A covalent network has strong covalent bonds throughout and no mobile charge carriers, so it is hard, has a very high melting point and is a non-conductor. An ionic lattice would conduct when molten, and a molecular solid would melt at a low temperature.
chem12a1-cl-31
Graphene is being investigated for use in flexible electronic displays. Link two structural features of graphene to the properties that make it suitable. (2 marks)

Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that is free to move across the sheet, so graphene conducts electricity [1]; the strong covalent bonds in the one-atom-thick hexagonal sheet make it strong yet flexible [1].
chem12a1-cl-32
Explain why graphite conducts electricity but silicon dioxide does not. (2 marks)

In graphite each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layers and carry charge [1]; in silicon dioxide all valence electrons are held in localised covalent bonds, so there are no mobile charge carriers [1].
vce-chem12-cl-c1
Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, because in graphite:
There are carbon ions between the layers that move when a voltage is applied
The covalent bonds are weaker, so electrons break free from them easily
Each carbon is bonded to four others, which spreads electrons through the lattice
Each carbon is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom
In diamond all four valence electrons are in localised covalent bonds. In graphite the fourth electron is delocalised within each layer.
vce-chem12-relative-masses-and-mass-spec: chem12a2-rm-1
Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, and a relative atomic mass of 35.45. Taking the relative isotopic masses as 35 and 37, what is the percentage abundance of ³⁵Cl?
Let x be the fraction of ³⁵Cl: 35x + 37(1 − x) = 35.45, so 37 − 2x = 35.45 and x = 0.775, i.e. 77.5%. 22.5% is the abundance of ³⁷Cl, not ³⁵Cl.
chem12a2-rm-2
In a mass spectrometer, what is actually detected and used to produce the mass spectrum?
Neutral atoms, separated according to their mass
Positively charged ions, separated according to their mass-to-charge ratio
Electrons removed from the sample, separated according to their energy
Negatively charged ions, separated according to their size

The sample is ionised to form positive ions, which are accelerated and deflected; the amount of deflection depends on m/z. Neutral atoms cannot be accelerated or deflected by electric or magnetic fields, so they are not detected.
chem12a2-rm-3
Relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass are both measured on a scale relative to:
one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
the mass of one hydrogen-1 atom
the mass of one proton
one-sixteenth of the mass of an atom of oxygen-16

The modern scale defines one-twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom as exactly 1 unit, so ¹²C has a relative isotopic mass of exactly 12. Hydrogen and oxygen scales were used historically but are not the current standard.
chem12a2-rm-4
Gallium consists of ⁶⁹Ga (60.1%) and ⁷¹Ga (39.9%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 69 and 71, the relative atomic mass of gallium is closest to:
Ar = (69 × 60.1 + 71 × 39.9) ÷ 100 = (4146.9 + 2832.9) ÷ 100 = 69.8. 70.0 would be the simple average, which ignores the higher abundance of ⁶⁹Ga.
chem12a2-rm-5

Bromine exists as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in almost equal amounts. The mass spectrum of Br₂ shows molecular-ion peaks at m/z 158, 160 and 162 in a ratio of about 1 : 2 : 1. The best explanation for the tallest peak at 160 is that:
160 is the relative molecular mass of the most abundant isotope of bromine
the ⁸¹Br–⁸¹Br molecule is the most stable
a ⁷⁹Br–⁸¹Br molecule can form in two ways (⁷⁹Br first or ⁸¹Br first), so it is twice as likely as either ⁷⁹Br–⁷⁹Br or ⁸¹Br–⁸¹Br
Br₂⁺ ions with m/z 160 are deflected the least

With a 50 : 50 isotope ratio, the combinations 79–79, 79–81, 81–79 and 81–81 are equally likely, so the mixed molecule (m/z 160) appears twice as often. Ions with m/z 160 are deflected in between the other two, not the least.
chem12a2-rm-6

Magnesium has three naturally occurring isotopes: ²⁴Mg (78.99%), ²⁵Mg (10.00%) and ²⁶Mg (11.01%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 24, 25 and 26, calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to four significant figures. (2 marks)
chem12a2-rm-7
Distinguish between relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass, and explain why the relative atomic mass of most elements is not a whole number. (3 marks)

Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one atom of a particular isotope relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom; relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the relative isotopic masses of all naturally occurring isotopes of the element, taking their abundances into account; because most elements are a mixture of isotopes, the weighted mean lies between the isotopic masses and is usually not a whole number.
chem12a2-rm-8

The mass spectrum of a metallic element X shows only two peaks: m/z 63 with a relative abundance of 69.2% and m/z 65 with a relative abundance of 30.8%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of X and identify the element. (3 marks)
Ar = (63 × 69.2 + 65 × 30.8) ÷ 100; = (4359.6 + 2002.0) ÷ 100 = 63.6; X is copper (Ar = 63.5 in the data book), the closest match.
chem12a2-rm-9
Lithium has two isotopes, ⁶Li (7.59%) and ⁷Li (92.41%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 6 and 7, the relative atomic mass of lithium is closest to:
Ar = (6 × 7.59 + 7 × 92.41) ÷ 100 = (45.54 + 646.87) ÷ 100 = 6.92. 6.50 is the simple average, which ignores that ⁷Li is far more abundant.
chem12a2-rm-10
Boron consists of ¹⁰B (19.9%) and ¹¹B (80.1%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 10 and 11, the relative atomic mass of boron is closest to:
Ar = (10 × 19.9 + 11 × 80.1) ÷ 100 = (199 + 881.1) ÷ 100 = 10.8. 10.2 results from swapping the abundances, and 10.5 is the unweighted average.
chem12a2-rm-11
Why does relative atomic mass have no units?
It is a ratio of masses, compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
It is measured in atomic mass units, which are left out by convention
It is the mass of a single atom, which is too small to have units
It is an average, and averages of masses have no units
A relative mass is the mass of an atom divided by a standard mass, so the units cancel. It is not a mass in grams or any other unit; an average of masses would still carry units.
chem12a2-rm-12
Singly charged ³⁵Cl⁺ and ³⁷Cl⁺ ions, travelling at the same speed, pass through the same magnetic field in a mass spectrometer. Which statement is correct?
³⁵Cl⁺ is deflected less because it has fewer neutrons
Both ions are deflected equally because they have the same charge
³⁵Cl⁺ is not deflected because it is lighter
³⁷Cl⁺ is deflected less because it has the greater mass
For ions of the same charge, the heavier ion has greater inertia and is deflected less. Having the same charge does not mean equal deflection, since deflection also depends on mass.
chem12a2-rm-13
In a mass spectrum, the vertical axis (the height of each peak) shows:
the charge on each ion
the energy of the ions as they hit the detector
the relative abundance of ions of that m/z value
the time taken for the ions to reach the detector
Peak height is proportional to the number of ions detected at that m/z, so it gives relative abundance. The horizontal axis, not the vertical, gives the mass-to-charge ratio.
chem12a2-rm-14
Antimony has two isotopes, ¹²¹Sb and ¹²³Sb, and a relative atomic mass of 121.76. Taking the relative isotopic masses as 121 and 123, the percentage abundance of ¹²¹Sb is:
Let x be the fraction of ¹²¹Sb: 121x + 123(1 − x) = 121.76, so 123 − 2x = 121.76 and x = 0.62, i.e. 62%. 38% is the abundance of ¹²³Sb, and 50% would give an Ar of 122.
chem12a2-rm-15
Chlorine molecules, Cl₂, are analysed in a mass spectrometer. Considering only ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, how many different molecular-ion peaks appear, and where?
Three peaks, at m/z 70, 72 and 74
Two peaks, at m/z 70 and 74
Two peaks, at m/z 35 and 37
Four peaks, at m/z 70, 72, 72 and 74
The possible molecules are ³⁵Cl–³⁵Cl (70), ³⁵Cl–³⁷Cl (72) and ³⁷Cl–³⁷Cl (74). The two ways of forming the mixed molecule give the same m/z, so they produce one peak, not two.
chem12a2-rm-16
Atoms of ¹²C and ¹⁴C differ in their:
number of protons
number of electrons
chemical properties
number of neutrons
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons (and electrons) but different numbers of neutrons. The same electron configuration means their chemical properties are essentially identical.
chem12a2-rm-17
The mass spectrum of silicon shows peaks at m/z 28 (92.2%), 29 (4.7%) and 30 (3.1%). The relative atomic mass of silicon is closest to:
Ar = (28 × 92.2 + 29 × 4.7 + 30 × 3.1) ÷ 100 = 28.11. 29.0 is the unweighted mean of the three values, which ignores the dominance of ²⁸Si.
chem12a2-rm-18
A sample of an element gives two peaks at m/z 107 (51.8%) and 109 (48.2%). Which element is it?
Palladium (Ar = 106.4)
Silver (Ar = 107.9)
Cadmium (Ar = 112.4)
Indium (Ar = 114.8)
Ar = (107 × 51.8 + 109 × 48.2) ÷ 100 = 107.96, matching silver. Palladium has an Ar below 107, which is impossible for a mixture of isotopes of mass 107 and 109.
chem12a2-rm-19
In a mass spectrometer, a ²⁴Mg atom loses two electrons to form a ²⁴Mg²⁺ ion. At what m/z value does this ion appear?
m/z is the mass number divided by the charge: 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Using 24 would ignore the 2+ charge.
chem12a2-rm-20
Taking hydrogen as ¹H only, the molecular-ion peaks for HCl (containing ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl) appear at m/z:
36 only
35 and 37
36 and 37
36 and 38
¹H³⁵Cl has m/z 36 and ¹H³⁷Cl has m/z 38. The peaks at 35 and 37 would be the Cl⁺ fragments, not the intact HCl molecular ions.
chem12a2-rm-21
The mass spectrum of an element shows peaks at m/z 50 (4%), 52 (84%), 53 (10%) and 54 (2%). Which prediction about its relative atomic mass is best?
Exactly 52, the mass of the tallest peak
Slightly above 52, because the heavier isotopes contribute more to the weighted mean than the lighter one
Well below 52, because the lightest isotope is at 50
52.25, the simple mean of the four m/z values
The weighted mean is dominated by the 52 peak, but the 53 and 54 isotopes pull it up more than the 50 isotope pulls it down (Ar ≈ 52.06). An unweighted mean ignores the abundances.
chem12a2-rm-22
Which statement about relative atomic mass is correct?
It always lies between the lightest and heaviest relative isotopic masses of the element
It always equals the mass number of the most abundant isotope
It is always higher than the mass number of the heaviest isotope
It is a whole number for any element with more than one isotope
A weighted mean must fall between the smallest and largest values being averaged. It is close to, but generally not equal to, the mass number of the most abundant isotope.
chem12a2-rm-23
Bromine consists of ⁷⁹Br (50.7%) and ⁸¹Br (49.3%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 79 and 81, calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine to four significant figures. (2 marks)
chem12a2-rm-24
Describe the main stages by which a mass spectrometer produces a mass spectrum of an element. (4 marks)

The sample is vaporised [1]; atoms are ionised (by electron bombardment) to form positive ions [1]; the ions are accelerated and deflected by a magnetic (or electric) field, with lighter ions deflected more than heavier ones of the same charge [1]; a detector records the ions at each m/z value, with peak height giving relative abundance [1].
chem12a2-rm-25

Potassium can be treated as consisting of two isotopes, ³⁹K and ⁴¹K, and has a relative atomic mass of 39.10. Taking the relative isotopic masses as 39 and 41, calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. (3 marks)
Let x be the fraction of ⁴¹K: 39(1 − x) + 41x = 39.10 [1]; 39 + 2x = 39.10, so x = 0.05 [1]; ⁴¹K = 5% and ³⁹K = 95% [1].
chem12a2-rm-26
State what the horizontal axis of a mass spectrum shows, and state its value for a singly charged ion of ⁶³Cu. (2 marks)
The horizontal axis shows the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of the ions [1]; for a ⁶³Cu⁺ ion, m/z = 63 [1].
chem12a2-rm-27

Neon has three isotopes: ²⁰Ne (90.5%), ²¹Ne (0.3%) and ²²Ne (9.2%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 20, 21 and 22, calculate the relative atomic mass of neon to four significant figures. (3 marks)
chem12a2-rm-28
³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl atoms have different masses but behave almost identically in chemical reactions. Explain both observations. (3 marks)

Both are isotopes of chlorine with 17 protons and 17 electrons [1]; they differ in neutron number (18 and 20), so their masses differ [1]; chemical properties depend on the electron configuration, which is the same for both [1].
chem12a2-rm-29
Rubidium consists of ⁸⁵Rb (72.2%) and ⁸⁷Rb (27.8%). Taking the relative isotopic masses as 85 and 87, the relative atomic mass of rubidium, to two decimal places, is
Ar = (85 × 72.2 + 87 × 27.8) ÷ 100 = 85.56. The simple average, 86.00, ignores the abundances, and 86.44 results from swapping the abundances.
chem12a2-rm-30
The mass spectrum of an element shows a single peak at m/z 31 for singly charged ions. Which conclusion is correct?
The element has two isotopes of masses 30 and 32.
The element has only one naturally occurring isotope.
The ions each contain 31 protons.
The sample was not ionised.

One peak means every atom has the same mass, so there is only one isotope present. Two isotopes would give two separate peaks, and the m/z value reflects the total of protons and neutrons, not protons alone.
chem12a2-rm-31
Element Q has two isotopes, ¹⁸⁴Q and ¹⁸⁶Q, and a relative atomic mass of 185.2. Taking the relative isotopic masses as 184 and 186, calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. (2 marks)
Let the abundance of ¹⁸⁴Q be x%: 185.2 = (184x + 186(100 − x)) ÷ 100 [1]; 18 520 = 18 600 − 2x, so x = 40.0, giving ¹⁸⁴Q 40.0% and ¹⁸⁶Q 60.0% [1].
chem12a2-rm-32
Explain why the sample in a mass spectrometer must be ionised and why the inside of the instrument is kept under a vacuum. (2 marks)

Only charged particles can be accelerated, deflected by the magnetic field and detected, so the atoms must be ionised [1]; a vacuum prevents the ions colliding with air particles, which would deflect them or neutralise them before they reach the detector [1].
vce-chem12-rm-c1
Boron is 19.9% ¹⁰B (isotopic mass 10.0) and 80.1% ¹¹B (isotopic mass 11.0). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.
Ar = (10.0 × 19.9 + 11.0 × 80.1) ÷ 100 = 10.8. It is closer to 11 because ¹¹B is more abundant.
vce-chem12-the-mole-and-molar-mass: How many molecules are present in 0.250 mol of carbon dioxide? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
N = n × NA = 0.250 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.51 × 10²³. 2.41 × 10²⁴ results from dividing NA by n rather than multiplying.
What is the molar mass of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂?
M = 40.1 + 2 × (14.0 + 3 × 16.0) = 40.1 + 124.0 = 164.1 g mol⁻¹. 102.1 g mol⁻¹ results from forgetting the subscript 2 outside the brackets.
Which sample contains the greatest total number of atoms?
Each of H₂O, CO₂ and CH₄ is 1.00 mol of molecules, but CH₄ has 5 atoms per molecule (5 mol of atoms) compared with 3 for H₂O and CO₂. 1.0 g of H₂ is 0.50 mol of molecules, or only 1.0 mol of atoms.
What is the mass of 0.0450 mol of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃?
How many oxygen atoms are present in 0.10 mol of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃?
Each formula unit contains 3 × 4 = 12 O atoms, so n(O) = 12 × 0.10 = 1.2 mol and N = 1.2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 7.2 × 10²³. 2.4 × 10²³ counts only the 4 O in one sulfate ion.
A sports drink contains 9.00 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. Calculate (a) the amount, in mol, of glucose and (b) the number of glucose molecules. (3 marks)
A sample of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, contains 1.20 × 10²⁴ hydrogen atoms. Calculate the mass of the ethanol sample. (3 marks)
n(H) = 1.20 × 10²⁴ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.99 mol; each ethanol molecule has 6 H atoms, so n(C₂H₅OH) = 1.99 ÷ 6 = 0.332 mol; M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.0 g mol⁻¹, so m = 0.332 × 46.0 = 15.3 g.
Define the mole, and explain why 1 mol of carbon has a mass of 12.0 g while 1 mol of magnesium has a mass of 24.3 g. (2 marks)

One mole is the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ (Avogadro's number of) specified particles; both samples contain the same number of atoms, but each magnesium atom on average has about twice the mass of a carbon atom, so the molar mass (numerically equal to Ar in grams) is larger for magnesium.
What amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide is present in 4.40 g of CO₂?
M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.40 ÷ 44.0 = 0.100 mol. 10.0 mol results from inverting the formula (M ÷ m).
What is the molar mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃?
M = 2(14.0) + 4(1.0) + 3(16.0) = 80.0 g mol⁻¹. 66.0 g mol⁻¹ counts only one nitrogen atom.
How many atoms are present in 0.500 mol of iron? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
N = n × NA = 0.500 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³. 1.20 × 10²⁴ results from dividing NA by n (6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 0.500) rather than multiplying.
What is the mass of 1.20 × 10²³ molecules of oxygen, O₂? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
n = 1.20 × 10²³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 0.199 mol, and m = 0.199 × 32.0 = 6.38 g. 3.19 g wrongly uses 16.0 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass of O atoms.
How many hydrogen atoms are present in 0.20 mol of ammonia, NH₃? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
n(H) = 3 × 0.20 = 0.60 mol, so N = 0.60 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.6 × 10²³. 1.2 × 10²³ is the number of NH₃ molecules, not H atoms.
Which sample has the greatest mass?
Masses are 18.0 g, 32.0 g, 79.8 g and 25.0 g respectively, so 0.50 mol of Fe₂O₃ (M = 159.6 g mol⁻¹) is greatest. Having the most moles (2.0 mol CH₄) does not mean the greatest mass.
What amount of chlorine atoms is present in 0.30 mol of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂?
Each formula unit contains 2 Cl, so n(Cl) = 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 mol. 0.90 mol counts all three ions or atoms in the formula.
What is the molar mass of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O?
M = 63.5 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) + 5(18.0) = 249.6 g mol⁻¹. 159.6 g mol⁻¹ is the anhydrous salt, ignoring the water of crystallisation.
What is the mass of 0.0250 mol of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃?
M = 27.0 + 3(16.0 + 1.0) = 78.0 g mol⁻¹, so m = 0.0250 × 78.0 = 1.95 g. 0.675 g uses only the mass of aluminium.
What is the total amount of atoms, in mol, in 9.0 g of water, H₂O?
n(H₂O) = 9.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.50 mol, and each molecule has 3 atoms, so n(atoms) = 1.5 mol. 0.50 mol counts molecules only.
Which statement about 1.00 mol of sodium and 1.00 mol of potassium is correct?
They have the same mass but different numbers of atoms.
They contain the same number of protons.
They contain different numbers of atoms because potassium atoms are heavier.
They contain the same number of atoms but have different masses.
One mole of any element contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, but the molar masses differ (23.0 and 39.1 g mol⁻¹). Heavier atoms do not change the number of atoms in a mole.
How many ions are present in 0.10 mol of sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
Each formula unit gives 2 Na⁺ and 1 SO₄²⁻, i.e. 3 ions, so n(ions) = 0.30 mol and N = 1.8 × 10²³. 4.2 × 10²³ counts all 7 atoms rather than 3 ions.
What is the approximate mass of a single water molecule? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
Mass of one molecule = M ÷ NA = 18.0 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.99 × 10⁻²³ g. 18.0 g is the mass of one mole, not one molecule.
What mass of nitrogen is present in 0.250 mol of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄?
Each formula unit has 2 N, so n(N) = 0.500 mol and m = 0.500 × 14.0 = 7.00 g. 3.50 g forgets the 2 N atoms per formula unit.
Calculate the mass of 0.350 mol of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. (2 marks)
Calculate the total number of atoms in 5.00 g of methane, CH₄. (3 marks)
M(CH₄) = 12.0 + 4(1.0) = 16.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 5.00 ÷ 16.0 = 0.313 mol [1]; each molecule contains 5 atoms, so n(atoms) = 5 × 0.3125 = 1.56 mol [1]; N = 1.56 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.41 × 10²³ atoms [1].
Distinguish between relative molecular mass and molar mass. (2 marks)

Relative molecular mass is the mass of a molecule relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom, so it is a ratio with no units [1]; molar mass is the mass of one mole of the substance, in g mol⁻¹, and is numerically equal to the relative molecular mass [1].
Calculate the mass of copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO₃)₂, that contains 0.600 mol of oxygen atoms. (3 marks)
Compare the number of molecules in 10.0 g of water, H₂O, with the number in 10.0 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂. Show your calculations and state which sample contains more molecules. (4 marks)

n(H₂O) = 10.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.556 mol [1]; N(H₂O) = 0.556 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.34 × 10²³ [1]; n(CO₂) = 10.0 ÷ 44.0 = 0.227 mol, so N(CO₂) = 0.227 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.37 × 10²³ [1]; the water sample contains more molecules because its molar mass is smaller [1].
A 3.20 g sample of a pure gas contains 3.01 × 10²² molecules. Calculate the molar mass of the gas and state whether it is O₂, N₂ or SO₂. (3 marks)
Calculate the number of aluminium atoms in a 1.00 kg block of aluminium. (2 marks)
Calculate the total number of ions in 2.34 g of sodium chloride, NaCl. (3 marks)
M(NaCl) = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 g mol⁻¹, so n = 2.34 ÷ 58.5 = 0.0400 mol [1]; each formula unit gives 2 ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻), so n(ions) = 0.0800 mol [1]; N = 0.0800 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 4.82 × 10²² ions [1].

A 2.86 g sample of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, is heated until all water is removed. Calculate the amount of the hydrated salt, the mass of water of crystallisation it contains, and the number of hydrogen atoms in that water. (4 marks)
What is the mass of 2.50 × 10²² molecules of nitrogen, N₂? (N = 14.0; NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
n = 2.50 × 10²² ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 0.0415 mol, and m = 0.0415 × 28.0 = 1.16 g. Using 14.0 g mol⁻¹ gives half the correct mass because N₂ molecules, not atoms, were counted.
How many oxygen atoms are in 0.50 mol of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂?
Each formula unit has 2 × 3 = 6 O atoms. n(O) = 0.50 × 6 = 3.0 mol; N = 3.0 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.8 × 10²⁴.
vce-chem12-percentage-composition-and-em: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃?
M(NH₄NO₃) = 2(14.0) + 4(1.0) + 3(16.0) = 80.0 g mol⁻¹; %N = 28.0 ÷ 80.0 × 100 = 35.0%. 17.5% counts only one of the two nitrogen atoms.
A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is:
In 100 g: C 40.0 ÷ 12.0 = 3.33 mol, H 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.7 mol, O 53.3 ÷ 16.0 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by 3.33 gives 1 : 2 : 1, so CH₂O. CHO would ignore the 2 : 1 ratio of H to C.
A hydrocarbon has the empirical formula CH₂ and a molar mass of 84.0 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is:
M(CH₂) = 14.0 g mol⁻¹ and 84.0 ÷ 14.0 = 6, so the molecular formula is (CH₂)₆ = C₆H₁₂. C₆H₁₄ has the right number of C atoms but its empirical formula is C₃H₇, not CH₂.
Which pair of compounds has the same empirical formula?
Both C₂H₂ and C₆H₆ reduce to CH. Propane (C₃H₈) and butane (empirical formula C₂H₅) have different simplest ratios even though they are in the same homologous series.

A student heated magnesium ribbon in a crucible to find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide. The calculated mole ratio Mg : O was 1 : 0.85 rather than 1 : 1. Which error best explains this result?
The magnesium ribbon was cleaned with sandpaper before weighing
The product absorbed water vapour from the air before the final weighing
Some magnesium remained unreacted at the end of heating
More oxygen was available than was needed to react with the magnesium

Unreacted magnesium means less oxygen combined, so the mass gain (and the calculated amount of O) is too low, giving a ratio below 1 : 1. Absorbing water would increase the final mass and make the O value too high, not too low.
A hydrocarbon used in the manufacture of a synthetic rubber contains 85.6% carbon and 14.4% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 56.0 g mol⁻¹. Determine its empirical and molecular formulas. (3 marks)

In 100 g: n(C) = 85.6 ÷ 12.0 = 7.13 mol and n(H) = 14.4 ÷ 1.0 = 14.4 mol; ratio 7.13 : 14.4 = 1 : 2.02 ≈ 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (M = 14.0 g mol⁻¹); 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.
A 2.50 g sample of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, was heated to constant mass, leaving 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄. Determine the value of x. (3 marks)

Haematite ore mined in Western Australia contains 80.0% Fe₂O₃ by mass. Calculate (a) the percentage by mass of iron in Fe₂O₃ and (b) the maximum mass of iron that could be extracted from 500 kg of the ore. (3 marks)
What is the percentage by mass of calcium in calcium carbonate, CaCO₃?
M(CaCO₃) = 40.1 + 12.0 + 3(16.0) = 100.1 g mol⁻¹; %Ca = 40.1 ÷ 100.1 × 100 = 40.1%. 12.0% is the percentage of carbon, not calcium.
A compound contains 32.4% sodium, 22.6% sulfur and 45.0% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is:
In 100 g: Na 32.4 ÷ 23.0 = 1.41 mol, S 22.6 ÷ 32.1 = 0.704 mol, O 45.0 ÷ 16.0 = 2.81 mol; dividing by 0.704 gives 2 : 1 : 4, so Na₂SO₄. NaSO₄ results from forgetting to scale the sodium value.
The empirical formula of a nitrogen oxide is NO₂ and its molar mass is 92.0 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is:
M(NO₂) = 46.0 g mol⁻¹ and 92.0 ÷ 46.0 = 2, so the molecular formula is (NO₂)₂ = N₂O₄. NO₂ is only the empirical formula and has a molar mass of 46.0 g mol⁻¹.
What mass of nitrogen is present in 50.0 g of urea, CO(NH₂)₂?
M(urea) = 12.0 + 16.0 + 2(14.0) + 4(1.0) = 60.0 g mol⁻¹; m(N) = 28.0 ÷ 60.0 × 50.0 = 23.3 g. 11.7 g counts only one of the two nitrogen atoms.
What is the percentage by mass of water in magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, MgSO₄·7H₂O?
M(MgSO₄·7H₂O) = 120.4 + 126.0 = 246.4 g mol⁻¹; %H₂O = 126.0 ÷ 246.4 × 100 = 51.1%. 104.7% comes from dividing by the mass of the anhydrous salt only, instead of the whole hydrate.
A sample of an aluminium oxide contains 5.40 g of aluminium combined with 4.80 g of oxygen. Its empirical formula is:
n(Al) = 5.40 ÷ 27.0 = 0.200 mol and n(O) = 4.80 ÷ 16.0 = 0.300 mol; the ratio 0.200 : 0.300 = 2 : 3 gives Al₂O₃. AlO would come from comparing the masses rather than the amounts.
Why can the formula NaCl for sodium chloride be described as an empirical formula?
Sodium chloride exists as separate NaCl molecules
Each compound contains exactly one atom of each element
The formula was found by mass spectrometry
It shows the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in the lattice
An ionic lattice has no discrete molecules, so its formula gives only the simplest ratio of ions (1 : 1). A molecule of NaCl does not exist, so the first option is incorrect.
A hydrocarbon sample contains 2.40 g of carbon and 0.600 g of hydrogen. Its empirical formula is:
n(C) = 2.40 ÷ 12.0 = 0.200 mol and n(H) = 0.600 ÷ 1.0 = 0.600 mol, a ratio of 1 : 3, so CH₃. C₂H₆ has the same ratio but is not the simplest whole-number ratio.
Which additional piece of information is needed to convert an empirical formula into a molecular formula?
The melting point of the compound
The molar mass of the compound
The state of the compound at room temperature

Dividing the molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives the whole-number multiple needed. Physical properties such as melting point or colour cannot show how many empirical units make up a molecule.
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂, and sulfur trioxide, SO₃, are both oxides of sulfur. Which statement about their sulfur content is correct?
SO₃ has the higher percentage of sulfur because it has more atoms
SO₃ has the higher percentage of sulfur because it contains more oxygen
SO₂ has the higher percentage of sulfur: 50.0% compared with 40.1%
The percentages are equal because each formula contains one sulfur atom
%S in SO₂ = 32.1 ÷ 64.1 × 100 = 50.0%, while %S in SO₃ = 32.1 ÷ 80.1 × 100 = 40.1%. The extra oxygen in SO₃ increases the total mass and so lowers the sulfur percentage.
A fertiliser is 90.0% ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, by mass. What mass of nitrogen is present in 100 kg of the fertiliser?
M((NH₄)₂SO₄) = 132.1 g mol⁻¹, so %N = 28.0 ÷ 132.1 = 21.2% and m(N) = 0.212 × 90.0 = 19.1 kg. 21.2 kg ignores that only 90.0% of the fertiliser is ammonium sulfate.
A student heated a hydrated salt but stopped before all the water had been driven off. How will this affect the calculated value of x in the formula salt·xH₂O?
x will be too low because the measured mass of water lost is too small
x will be too high because the mass of residue is too large
x will be unaffected because the ratio of water to salt is unchanged
x cannot be calculated from the results

Incomplete heating means the mass loss, and so the calculated amount of water, is too small, giving a value of x that is too low. The ratio is not unchanged because some water is still counted as part of the residue.
An iron oxide contains 70.0% iron and 30.0% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is:
n(Fe) = 70.0 ÷ 55.8 = 1.25 mol and n(O) = 30.0 ÷ 16.0 = 1.88 mol; the ratio 1 : 1.5 becomes 2 : 3, so Fe₂O₃. Fe₃O₄ would give 1 : 1.33, and FeO would give 1 : 1.
