A compound contains 54.5% carbon, 9.1% hydrogen and 36.4% oxygen by mass and has a molar mass of 88.0 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is:
Ratios of 4.54 : 9.1 : 2.28 mol give an empirical formula of C₂H₄O (44.0 g mol⁻¹); 88.0 ÷ 44.0 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈O₂. C₂H₄O is only the empirical formula.
Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃. (2 marks)
A sample of lead oxide contains 2.07 g of lead combined with 0.320 g of oxygen. Determine the empirical formula of the oxide. (3 marks)
n(Pb) = 2.07 ÷ 207 = 0.0100 mol [1]; n(O) = 0.320 ÷ 16.0 = 0.0200 mol [1]; ratio Pb : O = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is PbO₂ [1].

Complete combustion of 1.15 g of a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen produced 2.20 g of carbon dioxide and 1.35 g of water. Determine the empirical formula of the compound. (4 marks)
Hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, contains 62.9% water by mass. Determine the value of x. (3 marks)

In 100 g: m(H₂O) = 62.9 g and m(Na₂CO₃) = 37.1 g; n(H₂O) = 62.9 ÷ 18.0 = 3.49 mol [1]; M(Na₂CO₃) = 106.0 g mol⁻¹, so n(Na₂CO₃) = 37.1 ÷ 106.0 = 0.350 mol [1]; ratio H₂O : Na₂CO₃ = 3.49 ÷ 0.350 ≈ 10, so x = 10 [1].
The empirical formula of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is C₃H₄O₃ and its molar mass is 176 g mol⁻¹. Determine its molecular formula. (2 marks)
M(C₃H₄O₃) = 3(12.0) + 4(1.0) + 3(16.0) = 88.0 g mol⁻¹ [1]; 176 ÷ 88.0 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₆H₈O₆ [1].

A student determines the empirical formula of magnesium oxide by heating magnesium ribbon in a crucible. Explain why the student should (a) clean the ribbon with sandpaper before weighing and (b) heat the crucible repeatedly until constant mass is reached. (2 marks)

(a) Cleaning removes the layer of magnesium oxide already on the ribbon, so the initial mass is that of magnesium only and the mass of oxygen gained is not underestimated [1]; (b) constant mass shows that the reaction is complete and no more oxygen is being gained, so the mass of oxygen combined is accurate [1].

A 2.20 g sample of an iron sulfide contains 1.40 g of iron and the remainder is sulfur. Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the sample and determine the empirical formula of the compound. (3 marks)

A compound used as a moth repellent contains 49.0% carbon, 2.7% hydrogen and 48.3% chlorine by mass and has a molar mass of 147 g mol⁻¹. Determine its empirical formula and its molecular formula. (4 marks)

In 100 g: n(C) = 49.0 ÷ 12.0 = 4.08 mol, n(H) = 2.7 ÷ 1.0 = 2.7 mol, n(Cl) = 48.3 ÷ 35.5 = 1.36 mol [1]; dividing by 1.36 gives C : H : Cl = 3 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₃H₂Cl [1]; M(C₃H₂Cl) = 36.0 + 2.0 + 35.5 = 73.5 g mol⁻¹ [1]; 147 ÷ 73.5 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₆H₄Cl₂ [1].
When 1.35 g of aluminium reacts completely with chlorine, 6.67 g of aluminium chloride is formed. Determine the empirical formula of aluminium chloride. (Al = 27.0; Cl = 35.5) (3 marks)
Mass of chlorine = 6.67 − 1.35 = 5.32 g [1]; n(Al) = 1.35 ÷ 27.0 = 0.0500 mol and n(Cl) = 5.32 ÷ 35.5 = 0.150 mol [1]; ratio Al : Cl = 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is AlCl₃ [1].
A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g/mol. Find its empirical and molecular formulas.
Empirical formula CH₂O; molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆
Moles in 100 g: C 3.33, H 6.7, O 3.33; divide by 3.33 to get 1 : 2 : 1. M(CH₂O) = 30, and 180 ÷ 30 = 6.
vce-chem12-hydrocarbons-and-iupac-naming: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
The longest chain has 4 carbons (butane) with a methyl branch; numbering from the end nearest the branch gives the lowest locant, 2. 3-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end.
Which molecular formula could represent an alkene?
Alkenes with one C=C bond have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, which C₅H₁₀ fits. C₅H₁₂ and C₆H₁₄ fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (alkanes), and C₅H₈ fits CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (alkynes).
How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀?
Only butane (unbranched) and 2-methylpropane are possible. Drawing a 'bent' four-carbon chain does not create a new isomer, which is a common source of over-counting.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃?

The chain has 5 carbons with a C=C between C2 and C3 when numbered to give the double bond the lowest locant, so it is pent-2-ene. Pent-3-ene numbers from the wrong end; '-yne' indicates a triple bond.
The boiling points of the unbranched alkanes increase from methane to decane. This trend is best explained by:
the increasing number of covalent bonds that must be broken
the increasing strength of hydrogen bonds between molecules
the increasing polarity of the C–H bonds
the increasing strength of dispersion forces as the molecules become larger

Larger molecules have more electrons and greater surface contact, giving stronger dispersion forces that need more energy to overcome. Boiling does not break covalent bonds, and alkanes cannot hydrogen bond.
Give the IUPAC name for each of the following: (a) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, (b) CH≡CCH₂CH₃, (c) (CH₃)₃CH. (3 marks)
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane both have the formula C₅H₁₂, but their boiling points are 36 °C and 10 °C respectively. Explain this difference. (3 marks)

Both are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces are dispersion forces, and both have the same number of electrons; pentane is a linear (unbranched) molecule, so its molecules have a larger surface area of contact and can approach more closely; this gives stronger dispersion forces in pentane, needing more energy to separate the molecules, hence a higher boiling point than the compact, spherical 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Propane is the main component of LPG. (a) Write a balanced equation, with states at SLC, for the complete combustion of propane. (b) A student names a compound 3-methylbutane. Explain the error and give the correct name. (3 marks)
(a) C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l); (b) the chain should be numbered from the end that gives the branch the lowest locant; the correct name is 2-methylbutane.
What is the molecular formula of an alkane with 7 carbon atoms?
Alkanes follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so n = 7 gives C₇H₁₆. C₇H₁₄ is the formula of an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ).
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
The longest chain has 5 carbons (pentane) with a methyl branch on carbon 3. Naming it 2-ethylbutane picks a chain that is not the longest.
Which of the following is a saturated hydrocarbon?
C₃H₈ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so it contains only C–C single bonds and is saturated. C₂H₄ and C₂H₂ contain C=C and C≡C bonds respectively, and C₄H₆ is also unsaturated.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₃?
The chain has 5 carbons and a triple bond between C2 and C3 when numbered from the nearest end, giving pent-2-yne. Pent-3-yne numbers from the wrong end.
Propane has 3 carbons, and two methyl groups on carbon 2 give a central carbon bonded to four CH₃ groups, C(CH₃)₄. The first option is pentane and the second is 2-methylbutane.
How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of but-2-yne?
But-2-yne is CH₃C≡CCH₃, C₄H₆, fitting CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for alkynes. Eight hydrogens would be butene and ten would be butane.
Which pair of compounds are structural isomers of each other?
Both but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene are C₄H₈ with different arrangements of atoms. Butane (C₄H₁₀) and but-1-ene (C₄H₈) have different molecular formulas, so they are not isomers.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃?
The longest chain is butane, with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 3. 2-methylpentane would have only one branch and a 5-carbon chain.
Cyclohexane and hex-1-ene are best described as:
members of the same homologous series
Both have the formula C₆H₁₂ but different structures (a ring versus a chain with C=C), so they are structural isomers. They are in different homologous series, so they cannot be homologues.
Which statement about the forces between hexane molecules in the liquid state is correct?
Hydrogen bonds form between C–H groups.
Only dispersion forces act between the molecules.
Strong dipole–dipole forces act because C–H bonds are polar.
Covalent bonds form between neighbouring molecules.
Hexane is non-polar, so only weak dispersion forces act between its molecules. Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O or F, which hexane does not have.
Which unbranched alkane is a liquid at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa)?
Hexane has a boiling point of about 69 °C and so is a liquid at 25 °C. Ethane, propane and butane have boiling points below 25 °C and are gases.
Which set of products could form from the incomplete combustion of methane?
With limited oxygen, carbon monoxide (or carbon) forms along with water. Carbon dioxide and water only are the products of complete combustion.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?

The longest chain containing C=C has 4 carbons, with the double bond at C1 and a methyl on C2. 3-methylbut-1-ene places the branch on the wrong carbon, and a double bond at C3 does not give the lowest locant.
Distinguish between a saturated and an unsaturated hydrocarbon, giving one example of each. (2 marks)
Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single C–C bonds, e.g. propane [1]; unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one C=C or C≡C bond, e.g. ethene [1].
State the general formula for each of the following homologous series: alkanes, alkenes (one C=C) and alkynes (one C≡C). (3 marks)
Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ [1]; alkenes CₙH₂ₙ [1]; alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ [1].
Give the IUPAC name for each of the following: (a) CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, (b) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃, (c) CH₃C≡CCH₃. (3 marks)
Write a condensed structural formula for each of the following: (a) 2-methylbut-2-ene, (b) 3-methylpent-1-yne. (2 marks)
Hexane does not dissolve in water. Explain why in terms of intermolecular forces. (3 marks)

Hexane is non-polar and has only weak dispersion forces between its molecules [1]; water molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonds [1]; the forces that hexane could form with water are much weaker than the hydrogen bonds that would be broken, so hexane does not dissolve [1].
Propane burns completely in excess oxygen: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l). Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 11.0 g of propane burns completely. (3 marks)
Describe a simple test that distinguishes but-1-ene from butane, including the observations for each. (3 marks)

Add bromine water (a few drops, shaking) to a sample of each [1]; but-1-ene decolourises the orange-brown bromine water quickly because it is unsaturated [1]; butane causes no colour change in the dark because it is saturated [1].
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃?
The longest chain has six carbons, and numbering from the end nearer the branch places the methyl group on carbon 3. Numbering from the other end would give 4-methylhexane, which has a higher locant.
How many moles of oxygen are needed for the complete combustion of 1 mol of but-1-ene, C₄H₈?
C₄H₈ + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 4H₂O. The 4 CO₂ need 8 O atoms and the 4 H₂O need 4 O atoms, a total of 12 O atoms, which is 6 mol of O₂.

Ethane burns completely in oxygen: 2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l). Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, at SLC, produced by burning 5.00 g of ethane. (C = 12.0; H = 1.0; molar volume at SLC = 24.8 L mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
The correct IUPAC name for CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃ is:
The longest chain has 4 carbons (butane). Number from the end nearer the branches: two methyl groups on C2.
vce-chem12-functional-groups-and-homolog: Which functional group is present in ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH?
Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH (a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon). Although an –OH is present, the compound is not classified as an alcohol.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
It is a three-carbon alcohol with the –OH on carbon 1, so propan-1-ol. Propan-2-ol would have the –OH on the middle carbon, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.
Which statement about the members of a homologous series is correct?
They all have the same molecular formula
They all have the same boiling point
They are structural isomers of one another
Successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit and have similar chemical properties

A homologous series shares a general formula and functional group, with successive members differing by CH₂; their physical properties (e.g. boiling point) change gradually. Isomers have the same molecular formula, which homologues do not.
Chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, has a halogen atom replacing a hydrogen in an alkane. CH₃OH is an alcohol and CH₃COOH is a carboxylic acid.
The following compounds have similar molar masses. Which has the highest boiling point?

Propan-1-ol molecules can form hydrogen bonds through their –OH group, which are much stronger than the dipole–dipole and dispersion forces in chloroethane or the dispersion forces in butane. Chloroethane has the highest molar mass but no hydrogen bonding.
Explain why ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, is miscible with water but ethane, CH₃CH₃, is almost insoluble in water. (3 marks)

Ethanol has a polar –OH group with H bonded to highly electronegative O; it can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, which release enough energy to compensate for breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules, so ethanol mixes with water; ethane is non-polar with only dispersion forces, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and would disrupt the water hydrogen-bond network without compensating attractions, so it does not dissolve.

The alkanols (primary alcohols) form a homologous series with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, starting with methanol. Give the molecular formula and molar mass of the fifth member of the series. (2 marks)
Fifth member has n = 5: pentan-1-ol, C₅H₁₁OH (C₅H₁₂O); M = 5(12.0) + 12(1.0) + 16.0 = 88.0 g mol⁻¹.
For each compound, name the functional group present and give the IUPAC name of the compound: (a) CH₃CH₂COOH, (b) CH₃CHBrCH₃, (c) CH₂=CHCH₃. (3 marks)
(a) carboxyl group, propanoic acid; (b) bromo (halo) group, 2-bromopropane; (c) carbon–carbon double bond, propene (prop-1-ene).
Which functional group is present in methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃?
Methyl ethanoate has a C=O bonded to an O that is itself bonded to a carbon chain, which is the ester linkage, –COO–. A carboxyl group would have a hydrogen on that oxygen (–COOH).
Which molecular formula could represent an acyclic alkene with one carbon–carbon double bond?
Alkenes with one C=C have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, so five carbons gives C₅H₁₀. C₅H₁₂ fits an alkane (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂), and C₅H₈ has too few hydrogens for one double bond.
Which functional group is present in ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂?
Amines contain the amino group, –NH₂, bonded to a carbon chain. An amide would also have a C=O attached to the nitrogen, which ethylamine does not have.
Which pair of compounds belongs to the same homologous series?
Methanol and ethanol are both alkanols and differ by one –CH₂– unit. Ethanol and ethanoic acid have the same number of carbons but different functional groups, so they are in different series.
Which statement best explains why the boiling points of the alkanes increase from methane to decane?
The covalent C–C bonds become stronger
Hydrogen bonds form between the molecules
Dispersion forces increase as the molecules have more electrons

Alkanes are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces are dispersion forces, which strengthen as molecular size and electron number increase. Covalent bonds are not broken when a molecular substance boils.
What is the molar mass of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH? (C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0)
Propanoic acid is C₃H₆O₂, so M = 3(12.0) + 6(1.0) + 2(16.0) = 74.0 g mol⁻¹. 60.0 g mol⁻¹ is the value for ethanoic acid, which has one fewer carbon.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH?
The chain has four carbons including the carboxyl carbon, so the name is butanoic acid. Propanoic acid has three carbons, and butan-1-ol is an alcohol with an –OH group instead.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH?

The longest chain containing the carbon bonded to –OH has three carbons, with the –OH on carbon 1 and a methyl branch on carbon 2. Butan-1-ol has an unbranched four-carbon chain, so it is a different isomer.
What is the molecular formula of hexanoic acid?
Hexanoic acid is CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH, which has six carbons, twelve hydrogens and two oxygens. C₅H₁₀O₂ is pentanoic acid, which has one fewer carbon.
What is the IUPAC name of BrCH₂CH₂Br?
There is one bromine on each of the two carbons, so the locants are 1 and 2 and the prefix is di-. 1,1-dibromoethane would have both bromines on the same carbon.
Which two functional groups are present in aminoethanoic acid, H₂NCH₂COOH?
The molecule has an –NH₂ amino group and a –COOH carboxyl group. It has no C=O bonded to the nitrogen, so it does not contain an amide group.
Write the structural formulas and IUPAC names of the two structural isomers with molecular formula C₃H₇Cl. (2 marks)
An alkane contains 22 hydrogen atoms per molecule. Determine its molecular formula and name. (2 marks)
General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so 2n + 2 = 22 and n = 10, giving C₁₀H₂₂ [1]; the name is decane [1].
Describe how the structures of an alkane and an alkene differ, and how bromine water could be used to distinguish between hexane and hex-1-ene. (3 marks)

Alkanes contain only C–C single bonds whereas alkenes contain a C=C double bond [1]; hex-1-ene decolourises the orange/brown bromine water [1]; hexane does not react so the bromine water stays orange/brown [1].
Explain why butane (boiling point −1 °C) has a higher boiling point than propane (boiling point −42 °C). (2 marks)
Both are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces are dispersion forces [1]; butane has more electrons (larger molecules), so stronger dispersion forces that require more energy to overcome [1].
The compound HOCH₂CH₂COOH contains two functional groups. Name each group and give its formula. (2 marks)
Calculate the molar mass of 1-chlorobutane and the percentage by mass of chlorine in it. (C = 12.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5) (3 marks)
Methyl propanoate has the structural formula CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. Name its functional group and state the names of the alkanol and carboxylic acid from which it can be made. (3 marks)
Ester group, –COO– [1]; carboxylic acid is propanoic acid [1]; alkanol is methanol [1].
Explain why the solubility of the primary alkanols in water decreases as the length of the carbon chain increases, with reference to methanol and decan-1-ol. (3 marks)

The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water, so methanol, with a small non-polar part, mixes with water [1]; decan-1-ol has a long non-polar hydrocarbon chain that forms only dispersion forces with water [1]; the energy released by hydrogen bonding is not enough to disrupt the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, so decan-1-ol is insoluble [1].
The general formula for the alkanoic (carboxylic) acids, where n is the number of carbon atoms, is
Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, and propanoic acid, C₃H₆O₂, both fit CₙH₂ₙO₂. CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH is the formula of the alkanols.
Which compound is a structural isomer of butanoic acid, C₃H₇COOH?
Both butanoic acid and methyl propanoate have the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ but different functional groups. Methyl ethanoate is C₃H₆O₂, pentanoic acid is C₅H₁₀O₂ and butan-1-ol is C₄H₁₀O.
Give the IUPAC name and name the functional group of each compound: (a) CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH₃ and (b) CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. (2 marks)
(a) 2-chlorobutane, a haloalkane (chloro group, –Cl) [1]; (b) pentan-3-ol, an alkanol (hydroxyl group, –OH) [1].
Methylamine, CH₃NH₂ (boiling point −6 °C), has a much higher boiling point than ethane, CH₃CH₃ (boiling point −89 °C), although their molar masses are almost the same. Explain why. (2 marks)

Methylamine has an N–H group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, whereas ethane molecules are held together only by weak dispersion forces [1]; more energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds, so methylamine has the higher boiling point [1].
The molecular formula of the carboxylic acid with five carbon atoms (pentanoic acid) is:
Carboxylic acids follow CₙH₂ₙO₂ (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH with n − 1 carbons in the chain). C₅H₁₂O is an alcohol.
vce-chem12-addition-polymers: Which structural feature must a monomer have to undergo addition polymerisation?

In addition polymerisation one bond of the C=C breaks, allowing monomers to join into a chain with no other product. A halogen atom alone is not enough; chloroethene polymerises because of its C=C, not its Cl.
Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, is polymerised to form PVC. Which represents the repeating unit of the polymer?
The C=C opens and each monomer contributes a –CH₂–CHCl– unit with only single bonds in the chain. –CH=CCl– wrongly retains a double bond and has lost hydrogen.
A polymer has the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Its monomer is:
Restoring the C=C between the two chain carbons gives CH₂=CHCH₃, propene. Propane has no double bond, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation.
High-density polyethene (HDPE) has a higher density and softening temperature than low-density polyethene (LDPE). The best explanation is that HDPE:
is made from a different monomer
has little chain branching, so chains pack closely and have stronger dispersion forces between them
has hydrogen bonds between its chains

Both are made from ethene; HDPE chains are largely unbranched, so they align closely in crystalline regions, increasing density and the strength of dispersion forces. Polyethene has no cross-links and no hydrogen bonding.
A sample of polyethene has an average molar mass of 2.80 × 10⁵ g mol⁻¹. On average, how many ethene monomer units are in each chain?
M(C₂H₄) = 28.0 g mol⁻¹, and 2.80 × 10⁵ ÷ 28.0 = 1.00 × 10⁴. Because no atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, the chain mass is simply the number of units × 28.0.

Polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE) is used to coat non-stick frying pans. Give the structural formula of its monomer, the structure of its repeating unit, and explain why its formation is classified as addition polymerisation. (3 marks)

Monomer is tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂; repeating unit is –CF₂–CF₂–; the C=C double bond of each monomer breaks and monomers join end to end with no other product (no small molecule such as water is lost), so it is addition polymerisation.
Explain why a sample of polyethene with very long chains has a higher softening temperature than a sample with much shorter chains. (2 marks)

Longer chains have more electrons and greater contact area between chains, so the dispersion forces between chains are stronger in total; more energy is needed for the chains to slide past each other, so the polymer softens at a higher temperature.
Polystyrene is made from styrene (phenylethene), C₆H₅CH=CH₂. Write an equation showing n monomers forming the polymer, and state one property of polystyrene that relates to its structure. (3 marks)

n CH₂=CH(C₆H₅) → –[CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)]ₙ–; the repeating unit shows the double bond opened and a benzene ring (phenyl group) on every second carbon; e.g. it is rigid/brittle at room temperature because the bulky phenyl groups restrict chain movement (or it is a thermoplastic that softens on heating because there are no cross-links).
Which statement about the products of addition polymerisation of ethene is correct?
The polymer is the only product; no small molecule is released
Water is released for every bond formed
Hydrogen gas is released as the chain grows
Carbon dioxide is released as a by-product
The C=C of each monomer opens and the monomers join directly, so all atoms end up in the polymer. Release of water is characteristic of condensation polymerisation, not addition polymerisation.
Which of the following compounds could NOT be used as a monomer in addition polymerisation?
Hexane is a saturated alkane with only single bonds, so there is no C=C to open. The others each contain a C=C, even though they carry halogen atoms or a methyl group.
What is the systematic name of the monomer used to make PVC?
PVC is made from CH₂=CHCl, which is chloroethene (one chlorine on an ethene skeleton). Chloroethane is saturated and cannot polymerise by addition.
14.0 g of ethene is completely converted into polyethene by addition polymerisation. What is the mass of polyethene formed?

No atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, so mass is conserved and the polymer has the same mass as the monomer used. Doubling to 28.0 g would wrongly use the molar mass instead of the sample mass.
In the radical addition polymerisation of ethene, the role of the initiator is to:
supply the hydrogen atoms needed for the chain
produce a reactive radical that attacks the C=C and starts the chain
The initiator breaks down to form radicals, and a radical reacts with the C=C of a monomer to begin chain growth. It does not become a cross-linking agent or supply extra atoms to the chain.
Polyethene softens and can be moulded when heated. This is because:
the covalent bonds along each chain break at low temperatures
the C=C bonds reform on heating
ionic lattices in the polymer collapse
the weak dispersion forces between chains are overcome while the covalent bonds within chains stay intact

Heating supplies enough energy to overcome the intermolecular forces so chains can move past each other. The strong C–C covalent bonds along the chain are not broken, and there are no C=C bonds left in the polymer.
Acrylonitrile (propenenitrile), CH₂=CH–CN, is polymerised by addition polymerisation. Which represents its repeating unit?
The C=C opens, leaving a –CH₂–CH(CN)– unit with the CN group as a side group on every second carbon. A repeating unit containing C=C is wrong because the polymer chain is fully saturated.
A polyethene chain contains 500 ethene monomer units. How many carbon atoms are in its backbone?
Each ethene unit contributes two carbon atoms to the chain, so 500 × 2 = 1000. Counting one carbon per unit confuses the monomer with the number of carbon atoms it supplies.
Which equation correctly represents the formation of polyethene?
All atoms of the monomer end up in the saturated polymer, so there is no second product. Equations that release H₂ wrongly treat the reaction as one that loses small molecules.
PVC is harder and has a higher softening temperature than polyethene of similar chain length. The best explanation is that PVC has:
a higher number of C=C bonds in each chain
hydrogen bonds between the Cl atoms of neighbouring chains
polar C–Cl bonds, giving dipole–dipole forces in addition to dispersion forces between chains

The C–Cl bonds are polar, adding dipole–dipole attractions to the dispersion forces and so making the chains harder to separate. Cl bonded to carbon cannot form hydrogen bonds, and PVC chains contain no C=C bonds.
Aqueous bromine is added to a sample of polyethene and to a sample of ethene. What is observed?
The polyethene does not decolourise the bromine, but ethene does
Ethene has a C=C that reacts with bromine, decolourising it. In polyethene the C=C bonds were consumed during polymerisation, so the chain is saturated and does not react.
But-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, undergoes addition polymerisation. Which is its repeating unit?
Only the two carbons of the C=C form the chain backbone, and the remaining ethyl group becomes a side group. Putting all four carbons in the backbone ignores that the side group stays attached.
Discarded polyethene bags persist in the environment for a very long time. The best reason is that:
they dissolve to form toxic acids
the polymer contains many C=C bonds that are unreactive
its strong, non-polar saturated C–C and C–H backbone is not readily broken down by microorganisms
it reacts with oxygen to form a stable oxide layer
The saturated non-polar backbone of strong covalent bonds resists chemical attack and microbial breakdown. Polyethene does not contain C=C bonds, so this cannot be the cause.
Define the terms 'monomer' and 'polymer', and state what type of bond in the monomer allows addition polymerisation. (3 marks)

A monomer is a small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer [1]. A polymer is a very large molecule made of many repeating units joined together [1]. Addition polymerisation requires a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) in the monomer [1].
Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, is polymerised to form polypropene. Write the equation for the formation of the polymer from n monomer molecules, showing the repeating unit. (2 marks)
n CH₂=CH(CH₃) → –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ– [1] with the double bond opened and a methyl group on every second carbon of the chain, with no other product formed [1].
A sample of poly(vinyl chloride) has 2500 repeating units per chain. Calculate the molar mass of the polymer, in g mol⁻¹. (C = 12.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5) (3 marks)
Repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl– (same formula as chloroethene, C₂H₃Cl) [1]. M(C₂H₃Cl) = 2 × 12.0 + 3 × 1.0 + 35.5 = 62.5 g mol⁻¹ [1]. M(polymer) = 2500 × 62.5 = 1.56 × 10⁵ g mol⁻¹ [1].

5.60 kg of ethene is completely polymerised into polyethene. Calculate (a) the mass of polyethene formed and (b) the amount, in mol, of polymer chains if each chain contains 4.00 × 10³ ethene units. (M(C₂H₄) = 28.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)

(a) No atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, so mass of polyethene = 5.60 kg [1]. (b) n(C₂H₄) = 5600 ÷ 28.0 = 200 mol [1]; each chain uses 4.00 × 10³ monomer units, so n(chains) = 200 ÷ 4.00 × 10³ [1] = 0.0500 mol [1].
A polymer has the repeating unit –CH₂–CCl₂–. Which compound is its monomer?
Opening the C=C bond of CH₂=CCl₂ gives a chain of –CH₂–CCl₂– units. CHCl=CHCl would give –CHCl–CHCl– units, with one chlorine on each carbon.
A sample of polypropene has an average of 1500 repeating units per chain. What is its approximate average molar mass? (C₃H₆ = 42.0 g mol⁻¹)
Each repeating unit has the same formula as the monomer, C₃H₆, so M = 1500 × 42.0 = 6.30 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹. The value 4.20 × 10⁴ comes from using 28.0 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass of ethene.
The addition polymerisation of a single alkene monomer has an atom economy of 100%. This is because:
a catalyst is used, so no waste forms
all atoms in the monomers end up in the single polymer product
the polymer produced has a very high molar mass
Only one product forms and no small molecule is lost, so every reactant atom is incorporated into the polymer. A high molar mass or an exothermic reaction does not determine atom economy.
What is the percentage by mass of chlorine in PVC, (–CH₂–CHCl–)ₙ? (C = 12.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5)

The repeating unit C₂H₃Cl has M = 2 × 12.0 + 3 × 1.0 + 35.5 = 62.5, so the percentage is 35.5 ÷ 62.5 × 100 = 56.8%. The value 73.2% comes from leaving out one carbon and two hydrogens from the repeating unit.
Chloroethene is the monomer used to make PVC. Draw or describe a section of PVC containing three repeating units, and explain why the polymer chain contains no C=C double bonds. (3 marks)

The section is –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl– (three –CH₂–CHCl– units joined end to end) [1]; during polymerisation one bond of the C=C in each monomer breaks [1]; the freed electrons form new single bonds to neighbouring monomers, so the backbone contains only C–C single bonds [1].

A sample of PVC has an average molar mass of 1.25 × 10⁵ g mol⁻¹. The repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl–, with M = 62.5 g mol⁻¹. Calculate the average number of repeating units per chain and the number of carbon atoms in the backbone of an average chain. (2 marks)
Number of repeating units = 1.25 × 10⁵ ÷ 62.5 = 2.00 × 10³ [1]; each unit contributes two backbone carbon atoms, so 2 × 2.00 × 10³ = 4.00 × 10³ carbon atoms [1].
Which monomer forms a polymer with the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–?
Addition polymerisation opens the C=C bond. Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, gives polypropene. Propane has no double bond.
vce-chem12-thermoplastics-thermosets-and: chem12a2-tt-1
Which statement best describes the structure and behaviour of a thermoplastic?
Chains are joined by many covalent cross-links, so it chars rather than melts
It is a three-dimensional covalent network lattice
It contains ionic bonds between chains that break when heated
Chains are held together only by intermolecular forces, so it softens on heating and can be remoulded
Heating a thermoplastic overcomes the relatively weak intermolecular forces between chains, letting them slide and be reshaped. The cross-linked description in option A is a thermoset.
chem12a2-tt-2
Which feature distinguishes a thermosetting polymer from a thermoplastic?
It has a lower average molar mass
It has extensive covalent cross-links between polymer chains
It is always made from renewable raw materials
It can only be made by addition polymerisation

Covalent cross-links lock thermoset chains in place, so heating cannot make them flow; strong heating eventually breaks covalent bonds and the material decomposes. Raw material source does not define thermosets.
chem12a2-tt-3
Which practice best reflects the principles of a circular economy for plastics?
Burning all plastic waste in landfill gas flares
Producing single-use packaging that is thinner and cheaper
Designing products so their materials can be reused, repaired or recycled and kept in use for as long as possible
Exporting plastic waste overseas for disposal
A circular economy aims to design out waste and keep materials in use. The other options follow the linear 'take–make–dispose' model or simply move waste elsewhere.
chem12a2-tt-4
Which polymer is commonly produced from a renewable feedstock such as corn starch or sugarcane?
Polylactic acid (PLA)
Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
Polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE)
Polystyrene
PLA is made from lactic acid obtained by fermenting plant sugars, and is compostable under industrial conditions. PVC, PTFE and polystyrene are normally made from fossil fuel-derived monomers.
chem12a2-tt-5
Why can a thermoset such as cured epoxy resin not be recycled by melting and remoulding?
It is too dense to be shredded
It dissolves in water when heated
It contains no carbon
Its covalent cross-links prevent the chains from flowing, and heating strongly enough to break them decomposes the polymer
Melting requires chains to move past each other, which cross-links prevent; the material chars instead. Thermosets are carbon-based and do not dissolve in water.
chem12a2-tt-6
Compare the linear economy and the circular economy models as they apply to plastic drink bottles made of PET. (3 marks)

In a linear economy, fossil fuels are extracted to make PET, bottles are used once and then sent to landfill or become litter (take–make–dispose); in a circular economy, bottles are designed for recovery, collected (e.g. through container deposit schemes) and mechanically or chemically recycled into new bottles; this reduces demand for new raw materials, energy use and waste, keeping the material in use for longer.
chem12a2-tt-7
A car's brake pads contain a thermosetting resin. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why the resin does not soften when the brakes become very hot. (3 marks)

The resin chains are joined by covalent cross-links forming a rigid three-dimensional network; heating gives the chains energy, but the strong covalent cross-links prevent them from sliding past one another, so the material does not soften or melt; only at very high temperatures do covalent bonds break, causing decomposition (charring) rather than melting.
chem12a2-tt-8

Polyethene can be made from ethene obtained by dehydrating ethanol fermented from sugarcane ('bio-PE'). Explain why bio-PE is described as bio-based but not biodegradable, and state one environmental advantage it still offers. (3 marks)

Bio-based means the carbon comes from a renewable biological feedstock (sugarcane); however, bio-PE is chemically identical to fossil-derived polyethene, so microorganisms cannot readily break it down and it is not biodegradable; an advantage is that it reduces use of finite fossil fuels, and the CO₂ absorbed by the sugarcane during growth can offset some of the emissions (and it can be recycled with ordinary PE).
chem12a2-tt-9
Which of the following polymers is a thermoplastic?
Bakelite
Polyethene
Vulcanised rubber
Melamine–formaldehyde resin

Polyethene consists of separate chains held together by dispersion forces, so it softens on heating and can be remoulded. Bakelite, vulcanised rubber and melamine–formaldehyde are cross-linked thermosets.
chem12a2-tt-10
Natural rubber is vulcanised by heating it with sulfur. What does this process do to the rubber?
Breaks the polymer chains into monomers
Replaces the carbon–carbon double bonds with ionic bonds
Forms covalent sulfur cross-links between the polymer chains
Increases the length of each chain without joining them
Sulfur atoms form covalent bridges between neighbouring chains, making the rubber stronger and more elastic. The chains are joined to each other rather than broken apart or simply lengthened.
chem12a2-tt-11
Why is a thermoplastic such as high-density polyethene (HDPE) well suited to mechanical recycling?
It can be shredded, melted and reshaped because there are no covalent cross-links between its chains
It decomposes to its monomers when heated gently
It dissolves in water so impurities can be removed
It contains ionic bonds that can be broken by sorting
Only weak intermolecular forces hold the chains together, so heating lets the chains flow and be remoulded. HDPE does not depolymerise or dissolve in water on gentle heating.
chem12a2-tt-12
A manufacturer increases the extent of cross-linking in a polymer. Which change in properties is most likely?
It becomes more flexible and has a lower melting point
It becomes more soluble in non-polar solvents
Its average molar mass of individual chains decreases
It becomes harder and more rigid and is less able to soften on heating
More covalent cross-links restrict movement of the chains, giving a harder, more rigid material that resists softening. Greater flexibility and easier softening are features of fewer cross-links.
chem12a2-tt-13
In the waste hierarchy that underpins a circular economy, which action is the most preferred?
Recycling the material into new products
Reducing consumption so that less waste is created
Recovering energy by burning the waste
Disposing of the waste in landfill
Avoiding and reducing waste at the source is the top priority because no material or energy is needed to process it. Recycling is better than disposal but ranks below reduction and reuse.
chem12a2-tt-14
Which process describes chemical recycling of a condensation polymer such as PET?
Breaking the polymer down into its monomers or small molecules that are used to make new polymer
Melting the polymer and moulding it into a new shape
Burning the polymer to generate electricity
Burying the polymer so that microorganisms degrade it
Chemical recycling breaks bonds in the polymer (for example by hydrolysis) to recover monomers for repolymerisation. Melting and remoulding is mechanical recycling, and burning is energy recovery.
chem12a2-tt-15
Which statement correctly describes a biodegradable polymer?
It is always made from renewable plant materials
It cannot be recycled by any method
It is guaranteed to break down in landfill within a few months
It can be broken down by microorganisms into substances such as carbon dioxide, water and biomass

Biodegradability refers to breakdown by microorganisms, and depends on the polymer's structure and conditions, not its raw material. Some bio-based polymers are not biodegradable, and some biodegradable polymers come from fossil fuels.
chem12a2-tt-16
A plastic sample softens when heated and hardens again on cooling, and this can be repeated many times. What can be concluded?
It is a thermoset with extensive cross-linking
It is a thermoplastic with no extensive covalent cross-links between chains
It is a covalent network lattice
It is an ionic compound
Repeated softening and hardening shows the chains can move past each other when heated, so they are not covalently cross-linked. A cross-linked thermoset would char rather than soften.
chem12a2-tt-17
Which polymer type is most suitable for the handle of a saucepan that regularly gets hot?
A thermoset, because its cross-links stop it softening
A thermoplastic with a low melting point, because it is easily moulded
A thermoplastic, because its chains can slide to absorb heat
A biodegradable polymer, because it can be composted
A thermoset keeps its shape at high temperature because covalent cross-links hold the chains in place. A low-melting thermoplastic would soften and deform.
chem12a2-tt-18
How does a container deposit scheme support a circular economy?
It makes containers thinner so they use less plastic
It encourages burning of used containers for energy
It encourages return of used containers, providing a collected, relatively clean stream of material for recycling
It prevents any containers from being manufactured
A refundable deposit gives people an incentive to return containers, so they are collected and recycled rather than littered or landfilled. Burning is lower on the waste hierarchy than recycling.
chem12a2-tt-19
A recycling facility receives 250 t of PET bottles and produces 180 t of reusable recycled PET. What percentage of the PET was recovered?
Recovery = 180 ÷ 250 × 100 = 72%. The 28% figure is the proportion lost, and 139% results from dividing the wrong way round.
chem12a2-tt-20
Why must plastics generally be sorted by type before mechanical recycling?
Different polymers have different melting points and mix poorly, so a mixture gives a weak, inconsistent product
All plastics have the same density, so they cannot be separated otherwise
Sorting converts thermosets into thermoplastics
Sorting removes the carbon from the polymers
Different polymers melt at different temperatures and are often immiscible, so blends have poor properties. Plastics differ in density, and sorting does not change their chemical structure.
chem12a2-tt-21
What type of force mainly holds the polymer chains together in polyethene, allowing it to soften on heating?
Covalent cross-links
Dispersion forces
Ionic bonds
Hydrogen bonds

Polyethene chains are non-polar hydrocarbons, so only weak dispersion forces act between them. Covalent cross-links are found in thermosets, and polyethene has no O–H or N–H groups for hydrogen bonding.
chem12a2-tt-22
Why is burning waste plastic with energy recovery considered less desirable than recycling it in a circular economy?
It cannot release any energy
It only works for thermosets
It produces only water as a product
It destroys the material, so new raw materials are needed, and releases carbon dioxide from the carbon in the plastic
Combustion recovers some energy but the material is lost and CO₂ is released, whereas recycling keeps material in use. Plastics do release energy when burned, so that is not the drawback.
chem12a2-tt-23
Polyethene bags can be recycled by melting, but a vulcanised rubber tyre cannot. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding. (3 marks)

Polyethene is a thermoplastic whose chains are held together only by weak dispersion forces [1]; heating overcomes these forces so the chains can slide and the material can be melted and remoulded [1]; vulcanised rubber has covalent sulfur cross-links between chains, which hold the chains in place, so it cannot melt and decomposes when heated strongly [1].
chem12a2-tt-24
Distinguish between mechanical recycling and chemical recycling of PET. (3 marks)

Mechanical recycling involves sorting, cleaning, shredding and melting the PET so that it can be reshaped into new products without changing the polymer chemically [1]; chemical recycling breaks the polymer into monomers or small molecules (e.g. by hydrolysis) which are purified and repolymerised [1]; chemical recycling can give material equal in quality to new PET, whereas mechanical recycling often gives a lower-quality product because chains shorten and contaminants build up [1].
chem12a2-tt-25
Place the following in order from most preferred to least preferred in the waste hierarchy and justify the order: landfill, recycling, reducing consumption. (3 marks)

Order: reducing consumption, then recycling, then landfill [1]; reducing consumption is best because less material and energy is used and no waste is created [1]; recycling keeps materials in use and saves raw materials, whereas landfill loses the material permanently and uses land [1].
chem12a2-tt-26
A sorting plant receives 12.0 t of mixed plastic waste, of which 65% is PET. The plant recovers 70% of the PET as reusable material. Calculate the mass of PET recovered. (3 marks)
Mass of PET in waste = 0.65 × 12.0 [1] = 7.80 t [1]; mass recovered = 0.70 × 7.80 = 5.46 t [1].
chem12a2-tt-27
A company makes yoghurt tubs from a cross-linked thermosetting polymer. Suggest a change that would improve the recyclability of the tubs and justify it. (2 marks)
Make the tubs from a thermoplastic such as polypropene or PET instead [1]; a thermoplastic can be melted and remoulded because it has no covalent cross-links, so it can be mechanically recycled [1].
chem12a2-tt-28
Polylactic acid (PLA) is biodegradable, yet PLA cups sent to landfill often persist for years. Explain why, and state the advantage of sending them to industrial composting instead. (2 marks)

Landfill is cool and has little oxygen and moisture, so conditions are unsuitable for the microorganisms that degrade PLA, which needs the high temperatures and moisture of industrial composting [1]; composting allows PLA to break down into carbon dioxide, water and biomass, which can be returned to soil rather than being buried [1].
chem12a2-tt-29
Define the term 'downcycling' and explain why mechanical recycling of plastics often leads to it. (3 marks)

Downcycling is recycling a material into a product of lower quality or value than the original [1]; during melting and reprocessing, polymer chains can shorten and impurities or mixed polymers contaminate the plastic [1]; this reduces strength and clarity, so the material is used for less demanding products such as park benches rather than new food-grade bottles [1].
chem12a2-tt-30
Evaluate a container deposit scheme as a way of moving towards a circular economy for plastic drink bottles. Give two benefits and one limitation. (4 marks)

Benefit: the refund encourages people to return bottles, increasing collection rates and reducing litter and landfill [1]; benefit: returned bottles form a clean, single-type stream that is easier to recycle into food-grade material, reducing demand for new fossil-fuel-based PET [1]; limitation: it covers only certain containers and relies on consumer participation, and collection and transport cost energy and money [1]; overall it keeps materials in use for longer but should be combined with reduction and reuse strategies [1].
chem12a2-tt-31
Which process is an example of mechanical recycling of a thermoplastic such as HDPE?
Heating it with strong acid to regenerate the monomers
Burning it in an incinerator to generate electricity
Sorting, shredding, melting and remoulding the plastic into new items
Burying it in landfill so that it slowly breaks down

Mechanical recycling reshapes the polymer without changing its chemical structure, which works because heating weakens the intermolecular forces between chains. Burning recovers energy but does not keep the material in use.
vce-chem12-tt-c1
Why can thermoplastics be melted and remoulded, but thermosets cannot?
Thermoplastics have stronger covalent bonds within their chains, so they do not char when heated
Thermosets have covalent cross-links between chains; thermoplastics have only weak forces between chains
Thermosets are made from smaller monomers, so their chains are too short to flow when melted
Thermoplastics contain ions between their chains, which become mobile when the plastic is heated
Heating overcomes the weak intermolecular forces in thermoplastics. Thermosets char instead, which makes them harder to recycle in a circular economy.
vce-chem12-properties-of-water-and-hydro: chem12a2-wat-1
Water has a high specific heat capacity (4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) compared with most liquids. This is mainly because:
the O–H covalent bonds break when water is heated
water molecules are non-polar
extensive hydrogen bonding between molecules absorbs energy that would otherwise raise the kinetic energy of the molecules
water has a low molar mass
Much of the energy supplied is used to disrupt hydrogen bonds, so a larger energy input is needed to raise the temperature. Heating water does not break covalent O–H bonds, and water is polar.
chem12a2-wat-2
How much energy is needed to heat 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
q = mcΔT = 250 × 4.18 × 60.0 = 6.27 × 10⁴ J = 62.7 kJ. 20.9 kJ uses the initial temperature (20.0 °C) instead of ΔT; 6.27 × 10⁴ kJ forgets to convert J to kJ.
chem12a2-wat-3
Ice floats on liquid water because:
ice contains trapped air bubbles
the covalent bonds in ice are longer than in liquid water
ice molecules have a lower molar mass
hydrogen bonding holds the molecules in an open hexagonal lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water
In ice each molecule hydrogen-bonds to four neighbours in a regular, open arrangement with more space between molecules than in the liquid. The molar mass of H₂O is the same in both states.
chem12a2-wat-4
Consider the hydrides H₂O, H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te. Which has the highest boiling point, and why?
H₂Te, because it has the strongest dispersion forces
H₂O, because its molecules form hydrogen bonds
H₂S, because it has the most polar bonds
H₂Se, because it has an intermediate molar mass

Water boils at 100 °C, far higher than the others, because O is highly electronegative and small, allowing strong hydrogen bonds. H₂Te has the strongest dispersion forces of the group but these are weaker than water's hydrogen bonding.
chem12a2-wat-5
The molar heat of vaporisation of water at 100 °C is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is needed to vaporise 9.00 g of water at its boiling point?
366 kJ
n(H₂O) = 9.00 ÷ 18.0 = 0.500 mol; energy = 0.500 × 40.7 = 20.4 kJ. 366 kJ results from multiplying by the mass in grams rather than the amount in mol.
chem12a2-wat-6
Melbourne's coastal suburbs typically have a smaller daily temperature range than inland towns such as Mildura. Explain this, referring to a property of water and its cause. (3 marks)

Water has a high specific heat capacity; this is because energy is used to disrupt the extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so a large amount of energy is needed to change its temperature; large bodies of water such as Port Phillip Bay therefore absorb heat during the day and release it at night with only small temperature changes, moderating the air temperature of nearby land.
chem12a2-wat-7
Describe a hydrogen bond between two water molecules, and explain why each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds. (3 marks)

A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (O) in one molecule and a lone pair on an O atom of a neighbouring molecule; the large electronegativity difference makes H strongly δ+ and O strongly δ−; each water molecule has two H atoms (each can bond to another molecule) and two lone pairs on O (each can accept a hydrogen bond), giving up to four hydrogen bonds.
chem12a2-wat-8
15.0 kJ of energy is absorbed by 200 g of water initially at 18.0 °C. Calculate the final temperature of the water. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) (2 marks)
chem12a2-wat-9
Which pair of substances can form hydrogen bonds with each other?
CH₄ and H₂O
HCl and HCl
NH₃ and H₂O
CH₃Cl and CH₃Cl

NH₃ has an H atom bonded to N and a lone pair on N, and H₂O has H bonded to O and lone pairs on O, so hydrogen bonds can form between them. HCl is tempting because it is polar, but its H is bonded to Cl, not to N, O or F, and CH₄ and CH₃Cl have no H bonded to N, O or F either.
chem12a2-wat-10
A water molecule has a bent shape with a bond angle of about 104.5°. This is because the oxygen atom has:
two bonding pairs and two lone pairs of electrons, which repel to give a bent shape
two bonding pairs and no lone pairs, giving a linear shape
four bonding pairs, giving a tetrahedral molecule
two double bonds to hydrogen atoms

Four electron pairs around O (two bonding, two lone) repel to a tetrahedral arrangement, but the shape of the molecule is bent because only two of the pairs are bonded. With no lone pairs the molecule would be linear, but O in water has two.
chem12a2-wat-11
Water has a high surface tension. This is best explained by:
strong covalent bonds between the hydrogen and oxygen atoms in each molecule
hydrogen bonds pulling surface molecules inwards towards neighbouring molecules
the low density of liquid water
water molecules being non-polar

Molecules at the surface have no neighbours above them, so they are pulled inwards and sideways by hydrogen bonds, creating a tight 'skin'. The covalent bonds are within molecules and are not what holds the surface together.
chem12a2-wat-12
When liquid water boils at 100 °C, which of the following occurs?
The O–H covalent bonds break to form hydrogen and oxygen gas
The hydrogen atoms move to bond with different oxygen atoms
The covalent bonds become weaker but remain intact
Hydrogen bonds between water molecules are broken, but each molecule remains intact

Boiling is a physical change in which the intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome so molecules can separate as steam. The covalent O–H bonds are much stronger and stay intact, so no hydrogen or oxygen gas forms.
chem12a2-wat-13
How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 150 g of water by 25.0 °C? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
q = mcΔT = 150 × 4.18 × 25.0 = 15 675 J = 15.7 kJ. 0.627 kJ results from leaving out the temperature change, and 3.75 kJ from leaving out the specific heat capacity.
chem12a2-wat-14
A sample of water absorbs 5.00 kJ of energy and its temperature rises by 10.0 °C. What is the mass of the sample? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
m = q ÷ (cΔT) = 5000 ÷ (4.18 × 10.0) = 120 g. 0.120 g comes from using 5.00 J rather than converting kJ to J, and 2.09 × 10⁵ g from multiplying by c instead of dividing.
chem12a2-wat-15
Sweating cools the body mainly because:
water has a low specific heat capacity
evaporating sweat absorbs a large amount of energy from the skin to overcome hydrogen bonds
the covalent bonds in water release energy when they break
sweat is less dense than skin

Water has a high heat of vaporisation because many hydrogen bonds must be broken for it to evaporate, so evaporation removes a lot of energy from the body. Water's specific heat capacity is high, not low, and breaking bonds absorbs rather than releases energy.
chem12a2-wat-16
Methane (CH₄, M = 16) boils at −162 °C but water (H₂O, M = 18) boils at 100 °C. The main reason for this difference is that:
methane has a higher molar mass than water
methane molecules are polar and water molecules are not
methane has stronger dispersion forces than water
water molecules form hydrogen bonds, whereas methane has only weak dispersion forces

Water's molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonds, whereas non-polar methane has only weak dispersion forces, so far less energy is needed to separate methane molecules. The molar masses are similar, so dispersion forces cannot explain the 260 °C difference.
chem12a2-wat-17
The molar heat of vaporisation of water is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. What mass of water can be vaporised at 100 °C by 100 kJ of energy?
n = 100 ÷ 40.7 = 2.46 mol; m = 2.46 × 18.0 = 44.2 g. 2.46 g stops at the amount in mol without converting to mass.
chem12a2-wat-18
In liquid water, a hydrogen bond forms between:
the oxygen atom of one molecule and the oxygen atom of another molecule
the two hydrogen atoms of the same molecule
the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and a lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule
the hydrogen atom and oxygen atom within the same molecule
The hydrogen bond is an attraction between a δ+ H on one molecule and a lone pair on the δ− O of another. The attraction between H and O within a molecule is the covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.
chem12a2-wat-19
Propane (C₃H₈, M = 44), dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃, M = 46) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH, M = 46) have similar molar masses. Which has the highest boiling point?
propane, because it has the most hydrogen atoms
ethanol, because its molecules form hydrogen bonds
dimethyl ether, because it has a polar C–O bond
all are equal because their molar masses are similar

Ethanol has an H atom bonded to O, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the dipole–dipole forces in dimethyl ether or the dispersion forces in propane. Similar molar mass only means similar dispersion forces, not similar total intermolecular forces.
chem12a2-wat-20
Equal masses of water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) and ethanol (c = 2.44 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) at the same starting temperature absorb the same amount of energy. Which statement is correct?
The ethanol temperature rises by more, because it has a lower specific heat capacity
The water temperature rises by more, because it has hydrogen bonds
Both temperatures rise by the same amount
The ethanol temperature rises by less, because its molar mass is higher

ΔT = q ÷ (mc), so for the same q and m the substance with the lower c has the larger temperature rise. Water's high c, caused by hydrogen bonding, means it needs more energy per degree, so it warms less.
chem12a2-wat-21
Liquid water has a density of 1.00 g mL⁻¹ and ice has a density of 0.92 g mL⁻¹. What volume of ice forms when 100 mL of liquid water freezes?
100 mL
109 mL
Mass is conserved: m = 100 g, so V(ice) = 100 ÷ 0.92 = 109 mL. 92.0 mL multiplies by the density instead of dividing, which would wrongly suggest the water contracts on freezing.
chem12a2-wat-22
Which statement about the strength of the bonds and forces in water is correct?
The covalent O–H bonds within a molecule are weaker than the hydrogen bonds between molecules
Hydrogen bonds are weaker than the covalent bonds within molecules but stronger than dispersion forces between similar-sized non-polar molecules
Hydrogen bonds and covalent bonds have approximately the same strength
Hydrogen bonds are the weakest of all intermolecular forces

Hydrogen bonds are an intermolecular force, much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why boiling does not decompose water, yet they are stronger than the dispersion forces in non-polar substances of similar size. Dispersion forces in small non-polar molecules are weaker than hydrogen bonds.
chem12a2-wat-23
A water strider insect can walk on the surface of a pond without sinking. Explain this, referring to the intermolecular forces in water. (2 marks)

Water molecules at the surface are attracted inwards and sideways by hydrogen bonds to neighbouring molecules, producing high surface tension [1]; this forms a skin that can support the small mass of the insect without the surface breaking [1].
chem12a2-wat-24
Ammonia (NH₃) boils at −33 °C whereas phosphine (PH₃), which has a larger molar mass, boils at −88 °C. Explain this difference. (3 marks)

Nitrogen is small and highly electronegative, so the N–H bonds are very polar and NH₃ molecules form hydrogen bonds between them [1]; phosphorus is larger and less electronegative, so PH₃ cannot form hydrogen bonds and is held only by weaker dispersion forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions [1]; hydrogen bonds are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate NH₃ molecules, giving ammonia the higher boiling point despite its smaller molar mass [1].
chem12a2-wat-25

Calculate the total energy needed to heat 500 g of water from 15.0 °C to 100 °C and then vaporise all of it at 100 °C. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; molar heat of vaporisation = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹; M(H₂O) = 18.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a2-wat-26

An electric kettle with a power output of 2.00 kW (2000 J s⁻¹) heats 1.50 kg of water from 22.0 °C to 100 °C. Assuming all the energy heats the water, calculate the time taken. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) (3 marks)
chem12a2-wat-27
In cold climates, lakes freeze from the top down, and fish can survive in the liquid water beneath the ice. Explain why the ice forms at the surface, referring to hydrogen bonding. (3 marks)

In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in a rigid, open lattice with more space between molecules than in liquid water [1]; so ice has a lower density than liquid water and floats at the surface [1]; the floating layer of ice insulates the water below, so it remains liquid and aquatic life can survive [1].
chem12a2-wat-28
Explain why a water molecule is polar. (3 marks)

Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so each O–H bond is polar with O partially negative (δ−) and H partially positive (δ+) [1]; the molecule is bent (about 104.5°) because of the two lone pairs on oxygen [1]; because of the bent shape, the bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule has a net dipole [1].
chem12a2-wat-29
Distinguish between the covalent bonds in a water molecule and the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, and state which type is broken when water evaporates. (2 marks)

Covalent O–H bonds are strong bonds within a molecule formed by sharing of electrons, whereas hydrogen bonds are much weaker intermolecular attractions between δ+ H and a lone pair on O of a neighbouring molecule [1]; when water evaporates only the hydrogen bonds between molecules are broken, and the covalent bonds remain intact [1].
chem12a2-wat-30
100 g of water at 80.0 °C is mixed with 200 g of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) (3 marks)
Energy lost by the hot water equals energy gained by the cold water [1]; 100 × 4.18 × (80.0 − T) = 200 × 4.18 × (T − 20.0) [1]; 8000 − 100T = 200T − 4000, so T = 40.0 °C [1].
chem12a2-wat-31
Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why methanol, CH₃OH, is miscible with water but pentane, C₅H₁₂, is not. (3 marks)

Methanol has a polar O–H group that can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules [1]; the new methanol–water hydrogen bonds are comparable in strength to those broken in water and in methanol, so the two mix [1]; pentane is non-polar and can form only weak dispersion forces with water, which cannot compensate for the hydrogen bonds that would be broken between water molecules, so it does not mix [1].
vce-chem12-pw-c1
Ice floats on liquid water because:
Ice contains trapped air bubbles that make it less dense than the liquid water around it
Water molecules in ice are lighter, because some hydrogen atoms are lost on freezing
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice, so they are further apart than in the liquid
Covalent bonds within each molecule break on freezing, so the molecules spread further apart
The open hydrogen-bonded lattice makes ice less dense, so aquatic life survives beneath frozen surfaces.
vce-chem12-solubility-and-precipitation-: Which compound is insoluble in water?
Silver chloride is a classic insoluble chloride. All sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate compounds are soluble.
Solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate are mixed and a white precipitate forms. The ionic equation is:
The ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate, omitting spectator ions. Option B is the full (molecular) equation, not the ionic equation; NaCl and BaCl₂ are soluble.
When silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution, which ions are spectator ions?
Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ combine to form AgCl(s); Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain in solution unchanged. Option D wrongly includes Cl⁻, which is consumed in the precipitate.

The solubility of potassium nitrate is about 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and about 32 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A saturated solution containing 100 g of water is cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C. What mass of KNO₃ crystallises?
At 60 °C 110 g is dissolved; at 20 °C only 32 g can stay dissolved, so 110 − 32 = 78 g crystallises. 32 g is the amount that stays in solution.
Which pair of solutions forms a precipitate when mixed?
Pb²⁺ and I⁻ form insoluble yellow PbI₂(s). In the other pairs every possible combination of ions (e.g. NaNO₃, KCl, KNO₃) is soluble.
Explain, in terms of the particles involved, how solid sodium chloride dissolves in water. (3 marks)

Water molecules are polar; the δ− oxygen ends are attracted to Na⁺ ions and the δ+ hydrogen ends to Cl⁻ ions at the surface of the lattice (ion–dipole attractions); these attractions are strong enough to overcome the ionic bonding, so ions are pulled from the lattice and become surrounded by water molecules (hydrated), dispersing through the solution as Na⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq).
Copper(II) sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. Write the ionic equation with states, describe what is observed, and name the spectator ions. (3 marks)
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s); a pale blue precipitate forms (and the blue colour of the solution fades); the spectator ions are Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻.

A water sample is known to contain either Ag⁺ or Ba²⁺ ions. Adding dilute Na₂SO₄ solution gives a white precipitate, but adding NaCl solution to a fresh portion gives no precipitate. Identify the ion and explain, including an ionic equation. (3 marks)

The ion is Ba²⁺; barium sulfate is insoluble, so Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) explains the white precipitate; if Ag⁺ were present, adding chloride would have formed a white precipitate of AgCl, but none formed (BaCl₂ is soluble).
Lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution. What is the formula of the precipitate?
Pb²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine in a 1 : 2 ratio to form insoluble PbCl₂. NaNO₃ is soluble, so it stays in solution and is not the precipitate.
Iron(III) nitrate solution is added to sodium hydroxide solution and a brown solid forms. Which is the correct ionic equation?
The ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate, balanced for charge and atoms. The first option is the full equation, and the last is wrong because NaNO₃ is soluble.
Which pair of solutions does NOT form a precipitate when mixed?
The possible products, KNO₃ and NaOH, are both soluble, so no reaction occurs. The other pairs form AgBr, ZnS and Ca₃(PO₄)₂ respectively, which are all insoluble.
Excess sodium sulfate solution is added to 50.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ barium chloride solution. What mass of barium sulfate (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) precipitates?
n(BaCl₂) = 0.0500 × 0.100 = 0.00500 mol, and Ba²⁺ : BaSO₄ is 1 : 1, so m = 0.00500 × 233.4 = 1.17 g. Using 0.0100 mol (2.33 g) wrongly doubles the amount.
Which equation correctly represents the dissolving of solid sodium sulfate in water?
Each formula unit releases two Na⁺ ions and one SO₄²⁻ ion, and the equation must balance in atoms and charge. The second option is not balanced, and the third gives too many sulfate ions.
Which statement best describes a saturated solution?
It contains a very large amount of dissolved solute.
It contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature, so any extra solute remains undissolved.
It has a concentration greater than 1 mol L⁻¹.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature. It need not be highly concentrated, because a sparingly soluble salt can form a saturated solution that is very dilute.
The solubility of sodium nitrate is about 88 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. If 100 g of NaNO₃ is stirred into 100 g of water at 20 °C, which outcome is expected?
All 100 g dissolves to form an unsaturated solution.
A saturated solution forms with about 12 g of solid remaining undissolved.
A saturated solution forms with about 88 g of solid remaining undissolved.
A supersaturated solution forms with no solid remaining.
Only 88 g can dissolve at this temperature, so 100 − 88 = 12 g remains as solid in contact with the saturated solution. The 88 g figure is the amount that dissolves, not the amount left over.
Which anion, added as its sodium salt, would precipitate all of the Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺ and Ba²⁺ ions from a solution?
Magnesium, calcium and barium carbonates are all insoluble. Chloride and nitrate salts of these ions are soluble, and MgSO₄ is soluble so sulfate would not remove Mg²⁺.
Silver nitrate solution is added to sodium carbonate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction?
Two Ag⁺ ions are needed to balance the charge of one CO₃²⁻ ion, giving Ag₂CO₃. The first option has unbalanced charges, and sodium salts are soluble so they do not precipitate.
Which is the main reason an insoluble ionic compound such as CaCO₃ does not dissolve in water?
The ionic bonds in the lattice are stronger than the ion–dipole attractions that water molecules could form with the ions.
Water molecules are non-polar and cannot interact with ions.
The ions are too small to be surrounded by water molecules.
Calcium carbonate is a covalent network solid.
A compound dissolves only if hydration of its ions releases enough energy to overcome the lattice attractions. Water is polar, so the second option is wrong, and CaCO₃ is ionic.
Which is the correct ionic equation for the precipitation of magnesium phosphate when magnesium chloride and sodium phosphate solutions are mixed?
Three Mg²⁺ (+6) balance two PO₄³⁻ (−6), giving Mg₃(PO₄)₂. The other options have unbalanced charges, usually from swapping or ignoring the ion charges.
Which combination of solutions would form TWO different precipitates when mixed?
Barium hydroxide with copper(II) sulfate gives both BaSO₄ and Cu(OH)₂, which are insoluble. NaOH with CuSO₄ gives only Cu(OH)₂, and BaCl₂ with Na₂SO₄ gives only BaSO₄.
When sodium chloride dissolves in water, how are the water molecules oriented around each Na⁺ ion?
The δ+ hydrogen ends point towards the Na⁺ ion.
The δ− oxygen ends point towards the Na⁺ ion.
The molecules are oriented randomly with no preferred direction.
The water molecules form covalent bonds with the Na⁺ ion.
The positive Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water. The δ+ hydrogen ends point towards anions such as Cl⁻.
Solutions of calcium chloride and sodium carbonate are mixed. Write the ionic equation with states, state the colour of the precipitate, and name the spectator ions. (3 marks)
Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → CaCO₃(s) [1] A white precipitate forms [1] The spectator ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ [1]
A 25.0 mL sample of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ silver nitrate solution is added to excess sodium chloride solution. Calculate the mass of silver chloride (M = 143.4 g mol⁻¹) that precipitates. (3 marks)

You are given three colourless solutions labelled X, Y and Z. They are sodium chloride, sodium nitrate and sodium sulfate in an unknown order. Using only barium nitrate solution and silver nitrate solution, describe a procedure to identify each solution. (4 marks)

Add barium nitrate solution to a sample of each solution [1] The one that forms a white precipitate is sodium sulfate, because Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) [1] Add silver nitrate solution to samples of the other two solutions [1] The one that forms a white precipitate (AgCl) is sodium chloride and the one with no precipitate is sodium nitrate [1]
Silver chloride is insoluble in water, but sodium chloride is soluble. Explain this difference in terms of the attractions involved. (2 marks)

For an ionic compound to dissolve, the energy released by ion–dipole attractions between the ions and water molecules must be enough to overcome the attractions between ions in the lattice [1] In AgCl the attractions between the Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the lattice are stronger than the ion–dipole attractions with water, so it stays solid, whereas for NaCl the ion–dipole attractions are sufficient so it dissolves [1]

The solubility of potassium chloride is about 34 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C and about 46 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C. A saturated solution is made using 250 g of water at 60 °C and is then cooled to 20 °C. Calculate the mass of KCl that crystallises. (3 marks)
Mass dissolved at 60 °C = 46 × 2.5 = 115 g [1] Mass that can stay dissolved at 20 °C = 34 × 2.5 = 85 g [1] Mass crystallising = 115 − 85 = 30 g [1]

Water from a mine is contaminated with dissolved lead(II) ions. Describe how adding sodium carbonate solution could be used to remove the lead, including an ionic equation with states, and state how the solid would be separated. (3 marks)

Add sodium carbonate solution so that carbonate ions react with lead(II) ions: Pb²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → PbCO₃(s) [1] Lead(II) carbonate is insoluble so the lead is removed from solution as a precipitate, while the Na⁺ ions remain in solution as spectator ions [1] The precipitate is separated from the water by filtration [1]

50.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ barium chloride solution is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium sulfate solution. Write the ionic equation and calculate the concentrations of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the final solution after the precipitate is removed. (4 marks)

Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) [1] Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are each 0.00500 mol, so they react completely with none in excess [1] n(Na⁺) = 2 × 0.00500 = 0.0100 mol and n(Cl⁻) = 2 × 0.00500 = 0.0100 mol, in a total volume of 0.100 L [1] [Na⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 0.0100 ÷ 0.100 = 0.100 mol L⁻¹ [1]
Aluminium nitrate solution is mixed with potassium hydroxide solution. Write the balanced full (molecular) equation with states, and then the ionic equation. (3 marks)

Al(NO₃)₃(aq) + 3KOH(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s) + 3KNO₃(aq) [1] Ionic form: Al³⁺(aq) + 3NO₃⁻(aq) + 3K⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s) + 3K⁺(aq) + 3NO₃⁻(aq) [1] Cancelling spectator ions K⁺ and NO₃⁻ gives Al³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s) [1]
50.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) is added to an excess of NaCl(aq). What mass of PbCl₂ (M = 278.2 g mol⁻¹) precipitates?
n(Pb²⁺) = 0.0500 × 0.200 = 0.0100 mol, and Cl⁻ is in excess, so n(PbCl₂) = 0.0100 mol and m = 0.0100 × 278.2 = 2.78 g. The value 5.56 g wrongly assumes two moles of PbCl₂ form per mole of Pb²⁺.
Solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed. The ionic equation for the reaction is:
Lead(II) iodide is insoluble (a yellow precipitate); K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions. The full equation is correct but is not the ionic equation.
vce-chem12-bronsted-lowry-acids-and-base: According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a:
substance that produces OH⁻ ions in water
A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H⁺ (a proton) and a base accepts it. Producing OH⁻ in water is the older Arrhenius description of a base.
What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
A conjugate base has one fewer H⁺ than its acid: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. H₃PO₄ is its conjugate acid.
HCO₃⁻ can donate a proton (forming CO₃²⁻) or accept one (forming H₂CO₃). CO₃²⁻ has no H to donate, and Cl⁻ is an extremely weak base that does not act as an acid.
In the reaction NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), water acts as:
a base, because it accepts a proton
an acid, because it donates a proton to NH₃
H₂O loses H⁺ to become OH⁻, so it is the acid; NH₃ is the base. OH⁻ is the conjugate base of water, not the other way round.
Sulfuric acid can donate two protons per molecule. Ethanoic acid has four H atoms but only the one in –COOH is ionisable, so it is monoprotic; H₃PO₄ is triprotic.

The hydrogen carbonate ion, HCO₃⁻, is amphiprotic. Write balanced equations, with states, showing HCO₃⁻ reacting as (a) an acid with hydroxide ions and (b) a base with hydronium ions, and explain the term amphiprotic. (3 marks)

(a) HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l); (b) HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) → H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) (or → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)); an amphiprotic species can act as either a proton donor (acid) or a proton acceptor (base) depending on what it reacts with.
Identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs in: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). (2 marks)
CH₃COOH / CH₃COO⁻ (acid / conjugate base); H₃O⁺ / H₂O (conjugate acid / base).
Write balanced full equations, with states, for the reaction of hydrochloric acid with (a) solid magnesium carbonate and (b) zinc metal. State one observation common to both reactions. (3 marks)
(a) MgCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g); (b) Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g); in both, bubbles of gas (effervescence) are seen and the solid dissolves.
What is the conjugate acid of NH₃?
NH₃ accepts a proton to form NH₄⁺, its conjugate acid. NH₂⁻ would be the conjugate base, formed by losing a proton.
What is the conjugate base of H₂O?
Removing one H⁺ from H₂O gives OH⁻. H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid, formed by gaining a proton.
What is the conjugate acid of CO₃²⁻?
The conjugate acid has one more H⁺ than the base: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ gives HCO₃⁻. H₂CO₃ would require two protons to be added.
Which of the following is a monoprotic acid?
HCl donates one proton per molecule. H₂CO₃ and H₂S are diprotic and H₃PO₄ is triprotic.
Which species can act as both a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base?
Water can donate H⁺ (forming OH⁻) or accept H⁺ (forming H₃O⁺), so it is amphiprotic. NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ have no H to donate.
In the reaction HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), which is a conjugate acid–base pair?
HSO₄⁻ and SO₄²⁻ differ by one proton. HSO₄⁻ and H₃O⁺ are both acids, so they cannot be a conjugate pair.
What is the formula of the hydronium ion?
A hydronium ion is a water molecule that has gained a proton, H₂O + H⁺ = H₃O⁺. OH⁻ is the hydroxide ion formed when water loses a proton.
Nitric acid is added to solid calcium carbonate. Which products form?
Acid plus carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrogen gas forms only when an acid reacts with a reactive metal.
A gas released when an acid is added to a carbonate turns limewater milky. What is the gas?
Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes it cloudy. Hydrogen would instead burn with a squeaky pop.
A strong acid is best described as one that:
contains many hydrogen atoms per molecule
Strength refers to the extent of ionisation, not concentration. A dilute solution of a strong acid is still a strong acid.
The conjugate base of a strong acid is:
A strong acid donates protons so readily that its conjugate base has almost no tendency to accept one back. It is not a strong base.
In H₂S(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HS⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), which species is the conjugate base of H₂S?
H₂S loses one proton to form HS⁻. S²⁻ would need two protons to be lost, and H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of water.
In H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l), H₂PO₄⁻ acts as:
a base, because it gains a proton
an acid, because it donates a proton
an amphiprotic species that gains a proton
H₂PO₄⁻ loses H⁺ to OH⁻, so in this reaction it is the acid. It is amphiprotic in general, but here it only donates.
2.50 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess hydrochloric acid. How many moles of CO₂ form?
n(CaCO₃) = 2.50 ÷ 100.1 = 0.0250 mol, and the equation gives a 1:1 ratio to CO₂. The 0.0500 mol option wrongly uses a 1:2 ratio, which applies to HCl.
Define a Brønsted–Lowry base. Write an equation, with states, for the reaction of carbonate ions with water and identify the conjugate acid formed. (3 marks)
A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor [1]. CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) [1]. The conjugate acid formed is HCO₃⁻ [1].
Write an equation, with states, for the reaction of nitric acid with water and state why it is classified as a strong acid. (2 marks)
HNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) [1]. It is a strong acid because it ionises (donates protons to water) essentially completely, so the equation has a single arrow [1].
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. Write the equation for its reaction with water and explain why a reversible arrow is used. (2 marks)

CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) [1]. Only a small fraction of molecules ionise, so the reaction does not go to completion and an equilibrium with mostly unionised CH₃COOH is established [1].
Write balanced equations, with states, for the reaction of sulfuric acid with (a) sodium hydroxide solution and (b) solid copper(II) oxide. State one observation for (b). (3 marks)
