(a) H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l) [1]; (b) H₂SO₄(aq) + CuO(s) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) [1]; the black solid dissolves and the solution turns blue [1].
Write the net ionic equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate solution and identify the proton donor and proton acceptor. (2 marks)
2CH₃COOH(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → 2CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) [1]; CH₃COOH is the proton donor (acid) and CO₃²⁻ is the proton acceptor (base) [1].
Sulfuric acid is diprotic. Write equations, with states, for each stage of its ionisation in water. (2 marks)
H₂SO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) → HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) [1]; HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) [1].
A 25.0 mL sample of hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 18.5 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Write the balanced equation and calculate the concentration of the acid. (4 marks)
Water is amphiprotic. Write the equation for the self-ionisation of water and explain how it shows amphiprotic behaviour. (2 marks)
2H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) [1]; one water molecule donates a proton (acts as an acid) while the other accepts it (acts as a base) [1].
Explain why 0.1 M hydrochloric acid conducts electricity better than 0.1 M ethanoic acid. (2 marks)
HCl is a strong acid and ionises completely, giving a high concentration of ions [1]; ethanoic acid is weak and only partly ionises, so fewer mobile ions are present to carry charge [1].
In the reaction HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) → H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l), which statement is correct?
HCO₃⁻ acts as an acid and H₂CO₃ is its conjugate base
HCO₃⁻ acts as a base and H₂CO₃ is its conjugate acid
H₃O⁺ acts as a base and H₂O is its conjugate acid
HCO₃⁻ acts as a base and H₂O is its conjugate acid
HCO₃⁻ accepts a proton to form H₂CO₃, so it is the base and H₂CO₃ is its conjugate acid. A conjugate pair differs by one H⁺, so H₂O pairs with H₃O⁺, not with HCO₃⁻.
Which statement about H₂PO₄⁻ is correct?
It is amphiprotic: its conjugate base is H₃PO₄ and its conjugate acid is HPO₄²⁻
It is amphiprotic: its conjugate base is HPO₄²⁻ and its conjugate acid is H₃PO₄
It can only act as an acid, because it still has two hydrogens it can donate
It can only act as a base, because it already carries a negative charge
A conjugate base has one fewer H⁺; a conjugate acid has one more. H₂PO₄⁻ can do both.
vce-chem12-ph-and-strong-vs-weak-acids: chem12a2-ph-1
What is the pH of 0.010 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid at 25 °C?
HCl is a strong acid and ionises completely, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹ and pH = −log₁₀(0.010) = 2.0. 12.0 would be the pH of 0.010 mol L⁻¹ NaOH.
chem12a2-ph-2
A sample of rainwater has a pH of 4.0 at 25 °C. What is its hydronium ion concentration?
4.0 mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol L⁻¹
0.60 mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻⁴·⁰ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol L⁻¹ is the hydroxide ion concentration at 25 °C.
chem12a2-ph-3
Solutions of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ HCl and 0.10 mol L⁻¹ CH₃COOH are compared at 25 °C. Which statement is correct?
The HCl solution has the lower pH because HCl ionises completely in water, whereas CH₃COOH only partially ionises
Both solutions have the same pH because they have the same concentration
The CH₃COOH solution has the lower pH because each molecule contains four hydrogen atoms
The CH₃COOH solution is more concentrated than the HCl solution
Strength refers to the extent of ionisation: HCl is strong, so [H₃O⁺] ≈ 0.10 mol L⁻¹, while ethanoic acid is weak and produces a much smaller [H₃O⁺]. Equal concentrations do not mean equal pH.
chem12a2-ph-4
10.0 mL of hydrochloric acid with pH 1.0 is diluted with water to a final volume of 1.00 L. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
The solution is diluted 100-fold, so [H₃O⁺] falls from 0.10 to 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ and pH = 3.0. Each tenfold dilution of a strong acid raises the pH by 1, not by 10.
chem12a2-ph-5
What is the pH of a 0.0050 mol L⁻¹ solution of barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, at 25 °C? (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)
Each Ba(OH)₂ releases 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹; [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.010 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² mol L⁻¹, pH = 12.0. 11.7 ignores the factor of 2.
chem12a2-ph-6
Using examples, explain the difference between the terms 'strong' and 'concentrated' when describing an acid. (3 marks)

Strength describes the extent to which an acid ionises (donates protons) in water: a strong acid such as HCl ionises completely, while a weak acid such as CH₃COOH ionises only partially; concentration describes the amount of acid dissolved per litre of solution (mol L⁻¹); so an acid can be strong but dilute (e.g. 0.001 mol L⁻¹ HCl) or weak but concentrated (e.g. 10 mol L⁻¹ CH₃COOH).
chem12a2-ph-7
20.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl is mixed with 15.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH at 25 °C. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. (3 marks)

n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol and n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0150 = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol, so H₃O⁺ is in excess by 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol; total volume = 35.0 mL, so [H₃O⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.0350 = 1.43 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹; pH = −log₁₀(1.43 × 10⁻²) = 1.85.
chem12a2-ph-8
Calculate the pH of a 0.025 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C. (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) (2 marks)
chem12a2-ph-9
Which statement best defines a strong acid?
An acid with a high concentration in solution
An acid that contains many hydrogen atoms per molecule
An acid that ionises completely (donates its protons almost entirely) in water
An acid that reacts quickly with metals
A strong acid ionises essentially completely in water, regardless of how concentrated it is. A high concentration describes the amount dissolved, not the strength.
chem12a2-ph-10
What is the pH of 0.0010 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid, HNO₃, at 25 °C?
HNO₃ is a strong monoprotic acid, so [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ and pH = 3.0. 11.0 would be the pH of a 0.0010 mol L⁻¹ strong base such as NaOH.
chem12a2-ph-11
A solution has a pH of 9.0 at 25 °C. What is its hydroxide ion concentration? (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)
1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹
9.0 mol L⁻¹
5.0 mol L⁻¹
[H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹ is the hydronium concentration, not the hydroxide concentration.
chem12a2-ph-12
Which of the following is a weak acid?
HNO₃
HCl
HBr
CH₃COOH
Ethanoic acid ionises only partially in water, so it is a weak acid. HNO₃, HCl and HBr are all strong acids that ionise completely.
chem12a2-ph-13
The pH of a solution is raised from 3 to 5 by dilution. How does [H₃O⁺] change?
It decreases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 100
It increases by a factor of 100
It decreases by a factor of 5
Each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H₃O⁺], so a rise of 2 units means a 10² = 100-fold decrease. A change of 2 in pH is not a halving or a change of 2 mol L⁻¹.
chem12a2-ph-14
Equal volumes of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ HCl and 0.10 mol L⁻¹ HF are tested with a conductivity meter. Which result is expected?
HCl has the higher conductivity because it forms more ions
HF has the higher conductivity because it is more concentrated
Both have the same conductivity because the concentrations are equal
Neither conducts because acids are molecular

Complete ionisation of HCl gives a higher concentration of mobile ions than the partial ionisation of HF, so conductivity is higher. Equal concentrations of acid do not mean equal concentrations of ions.
chem12a2-ph-15
What is the pH of 0.0020 mol L⁻¹ calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, at 25 °C? (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)
Each Ca(OH)₂ releases 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.0040 mol L⁻¹, pOH = 2.40 and pH = 11.60. 11.30 results from forgetting the factor of 2.
chem12a2-ph-16
Solution X has a pH of 3 and solution Y has a pH of 6. How does [H₃O⁺] in X compare with Y?
3 times greater
30 times greater
1000 times greater
3 times smaller
The pH differs by 3 units, and each unit is a factor of 10, so [H₃O⁺] in X is 10³ = 1000 times greater. The pH scale is logarithmic, so a difference of 3 units is not a factor of 3.
chem12a2-ph-17
Which equation correctly represents the ionisation of the weak acid HF in water?
HF + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + F⁻
HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻
HF + H₂O ⇌ H₂F⁺ + OH⁻
HF → H⁺ + F⁻ (complete)
A weak acid donates a proton to water in a reversible reaction, shown with an equilibrium arrow. A single forward arrow would imply complete ionisation, as for a strong acid.
chem12a2-ph-18
50.0 mL of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of water. What is the pH of the resulting solution at 25 °C?
The volume doubles, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.050 mol L⁻¹ and pH = −log₁₀(0.050) = 1.30. A pH of 1.00 would be the undiluted solution.
chem12a2-ph-19
Equal volumes of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ HCl and 0.10 mol L⁻¹ CH₃COOH are each titrated with 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. Which statement is correct?
The HCl solution needs more NaOH because it is stronger
The CH₃COOH solution needs more NaOH because it is weaker
Neither can be neutralised completely
Both need the same volume of NaOH
Both acids are monoprotic and contain the same amount in moles, and the weak acid's ionisation shifts to replace H₃O⁺ as it is consumed. Strength affects the pH, not the amount of base needed.
chem12a2-ph-20
Pure water at 50 °C has a pH of 6.6. Which statement is correct?
The water is acidic because its pH is below 7
The water is basic because Kw has increased
The water is neutral because [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]
The water contains no hydroxide ions
Neutrality means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]; at higher temperature Kw increases, so the neutral pH falls below 7. A pH of 7 is neutral only at 25 °C.
chem12a2-ph-21
Which statement correctly compares 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NH₃ (a weak base) with 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaOH at 25 °C?
NH₃ has a lower pH because it only partially ionises, giving a lower [OH⁻]
NH₃ has a higher pH because it is a molecule
They have the same pH because concentrations are equal
NH₃ has a lower pH because it is acidic
NaOH dissociates completely, whereas NH₃ reacts only partially with water, so [OH⁻] and pH are lower for NH₃. NH₃ is still basic, with pH above 7.
chem12a2-ph-22
Which species is present in the highest concentration in a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of the weak acid HA (apart from water)?
H₃O⁺
A⁻
HA
OH⁻
A weak acid is only slightly ionised, so most of the acid remains as HA molecules while H₃O⁺ and A⁻ are present in small and equal amounts. H₃O⁺ would be highest only for a strong acid.
chem12a2-ph-23
Define the term 'strong acid' and write an equation for the ionisation of nitric acid, HNO₃, in water. (2 marks)
A strong acid is one that ionises (donates protons to water) completely in aqueous solution [1]; HNO₃ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + NO₃⁻ (single forward arrow) [1].
chem12a2-ph-24
10.0 mL of 0.50 mol L⁻¹ HCl is diluted with water to a final volume of 250 mL. Calculate the pH of the diluted solution at 25 °C. (3 marks)
chem12a2-ph-25
A sample of orange juice has a pH of 3.40 at 25 °C. Calculate its hydronium ion concentration. (2 marks)
chem12a2-ph-26
Write an equation for the ionisation of ethanoic acid in water, and explain why a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid solution is classed as a weak acid. (3 marks)

CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ [1]; the reversible arrow shows ionisation is incomplete, with the equilibrium lying well to the left [1]; so most ethanoic acid remains as molecules and [H₃O⁺] is much lower than the acid concentration [1].
chem12a2-ph-27
25.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH is mixed with 20.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl at 25 °C. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) (4 marks)
chem12a2-ph-28
A 0.15 mol L⁻¹ solution of ethanoic acid has a pH of 2.78 at 25 °C. Calculate [H₃O⁺] and the percentage of the acid that has ionised. (3 marks)
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻²·⁷⁸ = 1.66 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ [1]; fraction ionised = 1.66 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.15 = 0.0111 [1]; so about 1.1% ionised, confirming it is a weak acid [1].
chem12a2-ph-29
1.26 g of nitric acid, HNO₃ (M = 63.0 g mol⁻¹), is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. Calculate the pH at 25 °C. (3 marks)
vce-chem12-ph-c1
Calculate the pH of 0.0050 M Ba(OH)₂ solution at 25 °C.
Each Ba(OH)₂ releases 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.010 M. [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.010 = 10⁻¹² M, so pH = 12.0.
vce-chem12-redox-reactions-and-half-equa: In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), the oxidising agent is:
Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced) to form Cu, so it is the oxidising agent. Zn(s) loses electrons and is the reducing agent, not the oxidising agent.
What is the oxidation number of manganese in the permanganate ion, MnO₄⁻?
Each O is −2, giving −8 in total. The ion's charge is −1, so Mn + (−8) = −1 and Mn = +7. +2 is the oxidation number of Mn in Mn²⁺, the usual reduction product.
Which is the correctly balanced half-equation for the reduction of dichromate ions to chromium(III) ions in acidic solution?

Balance Cr (2), O with 7 H₂O, H with 14 H⁺, then charge: left side 14 − 2 = +12, right side +6, so 6 e⁻ are added to the left. Electrons on the product side would make it an oxidation, and 8 e⁻ leaves the charge unbalanced.
Which of the following is NOT a redox reaction?
The precipitation of AgCl involves no change in oxidation numbers (Ag stays +1, Cl stays −1), so it is not redox. In the other reactions, elements change oxidation number, e.g. Fe goes from +3 to 0.
When sulfur dioxide, SO₂, is converted to sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻, the sulfur:
In SO₂, S = +4; in SO₄²⁻, S + 4(−2) = −2 so S = +6. An increase in oxidation number is oxidation. An increase in oxidation number can never be reduction.

A strip of aluminium is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution and a brown solid forms. Write the oxidation half-equation, the reduction half-equation and the balanced overall ionic equation, including states. (3 marks)
Oxidation: Al(s) → Al³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻; Reduction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s); Overall (electrons balanced at 6): 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s).

Acidified potassium permanganate oxidises iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions and is itself reduced to Mn²⁺(aq). Write balanced half-equations for each process and combine them to give the overall equation, including states. (4 marks)

Reduction: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l); Oxidation: Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻; Multiply the oxidation by 5 so electrons cancel; Overall: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 5Fe³⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l).

Chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide: Cl₂(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cl⁻(aq) + OCl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a redox reaction and what is unusual about it. (3 marks)

Cl in Cl₂ has oxidation number 0; in Cl⁻ it is −1, so some chlorine is reduced; in OCl⁻ it is +1, so some chlorine is oxidised; the same species is both oxidised and reduced (disproportionation), and H, O and Na oxidation numbers do not change.
In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is defined as:
Oxidation is the loss of electrons and is accompanied by an increase in oxidation number. Gain of electrons is reduction, which is why it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
Each H is +1, giving +4 in total. The ion's charge is +1, so N + 4 = +1 and N = −3. +3 results from forgetting that the overall charge is +1 rather than 0 and adding the signs the wrong way.
What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂?
Each H is +1, so the two O atoms must total −2, giving −1 each. −2 is the usual oxidation number of oxygen but peroxides are an exception.
In the reaction 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s), the reducing agent is:
Mg loses electrons (0 to +2), so it is oxidised and is the reducing agent. O₂ gains electrons and is the oxidising agent, which is the common mix-up.
Which is the correctly balanced half-equation for the reduction of hydrogen peroxide to water in acidic solution?

Two H⁺ are needed to balance hydrogen (4 each side) and two electrons to balance charge (0 on both sides). Placing the electrons on the product side would describe oxidation, and omitting the H⁺ leaves H and charge unbalanced.
Chlorine gas reacts with bromide ions: Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq). How many electrons are accepted by each Cl₂ molecule?
Each Cl atom goes from 0 to −1, gaining one electron, so a Cl₂ molecule gains two. Answering 1 considers only a single atom rather than the whole molecule.
Which of the following changes represents a reduction?
Mn goes from +7 to +2, a decrease in oxidation number, so this is reduction. The other three each involve an increase in oxidation number (Fe +2 to +3, S +4 to +6, Cl −1 to 0) and are oxidations.
Which is the correct half-equation for the oxidation of iodide ions to iodine?

Two iodide ions each lose one electron, so two electrons appear on the product side with I balanced. I⁻ → I₂ + e⁻ is unbalanced in iodine atoms, and electrons on the reactant side would describe reduction.
In the combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), which statement is correct?
Carbon is −4 in CH₄ and +4 in CO₂, an increase, so it is oxidised. Oxygen goes from 0 to −2, which is reduction, and hydrogen stays at +1.
Zinc metal is added to silver nitrate solution. Which is the correctly balanced overall ionic equation?
Zn loses 2 electrons and each Ag⁺ gains only 1, so two Ag⁺ are needed. Equations with Zn + Ag⁺ in a 1:1 ratio are unbalanced in charge.
Which is the correctly balanced half-equation for the oxidation of sulfite ions to sulfate ions in acidic solution?

One H₂O supplies the extra oxygen, 2H⁺ balance hydrogen, and charge requires 2e⁻ on the product side (−2 on both sides). Putting the electrons on the left describes reduction, and a single electron leaves charge unbalanced.
In the reaction Fe(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + H₂(g), which species is reduced?
H in H⁺ goes from +1 to 0, a decrease, so H⁺ is reduced. Fe is oxidised (0 to +2); H₂ is the product of reduction, not the species reduced.
What is the oxidation number of chlorine in the chlorate ion, ClO₃⁻?
Three O atoms contribute −6 and the ion's charge is −1, so Cl = −1 + 6 = +5. +7 is the value in perchlorate, ClO₄⁻.
A piece of copper wire is placed in silver nitrate solution. Which observation is consistent with a redox reaction occurring?
The solution turns blue and a silver-coloured solid forms
The solution stays colourless and the copper wire is unchanged
The solution turns blue and a gas is released
The solution turns colourless and a brown solid forms
Cu is oxidised to blue Cu²⁺(aq) while Ag⁺ is reduced to solid silver: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag. A brown solid would be copper forming, which is the reverse reaction.
In acidic solution, nitrate ions are reduced to nitrogen monoxide: NO₃⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + ?e⁻ → NO(g) + 2H₂O(l). How many electrons are needed on the left side?
Left side charge is −1 + 4 = +3 and the right side is 0, so 3 electrons are required. This matches N changing from +5 to +2.
Determine the oxidation number of sulfur in each of H₂S, S₈, SO₂ and SO₄²⁻. (4 marks)
H₂S: S = −2 as each H is +1 [1]. S₈: S = 0 as it is an uncombined element [1]. SO₂: S = +4 as each O is −2 [1]. SO₄²⁻: S = +6 since S + 4(−2) = −2 [1].

Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfate ions by acidified permanganate ions, which are reduced to Mn²⁺. Write the balanced half-equation for the oxidation of SO₂ in acidic solution and combine it with the reduction half-equation to give the overall equation. (4 marks)

Oxidation: SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ [1]. Reduction: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) [1]. Multiply oxidation by 5 and reduction by 2 so 10 electrons cancel [1]. Overall: 5SO₂(g) + 2MnO₄⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 5SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) [1].
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and bubbles of gas form. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations, the overall ionic equation, and name the species oxidised. (4 marks)
Oxidation: Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ [1]. Reduction: 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) [1]. Overall: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g) [1]. Mg is the species oxidised (0 to +2) [1].
Use oxidation numbers to show that Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s) is a redox reaction, and identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (4 marks)
Fe changes from +3 to 0, so it is reduced [1]. Al changes from 0 to +3, so it is oxidised [1]. Oxidising agent is Fe₂O₃ [1]. Reducing agent is Al [1].
Explain, using oxidation numbers, why Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) is a redox reaction whereas NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) is not. (2 marks)

In the zinc reaction Zn changes from 0 to +2 and H changes from +1 to 0, so oxidation numbers change and it is redox [1]. In the NaOH and HCl reaction every element keeps its oxidation number (Na +1, O −2, H +1, Cl −1), so it is not redox [1].

A 0.486 g strip of magnesium reacts completely with excess copper(II) sulfate solution: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Calculate the mass of copper deposited. M(Mg) = 24.3 g mol⁻¹, M(Cu) = 63.5 g mol⁻¹. (3 marks)
Explain why oxidation and reduction must always occur together in a redox reaction. (2 marks)

Electrons lost in oxidation cannot exist freely in solution, so they must be gained by another species in reduction [1]. The number of electrons lost by the reducing agent equals the number gained by the oxidising agent [1].
In acidic solution, hydrogen peroxide oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and is itself reduced to water. Write the two half-equations and the overall balanced equation. (3 marks)
Reduction: H₂O₂(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O(l) [1]; oxidation: Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ [1]; overall (oxidation half-equation × 2): H₂O₂(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l) [1].
When the half-equation for MnO₄⁻(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) is balanced in acidic solution, the number of electrons is:
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons (reduction).
vce-chem12-reactivity-series-and-metal-d: chem12a3-rs-1
Which metal, when added to iron(II) sulfate solution, will displace iron?
Copper
Silver
Zinc
Lead

Zinc is a stronger reducing agent than iron (Zn²⁺/Zn lies below Fe²⁺/Fe in the electrochemical series), so it reduces Fe²⁺ to Fe. Lead is a weaker reductant than iron, so it does not react, and neither do Cu or Ag.
chem12a3-rs-2
A strip of copper is placed in silver nitrate solution. What would be observed over time?
No change, because copper is less reactive than silver
Grey-silver crystals form on the copper and the solution turns blue
A brown coating forms on the silver and the solution becomes colourless
Bubbles of hydrogen gas form on the copper
Cu is a stronger reductant than Ag, so Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). Silver deposits form and blue Cu²⁺ ions appear. Copper is more reactive than silver, so 'no change' is wrong.
chem12a3-rs-3
Using the electrochemical series, which of these is the strongest reducing agent?
Mg(s)
Zn(s)
Cu(s)
Ag(s)
Mg²⁺/Mg has the most negative E° (−2.37 V) of these, so Mg(s) loses electrons most readily. Ag(s) is the weakest reductant of the four.
chem12a3-rs-4
Metal X reacts with a solution of Y²⁺ ions, coating X with Y. Metal Z shows no reaction with solutions of X²⁺ or Y²⁺. What is the order of reactivity, from most to least reactive?
Z > Y > X
Y > X > Z
Z > X > Y
X > Y > Z
X displaces Y, so X is more reactive than Y. Z cannot displace either, so Z is the least reactive. Putting Z first reverses what the 'no reaction' results mean.
chem12a3-rs-5
Potassium is not used to displace less reactive metals from their aqueous salt solutions because:
potassium is too unreactive to reduce metal ions
potassium reacts vigorously with the water itself, producing hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions
potassium forms an insoluble coating that stops the reaction
K⁺ ions are very strong oxidising agents
Potassium is such a strong reductant that it reduces water (2K + 2H₂O → 2K⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂) rather than the metal ions, often violently. K⁺ is actually a very weak oxidising agent.
chem12a3-rs-6

A piece of zinc is placed in lead(II) nitrate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs, justify your prediction using the electrochemical series, and write the balanced ionic equation with states. (3 marks)

A reaction occurs; Pb²⁺(aq) (E° = −0.13 V) is a stronger oxidising agent than Zn²⁺(aq) (E° = −0.76 V), so Zn(s) is a stronger reductant than Pb(s) and can reduce Pb²⁺; Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s) (grey crystals of lead form as zinc dissolves).
chem12a3-rs-7
Explain why copper(II) sulfate solution should not be stored in an iron container. Include a balanced equation. (2 marks)

Iron is a stronger reducing agent than copper (Fe²⁺/Fe is below Cu²⁺/Cu in the electrochemical series), so iron is oxidised and the container corrodes while copper metal deposits; Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
chem12a3-rs-8

A student places four metals, A, B, C and D, into solutions of each other's nitrates (all ions are 2+). Metal A reacts with solutions of B²⁺, C²⁺ and D²⁺. Metal B reacts only with D²⁺. Metal C reacts with B²⁺ and D²⁺. Metal D reacts with none. (a) List the metals from most to least reactive. (b) Identify the strongest oxidising agent among the four ions. (3 marks)

(a) A > C > B > D, since each metal displaces only those below it; (b) D²⁺ is the strongest oxidising agent; because D is the weakest reductant, its ion most readily gains electrons (every other metal can reduce D²⁺).
chem12a3-rs-9
Which of these metals reacts with cold water to produce hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide solution?
Sodium
Iron
Copper
Lead
Sodium is a very strong reducing agent and reduces water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂. Iron reacts only very slowly with water (as rusting), and copper and lead do not react.
chem12a3-rs-10
A silver wire is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Which statement is correct?
Copper metal deposits on the wire and the solution becomes colourless
Hydrogen gas bubbles form on the wire
No reaction occurs, because Ag is a weaker reducing agent than Cu
The wire dissolves and the solution turns blue

Ag(s) is a weaker reductant than Cu(s), so it cannot reduce Cu²⁺ and there is no reaction. Copper deposition would require silver to be the more reactive metal, which is the reverse of the actual order.
chem12a3-rs-11
A clean iron nail is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is expected after some time?
No change, as iron is less reactive than copper
Silver crystals form on the nail and the solution turns colourless
The nail dissolves completely and the solution turns brown
A reddish-brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades to a pale green
Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): copper deposits as a reddish-brown layer and the blue Cu²⁺ is replaced by pale green Fe²⁺. 'No change' is wrong because iron is the stronger reductant.
chem12a3-rs-12
In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the oxidising agent?
Cu²⁺(aq)
Zn(s)
Zn²⁺(aq)
Cu(s)
Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidising agent. Zn(s) is oxidised and so is the reducing agent.
chem12a3-rs-13
Which of the following combinations will result in a displacement reaction?
Copper metal in zinc sulfate solution
Silver metal in lead(II) nitrate solution
Lead metal in silver nitrate solution
Iron metal in magnesium chloride solution
Pb is a stronger reducing agent than Ag, so Pb(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Pb²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). In each other option the metal is less reactive than the metal ion's parent metal, so there is no reaction.
chem12a3-rs-14
An iron nail is left in excess copper(II) sulfate solution until 0.100 mol of copper has deposited. What mass of iron has dissolved? (Fe = 55.8)
Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu is a 1 : 1 ratio, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.58 g. 6.35 g is the mass of copper formed, not iron dissolved.
chem12a3-rs-15
Metal M displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution but does not react with zinc sulfate solution. M is best placed:
between zinc and copper in the reactivity series
above zinc in the reactivity series
below copper in the reactivity series
at the same position as zinc
M reduces Cu²⁺, so it is more reactive than copper. It cannot reduce Zn²⁺, so it is less reactive than zinc. Hence it lies between zinc and copper.
chem12a3-rs-16
Which of these metals will NOT produce hydrogen gas when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
Magnesium
Iron
Copper
Zinc
Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) lies above H⁺/H₂ (0.00 V), so Cu is a weaker reductant than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺. Mg, Zn and Fe all lie below hydrogen and react.
chem12a3-rs-17
Aluminium is more reactive than zinc, yet aluminium cookware does not visibly react with water. The best explanation is that aluminium:
is a weaker reducing agent than zinc
has a thin, unreactive coating of aluminium oxide that protects the metal beneath
does not lose electrons to form ions
reacts with water to form a gas that blocks the surface
A tightly adhering Al₂O₃ layer forms on the surface and prevents contact with water and oxygen. The reactivity series is unchanged, so aluminium is still the stronger reductant than zinc.
chem12a3-rs-18
A copper wire is placed in excess silver nitrate solution and 0.0500 mol of copper reacts. What mass of silver is deposited? (Ag = 107.9)
Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, so n(Ag) = 2 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 107.9 = 10.8 g. 5.40 g comes from ignoring the 1 : 2 mole ratio.
chem12a3-rs-19
In a metal displacement reaction, a more reactive metal atom displaces a less reactive metal ion from solution because the more reactive metal:
gains electrons more readily than the less reactive metal ion
has a larger atomic mass than the metal ion
loses electrons to the less reactive metal ion, which is reduced to metal
is always a solid while the other metal is always a liquid

The more reactive metal is the stronger reductant, so it transfers electrons to the ion, which is reduced to the solid metal. Gaining electrons more readily describes the weaker reductant's ion, not the reactive metal.
chem12a3-rs-20
A piece of magnesium ribbon is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Describe two observations and write the balanced ionic equation with states. (3 marks)
A reddish-brown solid (copper) deposits on the magnesium [1]; the blue colour of the solution fades [1]; Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) [1].
chem12a3-rs-21
Describe an experiment, using only strips of Zn, Pb, Cu and Ag and solutions of their nitrates, to determine the order of reactivity of these four metals. State the expected order. (4 marks)

Place a strip of each metal into a solution of each of the other metals' nitrates (or a systematic set of pairs) and observe for deposits of metal [1]; a reaction (metal deposit on the strip) shows the strip is more reactive than the metal in solution [1]; zinc displaces all three others, silver displaces none [1]; order from most to least reactive: Zn > Pb > Cu > Ag [1].
chem12a3-rs-22
Aluminium foil is placed in copper(II) chloride solution. Write the oxidation half-equation, the reduction half-equation and the overall balanced ionic equation. (3 marks)
Oxidation: Al(s) → Al³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻ [1]; reduction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) [1]; overall: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s) [1].
chem12a3-rs-23
A 3.27 g piece of zinc (Zn = 65.4) is added to excess copper(II) sulfate solution and all of the zinc reacts. Calculate the mass of copper formed. (Cu = 63.5) (3 marks)
chem12a3-rs-24
Explain why zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas, but copper does not. (2 marks)

Zinc lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Zn is a stronger reducing agent than H₂ and can reduce H⁺ to H₂ [1]; copper lies above hydrogen, so it is a weaker reducing agent than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺ [1].
chem12a3-rs-25
Explain why an iron nail placed in magnesium sulfate solution shows no change. Refer to reducing agents in your answer. (2 marks)
Iron is a weaker reducing agent than magnesium (Fe²⁺/Fe lies above Mg²⁺/Mg in the electrochemical series) [1]; so Fe(s) cannot transfer electrons to Mg²⁺ and no displacement occurs [1].
chem12a3-rs-26
Define a metal displacement reaction in terms of electron transfer, and give one example with a balanced ionic equation. (2 marks)

A reaction in which a more reactive metal transfers electrons to the ion of a less reactive metal, so the more reactive metal is oxidised and the ion is reduced to the metal [1]; e.g. Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) [1].
chem12a3-rs-27
Which metal reacts with aqueous Pb(NO₃)₂ but not with aqueous Zn(NO₃)₂?
Cu
Ag
Mg
Fe
Iron is more reactive than lead, so it displaces Pb²⁺, but it is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace Zn²⁺. Magnesium is more reactive than zinc, so it would react with both solutions.
chem12a3-rs-28
Excess zinc powder is added to 50.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ CuSO₄(aq). What mass of copper (63.5 g mol⁻¹) is deposited?

n(Cu²⁺) = 0.0500 × 0.100 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol, and Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu gives 1 mol Cu per mol Cu²⁺, so m = 5.00 × 10⁻³ × 63.5 = 0.318 g. Doubling to 0.636 g assumes two moles of copper form per mole of Cu²⁺.
vce-chem12-rs-c1
Which combination will react?
Copper metal in zinc sulfate solution
Silver metal in copper(II) sulfate solution
Copper metal in silver nitrate solution
Lead metal in zinc nitrate solution
A metal displaces the ions of a less reactive metal. Copper is more reactive than silver, so silver crystals form and the solution turns blue.
vce-chem12-concentration-units-and-dilut: 5.85 g of sodium chloride (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water to make 250.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration?
n = 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol; c = 0.100 ÷ 0.2500 L = 0.400 mol L⁻¹. 0.100 mol L⁻¹ forgets to divide by the volume in litres.
25.0 mL of 2.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl is diluted with water to a final volume of 500.0 mL. What is the new concentration?
c₂ = c₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = 2.00 × 25.0 ÷ 500.0 = 0.100 mol L⁻¹. The amount of HCl is unchanged by dilution; only the volume increases twenty-fold.
A sample of drinking water contains 15 ppm of calcium ions. Assuming the density of the water is 1.00 g mL⁻¹, this is equivalent to:
1 ppm = 1 mg per kg, and 1 L of dilute aqueous solution has a mass of about 1 kg, so 15 ppm = 15 mg L⁻¹. 15 µg L⁻¹ would be 15 ppb.
What is the concentration of sulfate ions in a 0.200 mol L⁻¹ solution of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃?
Each Al₂(SO₄)₃ releases 3 SO₄²⁻ ions, so [SO₄²⁻] = 3 × 0.200 = 0.600 mol L⁻¹. 0.400 mol L⁻¹ is the Al³⁺ concentration.
12.0 g of glucose is dissolved to make 300 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % (m/v)?
% (m/v) = grams of solute per 100 mL: 12.0 g ÷ 300 mL × 100 = 4.00 %. 0.0400 omits the ×100 conversion.
A technician needs 2.00 L of 0.250 mol L⁻¹ NaOH, prepared from a 10.0 mol L⁻¹ stock solution. Calculate the volume of stock solution required and outline how the solution would be prepared. (2 marks)

V₁ = c₂V₂ ÷ c₁ = 0.250 × 2.00 ÷ 10.0 = 0.0500 L = 50.0 mL of stock; measure 50.0 mL accurately (pipette/burette), transfer to a 2.00 L volumetric flask and make up to the mark with deionised water, then mix.
A 200 mL sample of river water near a farm contains 0.48 mg of nitrate ions, NO₃⁻. Express the nitrate concentration in (a) ppm (mg L⁻¹) and (b) mol L⁻¹. (3 marks)
(a) 0.48 mg ÷ 0.200 L = 2.4 mg L⁻¹ = 2.4 ppm; (b) M(NO₃⁻) = 14.0 + 3 × 16.0 = 62.0 g mol⁻¹; c = 2.4 × 10⁻³ g L⁻¹ ÷ 62.0 g mol⁻¹ = 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹ (2 significant figures).

10.0 mL of 0.500 mol L⁻¹ CuSO₄ is diluted to 100.0 mL. Then 5.00 mL of this solution is diluted to 50.0 mL. Calculate the final concentration and the amount, in mol, of Cu²⁺ in the final 50.0 mL. (3 marks)

First dilution: 0.500 × 10.0 ÷ 100.0 = 0.0500 mol L⁻¹; second dilution: 0.0500 × 5.00 ÷ 50.0 = 0.00500 mol L⁻¹ (5.00 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹); n(Cu²⁺) = 0.00500 × 0.0500 L = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol (equal to the moles in the 5.00 mL aliquot).
A water sample contains 25 µg L⁻¹ of lead ions. What is this concentration in ppb?
1 ppb is 1 µg per litre (1 µg per kg of dilute aqueous solution), so 25 µg L⁻¹ is 25 ppb. 25 000 ppb would be 25 mg L⁻¹ (25 ppm).
4.00 g of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water to make 500.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration of the solution?
n = 4.00 ÷ 40.0 = 0.100 mol; c = 0.100 ÷ 0.5000 L = 0.200 mol L⁻¹. 2.00 mol L⁻¹ results from using 50.0 mL instead of 500.0 mL.
50.0 mL of 0.800 mol L⁻¹ KNO₃ solution is diluted with water to a total volume of 200.0 mL. What is the concentration of the diluted solution?
c₂ = 0.800 × 50.0 ÷ 200.0 = 0.200 mol L⁻¹, since the volume has increased four-fold. 3.20 mol L⁻¹ comes from multiplying by the dilution factor instead of dividing.
What is the concentration of chloride ions in a 0.150 mol L⁻¹ solution of calcium chloride, CaCl₂?
CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, so [Cl⁻] = 2 × 0.150 = 0.300 mol L⁻¹. 0.150 mol L⁻¹ is the Ca²⁺ concentration.
20.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl is to be diluted to 0.250 mol L⁻¹. Assuming volumes are additive, what volume of water must be added?
V₂ = 1.00 × 20.0 ÷ 0.250 = 80.0 mL final volume, so 80.0 − 20.0 = 60.0 mL of water is added. 80.0 mL is the final volume, not the volume of water added.
Which piece of glassware is most suitable for making up a standard solution to an accurately known final volume?
A volumetric flask is calibrated to contain one precise volume when filled to its mark. A measuring cylinder is graduated but much less accurate.
What mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹), is needed to prepare 250.0 mL of a 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution?
n = 0.100 × 0.2500 = 0.0250 mol; m = 0.0250 × 106.0 = 2.65 g. 10.6 g is the mass in one litre of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution, ignoring the actual volume.
15.0 mL of ethanol is mixed with water to make 250.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % (v/v)?
10.0 mL of a stock solution is diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL. What is the dilution factor?
Dilution factor = V₂ ÷ V₁ = 250.0 ÷ 10.0 = 25.0, so the concentration falls to one twenty-fifth of the original. 0.0400 is the inverse, the fraction of the original concentration remaining.
A water supply contains 2.0 ppm fluoride. What mass of fluoride is present in 5.0 L of this water (assume density 1.00 g mL⁻¹)?
2.0 ppm = 2.0 mg L⁻¹, so 5.0 L contains 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 mg. 10 g confuses mg with g.
What is the concentration, in g L⁻¹, of a 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ solution of potassium permanganate, KMnO₄ (M = 158.0 g mol⁻¹)?
Mass concentration = c × M = 0.0500 × 158.0 = 7.90 g L⁻¹. 3.16 × 10⁻⁴ results from dividing by the molar mass instead of multiplying.
When a solution is diluted by adding water, which quantity remains unchanged?
The amount of solute, in mol
Adding solvent does not add or remove solute particles, so n(solute) is constant, which is why c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Concentration and volume both change.
100.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ NaCl is mixed with 100.0 mL of 0.300 mol L⁻¹ NaCl. Assuming volumes are additive, what is the final concentration of NaCl?
n = 0.0200 + 0.0300 = 0.0500 mol in 0.2000 L, so c = 0.250 mol L⁻¹. 0.500 mol L⁻¹ simply adds the two concentrations without accounting for the larger volume.
A solution of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) has a concentration of 0.0400 g L⁻¹. What is its concentration in mol L⁻¹?
c = 0.0400 g L⁻¹ ÷ 40.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. 1.60 mol L⁻¹ results from multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing.
What volume of 12.0 mol L⁻¹ stock hydrochloric acid is required to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ HCl?
V₁ = c₂V₂ ÷ c₁ = 0.600 × 500.0 ÷ 12.0 = 25.0 mL. 250 mL is out by a factor of ten from a decimal slip.
Calculate the mass of potassium chloride, KCl (M = 74.6 g mol⁻¹), required to prepare 500.0 mL of a 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution. (2 marks)
The chloride concentration in a sample of river water is 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Calculate this concentration in ppm (mg L⁻¹). The molar mass of chlorine is 35.5 g mol⁻¹. (2 marks)
Mass concentration = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ × 35.5 g mol⁻¹ = 8.875 × 10⁻³ g L⁻¹ [1]; = 8.88 mg L⁻¹ = 8.88 ppm (assuming density 1.00 g mL⁻¹) [1].
A 0.250 mol L⁻¹ solution of sodium phosphate, Na₃PO₄, is prepared. Write the equation for its dissociation in water and determine the concentration of each ion in the solution. (3 marks)
20.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid is mixed with 30.0 mL of water. Assuming volumes are additive, calculate the concentration of the diluted acid. (3 marks)
Explain why a volumetric flask, rather than a beaker, is used to prepare a standard solution, and why the solvent is added in two stages (dissolving, then making up to the mark). (2 marks)

A volumetric flask is calibrated to hold one precise volume when filled to its mark, whereas a beaker's graduations are only approximate [1]; the solute is first dissolved in less water and then made up to the mark so that the total final volume of solution (not the volume of water added) is accurately known, giving an accurate concentration [1].
A stock solution contains 1000 ppm of copper(II) ions. Calculate the volume of stock needed to prepare 100.0 mL of a 25.0 ppm solution, and describe how the dilution is carried out. (3 marks)

Use c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ (concentration in ppm is directly proportional to the amount of solute per volume) [1]; V₁ = 25.0 × 100.0 ÷ 1000 = 2.50 mL [1]; pipette 2.50 mL of stock into a 100.0 mL volumetric flask, then add deionised water to the mark and mix by inverting [1].
50.0 mL of 0.400 mol L⁻¹ magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, solution is diluted to 200.0 mL with water. Calculate the concentration of Mg²⁺ and of Cl⁻ in the diluted solution. (3 marks)
A 1.5 L water sample contains 3.0 mg of dissolved lead. What is the lead concentration in ppm (mg kg⁻¹)? Assume the density of water is 1.00 g mL⁻¹.
1.5 L of water has a mass of 1.5 kg, so the concentration is 3.0 mg ÷ 1.5 kg = 2.0 mg kg⁻¹ = 2.0 ppm. Multiplying 3.0 by 1.5 gives 4.5, which is not a concentration.
25.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl is diluted to 500.0 mL. Find the new concentration. Separately, a 250 mL water sample contains 5.0 mg of lead: find its concentration in ppm.
c₁V₁ = c₂V₂: 2.00 × 25.0 = c₂ × 500.0, so c₂ = 0.100 M. For dilute water, ppm = mg/L: 5.0 mg ÷ 0.250 L = 20 ppm.
vce-chem12-stoichiometry-and-limiting-re: Methane burns completely: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). What mass of CO₂ is produced from 8.0 g of CH₄?
n(CH₄) = 8.0 ÷ 16.0 = 0.50 mol; the mole ratio is 1:1, so n(CO₂) = 0.50 mol; m = 0.50 × 44.0 = 22 g. 44 g assumes 1 mol of methane.
4.0 g of H₂ and 16.0 g of O₂ are mixed and ignited: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). Which statement is correct?
Neither is in excess; they are in stoichiometric amounts
The limiting reactant cannot be found without the volume of the vessel
n(H₂) = 2.0 mol and n(O₂) = 0.500 mol. 2.0 mol H₂ needs 1.0 mol O₂, but only 0.500 mol is present, so O₂ is limiting. Comparing masses (4.0 g vs 16.0 g) wrongly suggests H₂ is limiting.
3.27 g of zinc (M = 65.4 g mol⁻¹) is added to 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What amount of H₂ forms?
n(Zn) = 0.0500 mol and n(HCl) = 0.0500 mol. Zn needs 0.100 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting; n(H₂) = ½ × 0.0500 = 0.0250 mol. 0.0500 mol assumes Zn is limiting.
The theoretical yield of a product is 12.0 g but only 9.00 g is collected. What is the percentage yield?
Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 9.00 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 75.0 %. 133 % comes from inverting the ratio, and a yield above 100 % signals an error.
In a blast furnace, Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g). What amount of CO is needed to produce 0.60 mol of Fe?
n(CO) = 3/2 × n(Fe) = 1.5 × 0.60 = 0.90 mol. 0.40 mol uses the ratio upside down (2/3).

50.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ AgNO₃ is mixed with 30.0 mL of 0.150 mol L⁻¹ NaCl. Identify the limiting reactant, calculate the mass of AgCl precipitate (M = 143.4 g mol⁻¹), and state the amount of the excess ion remaining. (4 marks)

2.50 g of calcium carbonate (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) is added to 40.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Determine the limiting reactant and calculate the mass of CO₂ produced. (4 marks)

n(CaCO₃) = 2.50 ÷ 100.1 = 0.0250 mol; n(HCl) = 1.00 × 0.0400 = 0.0400 mol; 0.0250 mol CaCO₃ would need 0.0500 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting; n(CO₂) = ½ × 0.0400 = 0.0200 mol, m = 0.0200 × 44.0 = 0.880 g.
Give two reasons why the actual yield of a reaction carried out in a school laboratory is usually less than the theoretical yield. (2 marks)

Any two of: the reaction may not go to completion (e.g. it is reversible or too slow); side reactions form other products; product is lost during transfer, filtration or washing; reactants are impure, so fewer moles are present than assumed.
Ammonia is made by N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). What amount of NH₃ can be made from 1.5 mol of H₂ with excess N₂?
n(NH₃) = 2/3 × n(H₂) = 2/3 × 1.5 = 1.0 mol. 2.25 mol comes from using the ratio upside down (3/2).
Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What mass of MgO (M = 40.3 g mol⁻¹) forms when 4.86 g of Mg (M = 24.3 g mol⁻¹) burns completely?
n(Mg) = 4.86 ÷ 24.3 = 0.200 mol; the ratio Mg:MgO is 1:1, so m(MgO) = 0.200 × 40.3 = 8.06 g. 4.03 g wrongly halves the amount using the coefficient of O₂.
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). What volume of O₂ forms at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) from 0.200 mol of H₂O₂?
n(O₂) = ½ × 0.200 = 0.100 mol; V = 0.100 × 24.8 = 2.48 L. 4.96 L assumes a 1:1 ratio between H₂O₂ and O₂.
Which statement best describes the limiting reactant in a reaction?
The reactant with the smaller mass at the start
The reactant with the smaller coefficient in the balanced equation
The reactant with the lower molar mass
The reactant that is completely used up first, so no more product can form

The limiting reactant is the one fully consumed first, and it sets the maximum amount of product. Initial mass or coefficient alone does not identify it, because the amounts in mol and the ratio must be compared.
The theoretical yield of a salt is 25.0 g. If the percentage yield of the experiment is 84.0 %, what mass of salt is actually obtained?
Actual = 84.0 ÷ 100 × 25.0 = 21.0 g. 29.8 g comes from dividing by 0.840 instead of multiplying, which would give more than the theoretical maximum.
0.30 mol of Al reacts with 0.30 mol of Cl₂: 2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2AlCl₃(s). What amount of AlCl₃ forms?
0.30 mol Al needs 0.45 mol Cl₂, but only 0.30 mol is present, so Cl₂ is limiting: n(AlCl₃) = 2/3 × 0.30 = 0.20 mol. 0.30 mol wrongly takes Al as limiting.
2.0 mol of Mg and 0.50 mol of O₂ react completely: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What amount of the excess reactant remains?
O₂ is limiting and uses 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 mol of Mg, leaving 2.0 − 1.0 = 1.0 mol Mg. 1.5 mol results from subtracting 0.50 mol directly, ignoring the 2:1 ratio.
What volume of 0.250 mol L⁻¹ NaOH is needed to react completely with 20.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ H₂SO₄? H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
Excess Na₂SO₄ solution is added to a solution containing 0.0200 mol of BaCl₂. What mass of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) precipitates?
Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) is a 1:1 ratio, so n(BaSO₄) = 0.0200 mol and m = 0.0200 × 233.4 = 4.67 g. 9.34 g wrongly doubles the amount.
Propane burns: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g). At the same temperature and pressure, what volume of O₂ is needed to burn 10 L of propane completely?
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal amounts, so volume ratios match mole ratios: 10 × 5 = 50 L. 30 L uses the coefficient of CO₂ instead of O₂.
A student calculates a percentage yield of 108 % for a precipitate. Which is the most likely explanation?
The reaction did not go to completion
Some precipitate was lost during filtration
The precipitate was not fully dried and still contained water or impurities
A side reaction consumed some of the reactants
A yield above 100 % means more mass was measured than is theoretically possible, which happens when the product is wet or impure. The other options would all lower the measured mass.
In a balanced chemical equation, the coefficients represent the ratio of which quantity?
Amounts in moles of reactants and products
Volumes of all reactants and products, whatever their states
Numbers of atoms of each element in one formula unit
Coefficients give the mole ratio in which substances react and form. They do not give mass ratios, because molar masses differ.
1.215 g of Mg (M = 24.3 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess HCl: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What volume of H₂ forms at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹)?
n(Mg) = 0.0500 mol; the Mg:H₂ ratio is 1:1, so V = 0.0500 × 24.8 = 1.24 L. 2.48 L wrongly doubles the amount using the coefficient of HCl.
Explain why the limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product formed in a reaction. (2 marks)

The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely consumed first [1]; once it is used up the reaction stops, so no more product can form regardless of how much of the other reactants (in excess) remains [1].
Aluminium burns in oxygen: 4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s). Calculate the mass of Al₂O₃ (M = 102.0 g mol⁻¹) formed when 5.40 g of Al (M = 27.0 g mol⁻¹) burns completely in excess oxygen. (3 marks)

0.540 g of aluminium (M = 27.0 g mol⁻¹) is added to 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g). Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the volume of H₂ produced at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹). (4 marks)

20.0 mL of 0.500 mol L⁻¹ CuSO₄ is mixed with excess NaOH solution: CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq). After filtering and drying, 0.850 g of Cu(OH)₂ (M = 97.5 g mol⁻¹) is collected. Calculate the percentage yield. (3 marks)
A student has 10 g of substance X and 20 g of substance Y and states that X must be the limiting reactant because it has the smaller mass. Explain why this reasoning is flawed. (2 marks)

The limiting reactant depends on the amounts in mol available compared with the mole ratio in the balanced equation, not on mass [1]; substances have different molar masses and coefficients, so each mass must be converted to moles and compared with the stoichiometric ratio [1].
Ethanol burns completely: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). Calculate the volume of O₂ at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) required to burn 2.30 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹). (3 marks)

25.0 mL of 0.400 mol L⁻¹ Pb(NO₃)₂ is mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ KI: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). Determine the limiting reactant, calculate the mass of PbI₂ (M = 461.0 g mol⁻¹) formed, and find the concentration of Pb²⁺ remaining in the final solution (assume volumes are additive). (4 marks)
Limestone is heated: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). The percentage yield of CaO is 80.0 %. Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) required to obtain 5.61 g of CaO (M = 56.1 g mol⁻¹). (3 marks)

4.60 g of sodium (M = 23.0 g mol⁻¹) reacts with 0.150 mol of chlorine gas: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the mass of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) formed. (3 marks)
n(Na) = 4.60 ÷ 23.0 = 0.200 mol, which needs only 0.100 mol Cl₂ [1]; Cl₂ (0.150 mol) is in excess, so Na is the limiting reactant [1]; n(NaCl) = 0.200 mol, m = 0.200 × 58.5 = 11.7 g [1].
Heating 5.00 g of calcium carbonate gave 2.05 g of calcium oxide. Write the equation and calculate the percentage yield. (CaCO₃ = 100.1, CaO = 56.1 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) [1]; n(CaCO₃) = 5.00 ÷ 100.1 = 0.04995 mol, so theoretical m(CaO) = 0.04995 × 56.1 = 2.80 g [1]; percentage yield = 2.05 ÷ 2.80 × 100 = 73.2% [1].
10.0 g of hydrogen reacts with 64.0 g of oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of water forms?
Oxygen is limiting; 72.0 g of water
n(H₂) = 10.0 ÷ 2.0 = 5.00 mol, which needs 2.50 mol O₂. Only 64.0 ÷ 32.0 = 2.00 mol O₂ is present, so O₂ is limiting. n(H₂O) = 4.00 mol = 72.0 g.
vce-chem12-gas-laws-and-molar-volume: What volume does 0.250 mol of oxygen gas occupy at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa)?
V = n × Vm = 0.250 × 24.8 = 6.20 L. 5.60 L uses 22.4 L mol⁻¹, the molar volume at STP (0 °C), not at SLC.
A fixed amount of gas occupies 2.0 L at 100 kPa. At constant temperature it is compressed to 0.50 L. What is the new pressure?
Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so P₂ = 100 × 2.0 ÷ 0.50 = 400 kPa. Reducing the volume to a quarter quadruples the pressure; 25 kPa wrongly assumes pressure falls.
A 2.00 L flask contains a gas at 150 kPa and 300 K. Using R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what amount of gas is present?
n = PV ÷ RT = (150 kPa × 2.00 L) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 300 ÷ 2493 = 0.120 mol. kPa × L gives J, so no extra unit conversion is needed. 0.0120 mol comes from a units slip.
A balloon holds 500 mL of gas at 27 °C. At constant pressure it is warmed to 127 °C. What is its new volume?
Charles' law needs kelvin: V₂ = 500 × 400 K ÷ 300 K = 667 mL. 2350 mL comes from using Celsius temperatures (500 × 127 ÷ 27).
Equal volumes of hydrogen gas and carbon dioxide gas are at the same temperature and pressure. They contain the same:

Avogadro's hypothesis: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of particles (molecules). The atom count differs because H₂ is diatomic and CO₂ is triatomic, and the masses differ too.
Calculate the mass of 3.10 L of carbon dioxide gas at SLC. (2 marks)
A car airbag inflates when sodium azide decomposes: 2NaN₃(s) → 2Na(s) + 3N₂(g). Calculate the mass of NaN₃ needed to produce 60.0 L of N₂ at 25 °C and 120 kPa. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
Using the kinetic molecular theory, explain why the pressure of a fixed amount of gas in a sealed rigid container increases when it is heated. (3 marks)

Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the gas particles, so they move faster; they collide with the container walls more often and with greater force; because the volume is fixed, the force per unit area of wall (pressure) increases.
What amount of nitrogen gas is present in 12.4 L of N₂ at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa)?
n = V ÷ Vm = 12.4 ÷ 24.8 = 0.500 mol. 0.554 mol comes from using 22.4 L mol⁻¹, the molar volume at STP, instead of the SLC value.
What volume does 2.00 mol of methane gas occupy at STP (0 °C and 101.3 kPa)? (Vm = 22.4 L mol⁻¹)
V = n × Vm = 2.00 × 22.4 = 44.8 L. 49.6 L uses the SLC molar volume of 24.8 L mol⁻¹, and 11.2 L divides instead of multiplying.
A 300 mL sample of gas at 27 °C is cooled to −73 °C at constant pressure. What is its new volume?
Charles' law with kelvin temperatures: V₂ = 300 × 200 K ÷ 300 K = 200 mL. Using Celsius values gives a meaningless negative volume, and 450 mL inverts the temperature ratio.
A gas occupies 4.0 L at 100 kPa and 300 K. Its pressure is doubled to 200 kPa and its temperature is doubled to 600 K. What is the new volume?
V₂ = V₁ × (P₁ ÷ P₂) × (T₂ ÷ T₁) = 4.0 × ½ × 2 = 4.0 L. The halving from doubled pressure is cancelled by the doubling from doubled temperature.
What is the mass of 5.60 L of helium gas at STP? (Vm = 22.4 L mol⁻¹)
n = 5.60 ÷ 22.4 = 0.250 mol, so m = 0.250 × 4.00 = 1.00 g. 0.903 g comes from using 24.8 L mol⁻¹, which applies at SLC rather than STP.
What is the density of oxygen gas (O₂) at SLC, in g L⁻¹?
Density = M ÷ Vm = 32.0 ÷ 24.8 = 1.29 g L⁻¹. 0.775 g L⁻¹ inverts the ratio, and 32.0 is the molar mass, not a density.
In the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), what volume of oxygen reacts completely with 10 L of hydrogen, with all gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
At the same T and P, gas volumes are in the same ratio as the mole ratio, so V(O₂) = ½ × 10 = 5.0 L. Assuming equal volumes (10 L) ignores the 2 : 1 coefficients.
A 500 mL flask holds a gas at 100 kPa and 300 K. Using R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and kPa and L as pressure and volume units, what amount of gas is present?
Convert 500 mL to 0.500 L: n = PV ÷ RT = (100 × 0.500) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 0.0201 mol. Using 500 directly for the volume gives 20.1 mol, which is 1000 times too large.
For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, which graph is a straight line passing through the origin?
Boyle's law gives PV = constant, so V is directly proportional to 1 ÷ P. A plot of P against V is a curve (hyperbola), not a straight line.
Why is the molar volume of a gas at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹) greater than at STP (22.4 L mol⁻¹)?
The gas molecules are larger at SLC
The gas has a greater number of molecules at SLC
The gas particles have a greater mass at SLC
The temperature is higher, so the gas particles move faster and spread further apart

A higher temperature (25 °C rather than 0 °C) gives more energetic collisions, so a mole of gas occupies a larger volume. A mole always contains the same number of particles, and particle size and mass do not change with temperature.
What volume of carbon dioxide at SLC is produced when 10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid? CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
n(CaCO₃) = 10.0 ÷ 100.1 = 0.0999 mol, equal to n(CO₂) (1 : 1), so V = 0.0999 × 24.8 = 2.48 L. 2.24 L results from using the STP molar volume.
Four gas samples are at the same temperature and pressure. Which contains the greatest number of molecules?

By Avogadro's hypothesis, the number of molecules is proportional to volume at the same T and P, so the largest volume (3.0 L) has the most. The identity, mass or molecular size of the gas does not matter.
A sealed rigid container of gas at 300 K has its pressure doubled by heating. What is the final temperature?
At constant volume P ∝ T (in kelvin), so doubling P gives T = 600 K = 327 °C. 600 °C wrongly doubles a Celsius value.
Calculate the volume occupied by 8.00 g of methane, CH₄, at SLC. (2 marks)
A 3.0 L sample of gas at 150 kPa is compressed at constant temperature to 1.2 L. Calculate the final pressure. (2 marks)
Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ [1]; P₂ = 150 × 3.0 ÷ 1.2 = 375 kPa [1].
A 250 mL syringe of air at 15 °C is warmed to 45 °C at constant pressure. Calculate the final volume. (2 marks)
Temperatures in kelvin: T₁ = 288 K and T₂ = 318 K [1]; V₂ = 250 × 318 ÷ 288 = 276 mL [1].
A gas occupies 2.50 L at 27 °C and 200 kPa. Calculate its volume at 127 °C and 100 kPa. (3 marks)
Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K [1]; combined gas law: P₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂V₂ ÷ T₂ [1]; V₂ = 2.50 × (200 ÷ 100) × (400 ÷ 300) = 6.67 L [1].
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Calculate the mass of magnesium needed to produce 2.48 L of hydrogen gas at SLC. (3 marks)
A sample of unknown gas has a mass of 1.50 g and occupies 1.00 L at 27 °C and 100 kPa. Calculate the molar mass of the gas. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
Use the kinetic molecular theory to explain why the pressure of a fixed amount of gas increases when its volume is decreased at constant temperature. (2 marks)

With a smaller volume, the gas particles strike the container walls more frequently, as they have less distance to travel between collisions [1]; the average kinetic energy is unchanged (constant temperature), so the greater collision rate per unit area increases the pressure [1].
Explain why 1.0 L of hydrogen and 1.0 L of carbon dioxide at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, even though CO₂ molecules are larger and heavier. (2 marks)

Gas particles are very far apart, so the volume of the gas is mostly empty space and the size of individual particles is negligible [1]; the volume of a gas therefore depends only on the number of particles (at fixed T and P), not on their identity (Avogadro's hypothesis) [1].

Propane burns according to: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g). If 4.0 L of propane is burned completely, all gases being measured at the same temperature and pressure, calculate the volume of oxygen consumed and the volume of carbon dioxide produced. (3 marks)
At the same T and P, gas volumes are in the same ratio as the coefficients, so C₃H₈ : O₂ : CO₂ = 1 : 5 : 3 [1]; V(O₂) = 5 × 4.0 = 20 L [1]; V(CO₂) = 3 × 4.0 = 12 L [1].
Calculate the pressure, in kPa, of 0.0500 mol of an ideal gas in a 1.50 L container at 27 °C. (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) (2 marks)
How many moles of gas are in a 2.00 L container at 150 kPa and 27 °C?
n = PV/(RT) = 150 × 2.00 ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 0.120 mol. Use kPa with litres, and convert °C to K.
vce-chem12-volumetric-analysis-and-titra: chem12a3-vt-1
In a titration, which piece of glassware is used to transfer an accurately known volume (an aliquot) of solution into the conical flask?
Burette
Pipette
Volumetric flask
Measuring cylinder
A pipette delivers a single fixed, accurate volume (the aliquot). The burette delivers the titrant and measures the titre. A measuring cylinder is not accurate enough.
chem12a3-vt-2
A student rinses the burette with deionised water but not with the titrant before filling it. Compared with the true value, the result for the analyte concentration will be:
unchanged, because the amount of titrant is the same
too low, because the titre is smaller
too high, because the diluted titrant gives a larger titre
too low, because the diluted titrant gives a larger titre

Water left in the burette dilutes the titrant, so a larger volume is needed to reach the end point. The calculation uses the original (higher) concentration, which overestimates the moles of titrant and hence the analyte concentration.
chem12a3-vt-3
A 20.00 mL aliquot of NaOH solution is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl. The mean concordant titre is 18.40 mL. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
0.0920 mol L⁻¹
0.109 mol L⁻¹
0.184 mol L⁻¹
0.0460 mol L⁻¹
n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.01840 = 1.84 × 10⁻³ mol = n(NaOH) (1:1 ratio); c = 1.84 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02000 = 0.0920 mol L⁻¹. 0.109 mol L⁻¹ comes from inverting the volumes.
chem12a3-vt-4
A 25.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid is neutralised by 22.50 mL of 0.150 mol L⁻¹ NaOH: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l). What is the concentration of the H₂SO₄?
0.135 mol L⁻¹
0.150 mol L⁻¹
0.0338 mol L⁻¹
0.0675 mol L⁻¹
chem12a3-vt-5
Titres are usually considered concordant if they agree within 0.10 mL. Which set of titres is concordant?
The range of 21.30 to 21.40 mL is 0.10 mL, so these three are concordant. The first set contains 22.10 mL, which is often a rough first titre and should be left out of the mean.
chem12a3-vt-6

25.00 mL of vinegar is diluted to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 20.00 mL aliquots of the diluted solution are titrated with 0.1050 mol L⁻¹ NaOH, giving a mean titre of 16.85 mL. Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH, M = 60.0 g mol⁻¹) in the original vinegar in mol L⁻¹ and in % (m/v). (4 marks)
chem12a3-vt-7
For the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide, explain whether phenolphthalein (colour change pH 8.3–10.0) or methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) is the more suitable indicator. (3 marks)

Phenolphthalein; at equivalence the solution contains ethanoate ions, a weak base, so the equivalence point pH is above 7 (about 8–9); the indicator must change colour within the steep pH change at equivalence, which phenolphthalein does, whereas methyl orange would change colour well before equivalence, giving a titre that is too small.
chem12a3-vt-8
State three properties of a primary standard and explain why solid sodium hydroxide is not suitable as one. (3 marks)

Any three: high purity; known, stable chemical formula; does not absorb water or react with air (not hygroscopic or deliquescent); high molar mass to reduce weighing error; readily soluble; NaOH is unsuitable because it absorbs water from the air and reacts with atmospheric CO₂ (forming Na₂CO₃), so its mass does not reliably match the amount of NaOH.
chem12a3-vt-9
What is a standard solution in volumetric analysis?
A solution whose concentration is accurately known
A solution that has been made up to exactly 1.00 L
A solution of a primary standard only
A solution with a pH of exactly 7

A standard solution has an accurately known concentration, so it can be used to determine the concentration of an unknown. It can be prepared from a primary standard or standardised against one, and it need not be neutral or 1.00 L.
chem12a3-vt-10
How should the volume be read from a burette containing a colourless solution?
At the top of the meniscus, with the eye above the liquid
At the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye level with the meniscus
At the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye looking down from above
At the top of the meniscus, with the eye level with the meniscus
The reading is taken at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye at the same level, which avoids parallax error. Reading from above or below makes the reading appear higher or lower than it really is.
chem12a3-vt-11
What is the difference between the end point and the equivalence point of a titration?
They are always the same point by definition
The end point is where the reactants are in exact stoichiometric ratio; the equivalence point is where the indicator changes colour
The equivalence point is where the reactants are in exact stoichiometric ratio; the end point is where the indicator changes colour
The end point occurs before the first drop of titrant is added

The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point calculated from the equation, while the end point is the observed colour change of the indicator. A good indicator makes the two very close, but they are not defined as identical.
chem12a3-vt-12
A 25.00 mL aliquot of HCl is titrated with 0.0800 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. The mean titre is 20.50 mL. What is the concentration of the HCl?
0.0328 mol L⁻¹
0.0976 mol L⁻¹
0.131 mol L⁻¹
0.0656 mol L⁻¹
n(NaOH) = 0.0800 × 0.02050 = 1.64 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl) (1:1); c(HCl) = 1.64 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0656 mol L⁻¹. 0.0976 mol L⁻¹ comes from dividing by the titre instead of the aliquot volume.
chem12a3-vt-13
Just before a titration, a student rinses the conical flask with deionised water and leaves some water in it. What effect does this have on the calculated concentration of the analyte?
No effect, because the amount of analyte in the flask is unchanged
The concentration will be too high, because the titre is larger
The concentration will be too low, because the analyte is diluted
The concentration will be too low, because the titre is smaller

The extra water does not change the number of moles of analyte in the aliquot, so the same volume of titrant is needed to reach the end point. Dilution in the flask therefore does not affect the result.
chem12a3-vt-14
A student rinses the pipette with deionised water, not with the analyte solution, before measuring the aliquot. The calculated analyte concentration will be:
too high, because the titre is larger
too low, because the aliquot contains fewer moles of analyte
unchanged, because the pipette volume is fixed
too high, because the water adds to the moles of analyte
Residual water dilutes the aliquot, so it contains fewer moles of analyte than expected and the titre is smaller. The calculation assumes the original aliquot concentration, so the result is too low.
chem12a3-vt-15
An air bubble is trapped in the tip of a burette at the start of a titration and is dislodged and escapes during the titration. How is the calculated analyte concentration affected?
Too low, because less titrant was delivered than was read
Unchanged, because air has no mass
Too high, because the measured titre is larger than the volume of titrant actually delivered
Too low, because the titre is smaller than expected

Some of the volume read off the burette was air, so the recorded titre is larger than the volume of liquid delivered. This overestimates the moles of titrant and gives an analyte concentration that is too high.
chem12a3-vt-16
A 20.00 mL aliquot of Na₂CO₃ solution is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). The mean titre is 24.00 mL. What is the concentration of the Na₂CO₃?
0.120 mol L⁻¹
0.0480 mol L⁻¹
0.0300 mol L⁻¹
0.0600 mol L⁻¹
chem12a3-vt-17
Which substance is the most suitable primary standard for making up a standard acid solution?
Anhydrous sodium carbonate
Solid sodium hydroxide
Concentrated hydrochloric acid
Potassium permanganate

Anhydrous sodium carbonate is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic and has a known formula. Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and CO₂, and concentrated hydrochloric acid loses HCl gas, so neither has a reliably known amount.
chem12a3-vt-18
1.325 g of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water and made up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. What is the concentration of the solution?
0.0125 mol L⁻¹
0.0500 mol L⁻¹
0.0100 mol L⁻¹
n = 1.325 ÷ 106.0 = 0.0125 mol; c = 0.0125 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.0500 mol L⁻¹. 0.0125 is the number of moles, not the concentration, because the volume was not used.
chem12a3-vt-19
Ammonia solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid. Which indicator is more suitable, and why?
Phenolphthalein, because its colour change is at pH 8.3–10.0
Either indicator, because the equivalence point is at pH 7
Phenolphthalein, because ammonia is a base
Methyl orange, because the solution at equivalence contains NH₄⁺ and is acidic

At equivalence the solution contains NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so the pH is below 7 and methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) changes colour in the steep region. Phenolphthalein would change colour well before the equivalence point is reached.
chem12a3-vt-20
Four titres are recorded: 23.60 mL, 22.45 mL, 22.40 mL and 22.50 mL. The first is a rough titre. What mean titre should be used in the calculation?
The rough titre is discarded and the concordant titres (22.45, 22.40, 22.50 mL, all within 0.10 mL) are averaged to give 22.45 mL. 22.74 mL results from including the rough titre.
chem12a3-vt-21
A 20.00 mL aliquot of KOH solution is titrated with 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ H₂SO₄. The mean titre is 15.60 mL. What is the concentration of the KOH? (H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l))
0.0390 mol L⁻¹
0.0780 mol L⁻¹
0.156 mol L⁻¹
0.0641 mol L⁻¹
chem12a3-vt-22
Why should only a few drops of indicator be added to the analyte in the conical flask?
More indicator makes the colour change impossible to see
Indicators only work in very small amounts of water
Indicators are weak acids or bases, so a larger amount would react with the titrant and alter the titre
The indicator would otherwise change the concentration of the standard solution
Most indicators are themselves weak acids or bases, so excess indicator consumes some titrant and gives a titre that is too large. The amount is kept small to make this effect negligible.
chem12a3-vt-23
Describe how the burette, the pipette and the conical flask should each be rinsed before a titration, and justify the choice for the conical flask. (3 marks)

Burette is rinsed with a small amount of the titrant (standard solution) [1]; pipette is rinsed with a small amount of the analyte solution it will measure [1]; conical flask is rinsed with deionised water only, because the water does not change the moles of analyte in the aliquot, whereas rinsing with analyte would add extra moles and make the titre too large [1].
chem12a3-vt-24
Explain why a rough titration is carried out first and why further titres must be concordant. (2 marks)

The rough titre gives an approximate end point so that later titrations can add titrant dropwise near the end point for accuracy [1]; concordant titres (within 0.10 mL) show that the results are reproducible and that random errors are small, so the mean is reliable [1].
chem12a3-vt-25
Distinguish between the accuracy and the precision of a titration result, and explain how a titration could be precise but not accurate. (3 marks)

Accuracy is how close the result is to the true value [1]; precision is how close repeated measurements (titres) are to each other [1]; a systematic error, such as a burette not rinsed with titrant or a consistently misread meniscus, shifts all titres the same way so they are concordant (precise) but the result is wrong (inaccurate) [1].
chem12a3-vt-26

10.00 mL of household ammonia (NH₃) cleaner is diluted to 500.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 25.00 mL aliquots of the diluted solution are titrated with 0.0950 mol L⁻¹ HCl, giving a mean titre of 21.30 mL. NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq). Calculate the concentration of NH₃ in the original cleaner in mol L⁻¹ and g L⁻¹ (M(NH₃) = 17.0 g mol⁻¹). (4 marks)
chem12a3-vt-27

Explain why bromothymol blue (colour change pH 6.0–7.6) is suitable for the titration of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, and why the choice of indicator is less critical for this titration than for ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide. (3 marks)

The equivalence point of a strong acid with a strong base is at pH 7, which lies within the range of bromothymol blue [1]; the pH changes very steeply (from about 3 to 11) near equivalence, so a drop of titrant moves the pH through the whole range of the indicator [1]; therefore several indicators (such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange) give a nearly identical titre, whereas a weak acid has a smaller, higher-pH steep region so only some indicators are suitable [1].
chem12a3-vt-28

0.6300 g of oxalic acid dihydrate, H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O (M = 126.0 g mol⁻¹), is dissolved and made up to 100.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot is titrated with NaOH solution and the mean titre is 19.40 mL. H₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l). Calculate the concentration of the NaOH. (4 marks)
chem12a3-vt-29
Outline the steps for preparing 250.0 mL of a standard solution from a solid primary standard using a volumetric flask. (4 marks)

Accurately weigh the required mass of the primary standard (for example by difference) [1]; dissolve it in a beaker with deionised water, then transfer the solution to the volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker and funnel into the flask [1]; add deionised water until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the calibration mark at eye level [1]; stopper and invert the flask several times to mix thoroughly [1].
vce-chem12-va-c1
A 20.00 mL aliquot of sodium carbonate solution needs 18.40 mL of 0.100 M HCl to react completely: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O. Find the concentration of the sodium carbonate.
vce-chem12-gravimetric-analysis: chem12a3-ga-1
In gravimetric analysis, the precipitate is repeatedly dried and weighed until it reaches constant mass. This is done to:
make the precipitate crystals larger
remove soluble impurities from the precipitate
ensure all water has been removed from the precipitate
convert the precipitate to its oxide
Heating to constant mass confirms that no more water is being lost, so the recorded mass is of dry precipitate only. Removing soluble impurities is the job of washing, not drying.
chem12a3-ga-2
To find the chloride content of a sample, an excess of silver nitrate solution is added. The excess is used to:
ensure that all chloride ions are precipitated as AgCl
increase the solubility of AgCl
prevent the AgCl from being washed away
react with any sodium ions present
An excess of Ag⁺ makes chloride the limiting reactant, so all of it is precipitated and the mass of AgCl reflects the total chloride. Na⁺ does not react with Ag⁺.
chem12a3-ga-3
A 2.00 g sample produces 0.287 g of dry AgCl (M = 143.4 g mol⁻¹). What is the percentage by mass of chloride in the sample?
m(Cl) = 0.287 × 35.5 ÷ 143.4 = 0.0711 g; % = 0.0711 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = 3.55 %. 14.4 % takes the mass of AgCl as if it were all chloride.
chem12a3-ga-4
A barium sulfate precipitate is not washed before drying, and soluble sodium chloride stays on it. How will this affect the calculated percentage of sulfate?
It will be too low, because some BaSO₄ dissolves
No effect, because NaCl is soluble
It will be too low, because the precipitate mass decreases
It will be too high, because the dried precipitate mass includes NaCl
Impurities that dry onto the precipitate add mass, which is wrongly counted as BaSO₄, so the sulfate result is too high. NaCl being soluble does not help unless it is washed off.
chem12a3-ga-5
Excess BaCl₂ solution is added to a dissolved fertiliser sample and 0.466 g of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) is collected. What mass of sulfate (SO₄²⁻, M = 96.1 g mol⁻¹) was in the sample?
n(BaSO₄) = 0.466 ÷ 233.4 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(SO₄²⁻); m = 2.00 × 10⁻³ × 96.1 = 0.192 g. 0.466 g is the mass of the whole precipitate, including barium.
chem12a3-ga-6
2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ (M = 159.6 g mol⁻¹). Determine the value of x. (3 marks)
chem12a3-ga-7

Excess barium chloride solution is added to a 200.0 mL sample of mineral water. The washed and dried BaSO₄ precipitate has a mass of 0.0583 g. Calculate the sulfate ion concentration in the water in mg L⁻¹ (ppm). (M(BaSO₄) = 233.4 g mol⁻¹; M(SO₄²⁻) = 96.1 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a3-ga-8
Describe two sources of error in a gravimetric analysis and state the effect of each on the calculated result. (3 marks)

Any two with effect: the precipitate is not dried to constant mass, so the mass is too high and the result is overestimated; fine precipitate passes through the filter paper, or some precipitate stays dissolved, so the mass is too low and the result is underestimated; soluble impurities are not washed off or are co-precipitated, so the result is too high; not enough precipitating agent is added, so precipitation is incomplete and the result is too low.
chem12a3-ga-9
Gravimetric analysis determines the amount of an analyte by:
measuring the volume of a standard solution needed to react with it
converting it to a pure solid of known formula and measuring its mass
measuring the intensity of light absorbed by its solution
measuring the electrical conductivity of its solution

In gravimetric analysis the analyte is isolated as a pure, stable solid and weighed, and its amount is calculated from that mass. Measuring a volume of reagent describes titration, not gravimetric analysis.
chem12a3-ga-10
Which solution could be added to a water sample to precipitate sulfate ions for gravimetric analysis?
sodium nitrate
potassium chloride
barium chloride
hydrochloric acid
Ba²⁺ forms insoluble BaSO₄ with sulfate ions. Sodium nitrate, potassium chloride and hydrochloric acid contain no cation that forms an insoluble sulfate.
chem12a3-ga-11
In a gravimetric analysis, the clear liquid that passes through the filter paper is called the:
residue
precipitate
supernatant solid
filtrate
The filtrate is the liquid that passes through the filter paper. The precipitate (residue) is the solid that is retained on the paper.
chem12a3-ga-12
Excess sodium carbonate solution is added to a solution of calcium chloride and 0.250 g of dry CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) is collected. What mass of calcium (M = 40.1 g mol⁻¹) was in the solution?
n(CaCO₃) = 0.250 ÷ 100.1 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Ca²⁺); m(Ca) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ × 40.1 = 0.100 g. 0.250 g is the mass of the whole precipitate, which includes carbonate.
chem12a3-ga-13

A sample containing sodium chloride is dissolved in water and treated with excess silver nitrate, giving 1.434 g of dry AgCl (M = 143.4 g mol⁻¹). What mass of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) was in the sample?
n(AgCl) = 1.434 ÷ 143.4 = 0.0100 mol = n(NaCl); m(NaCl) = 0.0100 × 58.5 = 0.585 g. 0.355 g is the mass of chloride only, not NaCl.
chem12a3-ga-14
Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a precipitate used in gravimetric analysis?
It has a very low solubility in the solution
It has a known, fixed formula
It is stable when dried
It is soluble in water so that it is easy to wash
The precipitate must be insoluble so that essentially none is lost in the filtrate or during washing. Being soluble in water would make it unsuitable.
chem12a3-ga-15
A crucible is heated, cooled and weighed repeatedly until its mass is constant before it is used to collect a precipitate. This is done so that:
the crucible mass does not change during the experiment
the crucible becomes coated with a layer of precipitate
the precipitate dissolves more easily
the crucible reacts with the analyte

A crucible at constant mass will not gain or lose mass (for example, by losing moisture) during heating, so any later mass change comes from the precipitate. It has nothing to do with dissolving the precipitate.
chem12a3-ga-16
During transfer, some of the precipitate is left behind in the beaker and is not collected on the filter paper. The calculated percentage of the analyte in the sample will be:
too high, because the filtrate contains extra solid
