unaffected, because the precipitate is still produced
too high, because the beaker adds mass
too low, because the measured mass of precipitate is less than the actual mass
Lost precipitate means a smaller mass is weighed, so the calculated amount of analyte is too low. The reaction still produced the full amount, but it was not all weighed.
chem12a3-ga-17

A 0.500 g sample containing barium is dissolved and excess sulfate ions are added. The dried BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) has a mass of 0.2334 g. What is the percentage by mass of barium (M = 137.3 g mol⁻¹) in the sample?
n(BaSO₄) = 0.2334 ÷ 233.4 = 1.000 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Ba); m(Ba) = 0.1373 g; % = 0.1373 ÷ 0.500 × 100 = 27.5 %. 58.8 % is the percentage of barium in pure BaSO₄, not in the sample.
chem12a3-ga-18
After filtering a BaSO₄ precipitate, a student wants to check that all the sulfate has been precipitated. The best test is to:
add a few more drops of barium chloride to the filtrate and see whether more precipitate forms
heat the filtrate until it boils dry
add sodium hydroxide to the filtrate
weigh the filtrate
If no further precipitate forms when more Ba²⁺ is added to the filtrate, no sulfate remains and precipitation was complete. Weighing or boiling the filtrate does not show whether sulfate ions remain.
chem12a3-ga-19
Excess potassium iodide is added to 50.0 mL of lead(II) nitrate solution, producing 0.461 g of dry PbI₂ (M = 461.0 g mol⁻¹). What was the concentration of Pb²⁺ in the original solution?
0.0100 mol L⁻¹
0.0200 mol L⁻¹
0.0400 mol L⁻¹
n(PbI₂) = 0.461 ÷ 461.0 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Pb²⁺); c = 1.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0500 = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹. Doubling the answer wrongly applies a 2:1 ratio, but Pb²⁺ and PbI₂ are in a 1:1 ratio.
chem12a3-ga-20
A precipitate is dried, cooled and weighed repeatedly, giving masses of 0.512 g, 0.498 g, 0.497 g and 0.497 g. Which statement is correct?
The precipitate has reached constant mass and 0.497 g should be used
The precipitate should be dried until the mass reaches 0.512 g
The precipitate has not reached constant mass because the values are not all the same
The average of all four masses should be used

The last two masses agree, which shows all the water has been removed, so 0.497 g is the dry mass. Averaging includes the earlier masses of a still-damp precipitate and gives a value that is too high.
chem12a3-ga-21
A 5.00 g sample of a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass, leaving 4.10 g of anhydrous solid. What is the percentage by mass of water in the hydrated salt?
Mass of water lost = 5.00 − 4.10 = 0.90 g; % = 0.90 ÷ 5.00 × 100 = 18.0 %. 22.0 % divides by the mass of the anhydrous solid instead of the original hydrated sample.
chem12a3-ga-22
Explain why a precipitate is washed with distilled water before it is dried and weighed in a gravimetric analysis. (2 marks)

Washing removes soluble impurities (such as excess precipitating reagent or spectator ions) that are stuck to the surface of the precipitate [1]; if left, these would dry onto the precipitate, adding mass and making the calculated amount of analyte too high [1].
chem12a3-ga-23
Outline the main steps in a gravimetric analysis to determine the percentage of chloride in a solid salt sample. (4 marks)

Accurately weigh the sample and dissolve it in distilled water [1]; add excess silver nitrate solution so that all chloride ions precipitate as AgCl [1]; filter the mixture and wash the precipitate with distilled water [1]; dry the precipitate to constant mass, weigh it and use the mole ratio n(Cl⁻) = n(AgCl) to calculate the percentage of chloride [1].
chem12a3-ga-24

A 1.250 g sample of a salt mixture containing sodium chloride is dissolved in water and excess silver nitrate solution is added. The dried precipitate of AgCl has a mass of 2.868 g. Calculate the percentage by mass of NaCl in the sample. (M(AgCl) = 143.4 g mol⁻¹; M(NaCl) = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a3-ga-25

Excess sodium carbonate solution is added to a 25.0 mL sample of calcium chloride solution. The dried CaCO₃ precipitate has a mass of 0.350 g. Calculate the concentration of Ca²⁺ in the original solution in mol L⁻¹. (M(CaCO₃) = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
chem12a3-ga-26
4.92 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 2.40 g of anhydrous MgSO₄ (M = 120.4 g mol⁻¹). Determine the value of x. (M(H₂O) = 18.0 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
chem12a3-ga-27
A student adds too little precipitating agent to a sample solution in a gravimetric analysis. Explain the effect on the calculated mass of analyte in the sample. (2 marks)

Not all of the analyte ions are precipitated, because the precipitating agent is the limiting reactant [1]; the mass of precipitate is lower than it should be, so the calculated mass of analyte is too low [1].
chem12a3-ga-28

A student heats a precipitate in a crucible and records masses of 18.642 g, then 18.615 g, then 18.598 g after successive heating and cooling. Explain what these results show and describe what the student should do next. (3 marks)

The mass is still decreasing, so the precipitate has not reached constant mass and still contains water [1]; the student should reheat the precipitate and cool it in a desiccator to prevent water being reabsorbed [1]; then reweigh, repeating until two successive masses agree [1].
chem12a3-ga-29
State two properties that a precipitate must have to be suitable for gravimetric analysis and explain why each is needed. (2 marks)

It must be very insoluble, so that almost none is lost in the filtrate or during washing [1]; it must have a known formula (composition), so that the amount of analyte can be calculated from its mass [1].
chem12a3-ga-30

Excess silver nitrate solution is added to a 250.0 mL sample of river water. The washed and dried AgCl precipitate has a mass of 0.0287 g. Calculate the concentration of chloride ions in the river water in mg L⁻¹. (M(AgCl) = 143.4 g mol⁻¹; M(Cl) = 35.5 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a3-ga-31
Excess BaCl₂(aq) is added to a solution containing 0.0500 mol of Na₂SO₄. What mass of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) is obtained?
Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ is 1 : 1, so n(BaSO₄) = 0.0500 mol and m = 0.0500 × 233.4 = 11.7 g. The value 7.10 g is the mass of Na₂SO₄ itself, not of the precipitate.
vce-chem12-ga-c1
Excess silver nitrate is added to 50.0 mL of a water sample, and 0.287 g of dried AgCl (M = 143.4 g/mol) forms. Find the chloride concentration in g/L.
vce-chem12-colorimetry-and-uv-visible-sp: chem12a3-cu-1
A colorimeter is used to find the concentration of a blue copper(II) solution. Which colour of light should be selected, and why?
Blue light, because the solution is blue
Orange light, because the solution absorbs it most strongly
White light, because it contains all wavelengths
Green light, because it is in the middle of the visible spectrum

A solution looks blue because it transmits blue light and absorbs the complementary colour, orange. Measuring at the wavelength absorbed most strongly gives the greatest sensitivity. Blue light would mostly pass straight through.
chem12a3-cu-2

A calibration curve for a dye is a straight line through the origin. A 4.0 mg L⁻¹ standard has an absorbance of 0.40. An unknown sample has an absorbance of 0.26. What is the concentration of the unknown?
2.6 mg L⁻¹
0.65 mg L⁻¹
6.2 mg L⁻¹
1.04 mg L⁻¹
Absorbance is proportional to concentration: c = 0.26 ÷ 0.40 × 4.0 = 2.6 mg L⁻¹. 6.2 mg L⁻¹ comes from inverting the ratio.
chem12a3-cu-3
Before measuring standards and samples, a cuvette containing only the solvent (a blank) is placed in the spectrophotometer. Its purpose is to:
calibrate the wavelength of the light source
find the concentration of the most dilute standard
check that the analyte is coloured
set absorbance to zero, so that any absorbance by the solvent and cuvette is not counted
The blank sets the baseline (A = 0), so measured absorbances come only from the analyte. It does not set the wavelength or measure a concentration.
chem12a3-cu-4
The absorbance of an unknown sample is higher than that of the most concentrated standard on the calibration curve. The most appropriate action is to:
extend the calibration line to estimate the concentration
use a different wavelength at which the sample absorbs more
dilute the sample by a known factor, remeasure, and multiply by the dilution factor
report the concentration as equal to the highest standard

Results are only reliable within the range of the standards, because the absorbance–concentration relationship may stop being linear. Diluting by a known factor brings the reading within range. Extrapolation assumes linearity that may not hold.
chem12a3-cu-5
UV-visible spectroscopy is based on the absorption of radiation that causes:
bonds within molecules to vibrate
electrons to move to higher energy levels
nuclei to change their spin state
molecules to fragment into charged ions
UV and visible photons have the right energy to promote electrons to higher energy levels. Bond vibrations are caused by infrared radiation, and fragmentation into ions describes mass spectrometry.
chem12a3-cu-6

Iron in tank water is reacted to form a red complex. Standards of 0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0 and 8.0 mg L⁻¹ iron give absorbances of 0.00, 0.11, 0.22, 0.33 and 0.44. A 5.0 mL sample of tank water is treated and diluted to 50.0 mL, giving an absorbance of 0.15. Calculate the iron concentration in the original tank water. (3 marks)
The calibration is linear with slope 0.11 ÷ 2.0 = 0.055 per mg L⁻¹; diluted sample c = 0.15 ÷ 0.055 = 2.7 mg L⁻¹; dilution factor 50.0 ÷ 5.0 = 10, so original = 27 mg L⁻¹.
chem12a3-cu-7
Explain why the wavelength of maximum absorbance (λmax) of the analyte is normally chosen for a UV-visible spectroscopic analysis. (2 marks)

At λmax the absorbance changes most for a given change in concentration, giving the greatest sensitivity and the lowest detection limit; the absorption peak is flattest there, so small shifts in wavelength have little effect on readings, which improves precision (it may also reduce interference from other species).
chem12a3-cu-8

Explain why a set of standard solutions must be measured to produce a calibration curve each time an analysis is done, and why sample absorbances should fall within the range of the standards. (3 marks)

Absorbance depends on the instrument, wavelength, cuvette path length and the analyte, so the relationship between absorbance and concentration must be found under the same conditions; the curve converts sample absorbance into concentration; the relationship is only known to be linear over the range measured, and at high concentrations it may stop being linear, so extrapolating beyond the standards is unreliable.
chem12a3-cu-9
Which range of wavelengths corresponds to visible light?
Visible light spans roughly 400–700 nm. Wavelengths below 400 nm are ultraviolet, and those above 700 nm are infrared.
chem12a3-cu-10
A dye solution within the linear range of a spectrophotometer has an absorbance of 0.80. A 10.0 mL portion is diluted to 20.0 mL with water. What absorbance is expected for the diluted solution?
Diluting by a factor of 2 halves the concentration, and absorbance is proportional to concentration, so A = 0.40. 1.6 comes from multiplying instead of dividing by the dilution factor.
chem12a3-cu-11
What are the units of absorbance?
mol L⁻¹
nm
It has no units
cm⁻¹
Absorbance is a logarithm of a ratio of light intensities, so it is dimensionless. Wavelength is measured in nm, which is a different quantity.
chem12a3-cu-12
Why is a quartz cuvette, rather than a glass or plastic one, required for measurements in the ultraviolet region?
Quartz is cheaper and easier to clean
Quartz scatters light, which increases sensitivity
Quartz absorbs visible light, which removes interference
Quartz is transparent to UV radiation, whereas glass and most plastics absorb it
Glass and most plastics absorb UV radiation, so they would block the beam and give false absorbances. Quartz transmits UV and visible light.
chem12a3-cu-13
Which statement correctly distinguishes a UV-visible spectrophotometer from a simple colorimeter?
A colorimeter measures emitted light, whereas a spectrophotometer measures absorbed light
A colorimeter works only on colourless solutions
A spectrophotometer cannot be used with a calibration curve
A spectrophotometer can select any wavelength across the UV and visible range, whereas a colorimeter uses a few fixed filters in the visible range

A spectrophotometer uses a monochromator to select any wavelength, including UV, while a colorimeter typically uses filters or LEDs for a few visible wavelengths. Both measure absorbance and both use calibration curves.
chem12a3-cu-14
When a calibration curve is plotted for a colorimetric analysis, which choice is standard?
Concentration on the y-axis and absorbance on the x-axis
Absorbance on the y-axis and concentration of the standards on the x-axis
Absorbance on the y-axis and wavelength on the x-axis
Transmittance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis
Absorbance (measured response) is plotted against the known concentration of the standards. Absorbance against wavelength is an absorption spectrum, not a calibration curve.
chem12a3-cu-15
Which of the following ions in aqueous solution could NOT be determined directly by visible colorimetry, without first reacting it to form a coloured species?
Cu²⁺ (blue)
MnO₄⁻ (purple)
Zn²⁺ (colourless)
Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange)
Zn²⁺(aq) does not absorb visible light, so a reagent must be added to make a coloured complex. The other ions already absorb strongly in the visible region.
chem12a3-cu-16
A solution is measured and found to have an absorbance of 0 at the chosen wavelength, relative to a blank. This means that:
the sample absorbs no more light at that wavelength than the blank does
the sample absorbs all of the light at that wavelength
the concentration of the sample is 1.0 mol L⁻¹
the instrument has failed
An absorbance of 0 means the same intensity is transmitted as for the blank, so the analyte absorbs no measurable light. Total absorption would give a very large absorbance, not zero.
chem12a3-cu-17
What is plotted on the axes of a UV-visible absorption spectrum?
Concentration against absorbance
Absorbance against time
Wavelength against concentration
Absorbance against wavelength
An absorption spectrum shows how absorbance varies with wavelength, and the peak gives λmax. Absorbance against concentration is a calibration curve.
chem12a3-cu-18
Another species in a water sample absorbs light at the same wavelength as the analyte being measured. How will this affect the calculated concentration of the analyte?
It will be too low, because less analyte absorbs light
It will be too high, because the measured absorbance includes the other species
It will be unaffected, because only the analyte is coloured
It will be zero
Absorbances from different species at the same wavelength add together, so the reading is higher than the analyte alone would give. This overestimates the concentration.
chem12a3-cu-19
A student prepares standards and measures them in 1.0 cm cuvettes, but measures the sample in a 2.0 cm cuvette. The sample concentration read from the calibration curve will be:
half the true value
unchanged, since concentration does not depend on cuvette
about double the true value
zero, as the beam cannot pass through
Absorbance is proportional to path length, so doubling the path doubles the absorbance and the concentration read from the curve. Halving would occur only if the path were shorter.
chem12a3-cu-20
Why should a cuvette be held only by its frosted (non-optical) sides?
Fingerprints on the clear faces absorb and scatter light, giving a falsely high absorbance
The frosted sides contain the sample
Oil from fingers reacts with the analyte to change its colour
The frosted sides are the only ones that are sterile
Marks, smudges and fingerprints on the clear faces scatter and absorb the beam, adding to the absorbance. They do not change the chemistry of the analyte.
chem12a3-cu-21
Compared with visible light, ultraviolet radiation has:
longer wavelength and higher energy per photon
longer wavelength and lower energy per photon
the same energy but a lower frequency
shorter wavelength and higher energy per photon

UV radiation has wavelengths below about 400 nm, and energy is inversely related to wavelength, so each photon carries more energy. Higher energy is why UV can excite electrons in many colourless compounds.
chem12a3-cu-22
Describe how a student could prepare 100.0 mL of a 20 mg L⁻¹ standard solution from a 100 mg L⁻¹ stock solution. Include the volume of stock required. (3 marks)

Use c₁V₁ = c₂V₂: V₁ = 20 × 100.0 ÷ 100 = 20 mL of stock required [1]. Measure 20.0 mL of the stock accurately using a pipette (or burette) and transfer it to a 100.0 mL volumetric flask [1]. Add deionised water up to the mark, stopper and invert several times to mix thoroughly [1].
chem12a3-cu-23

Standard solutions of 0.50, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mmol L⁻¹ of a coloured complex give absorbances of 0.12, 0.24, 0.36 and 0.48 respectively. A 25.0 mL sample gives an absorbance of 0.30. Calculate the amount, in mol, of the complex in the 25.0 mL sample. (3 marks)
The calibration is linear through the origin with a slope of 0.24 per mmol L⁻¹ (0.12 ÷ 0.50) [1]. c = 0.30 ÷ 0.24 = 1.25 mmol L⁻¹ [1]. n = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ mol [1].
chem12a3-cu-24
A colourless analyte is to be determined by visible colorimetry. Explain why it is first reacted with a reagent, and why the amount of reagent is controlled. (2 marks)

The reagent reacts with the analyte to form a coloured species that absorbs in the visible region, so absorbance can be measured [1]. The reagent is added in excess/fixed amounts so that all the analyte reacts and the colour intensity (absorbance) is proportional to the analyte concentration [1].
chem12a3-cu-25

A calibration graph of absorbance against concentration curves towards the horizontal axis at high concentrations. Explain why this limits the analysis and state what should be done with a sample of high concentration. (2 marks)

The absorbance is no longer proportional to concentration at high concentrations, so the calibration is unreliable beyond the linear range and concentrations cannot be read accurately [1]. The sample should be diluted by a known factor so that its absorbance falls within the linear range, then the dilution factor is applied to the result [1].
chem12a3-cu-26

A 0.500 g sample of brass is dissolved and made up to 250.0 mL. A 1.00 mL aliquot is diluted to 100.0 mL and its copper concentration is determined by colorimetry. A calibration line through the origin has a slope of 0.040 absorbance units per mg L⁻¹, and the diluted solution has an absorbance of 0.48. Calculate the percentage of copper by mass in the brass. (4 marks)

Concentration of diluted solution = 0.48 ÷ 0.040 = 12 mg L⁻¹ [1]. Dilution factor = 100.0 ÷ 1.00 = 100, so the 250.0 mL solution is 1200 mg L⁻¹ [1]. Mass of Cu = 1200 mg L⁻¹ × 0.2500 L = 300 mg [1]. % Cu = 300 ÷ 500 × 100 = 60% [1].
chem12a3-cu-27
State two precautions that should be taken when filling and placing a cuvette in a spectrophotometer to ensure accurate absorbance readings. (2 marks)

Rinse the cuvette with a small amount of the solution to be measured, and avoid air bubbles in the light path [1]. Wipe the clear faces clean and handle only by the frosted sides; place the cuvette in the same orientation each time [1].
chem12a3-cu-28
An aqueous solution of potassium permanganate appears purple. Explain this observation in terms of the light absorbed and transmitted by the solution. (3 marks)

White light contains all visible wavelengths, and the solution absorbs light of some wavelengths (mainly green, around 530 nm) as electrons are promoted to higher energy levels [1]. The remaining wavelengths (red and blue/violet) are transmitted [1]. The transmitted light combines to give the complementary colour, so the solution appears purple [1].
chem12a3-cu-29
State how absorbance depends on the concentration of the analyte and on the path length of the cuvette, for a dilute solution at a fixed wavelength. (2 marks)
Absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing species [1]. Absorbance is also directly proportional to the path length of the cuvette [1].
chem12a3-cu-30
Describe how a calibration curve is used to determine the concentration of Cu²⁺ in a water sample by colorimetry. (3 marks)

Prepare standard solutions of known Cu²⁺ concentration and measure their absorbance at the wavelength of maximum absorbance [1]; plot absorbance against concentration to give a straight-line calibration curve [1]; measure the absorbance of the sample (diluting if it is out of range) and read its concentration from the curve, allowing for any dilution [1].
vce-chem12-uv-c1
A calibration curve gives an absorbance of 0.080 per mg/L of copper(II). A sample diluted by a factor of 10 has an absorbance of 0.36. Find the copper concentration in the original sample.
45 mg/L
Diluted sample: 0.36 ÷ 0.080 = 4.5 mg/L. Multiply by the dilution factor: 4.5 × 10 = 45 mg/L.
vce-chem12-greenhouse-gases-and-ocean-ac: chem12a3-go-1
Which of the following gases in the atmosphere is NOT a greenhouse gas?
Methane, CH₄
Water vapour, H₂O
Nitrogen, N₂
Nitrous oxide, N₂O
N₂ is a symmetrical diatomic molecule that does not absorb infrared radiation, so it is not a greenhouse gas. Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas.
chem12a3-go-2
Greenhouse gases warm the lower atmosphere mainly because they:
absorb incoming ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
absorb infrared radiation emitted from Earth's surface and re-emit some of it back towards the surface
reflect visible sunlight back to Earth
destroy the ozone layer, letting more radiation in

Earth's surface emits infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb it and re-radiate energy in all directions, including back down. UV absorption is mainly due to ozone, and ozone depletion is a separate issue.
chem12a3-go-3
As atmospheric CO₂ rises, more CO₂ dissolves in the oceans. What happens to the concentration of carbonate ions, CO₃²⁻, in seawater?
It increases, because CO₂ forms carbonic acid which ionises to carbonate
It is unchanged, because the ocean is buffered
It increases, because more calcium carbonate dissolves
It decreases, because the extra H₃O⁺ reacts with CO₃²⁻ to form HCO₃⁻

Dissolved CO₂ forms H₂CO₃, which donates protons; the extra H₃O⁺ reacts with carbonate (H₃O⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻ + H₂O), lowering [CO₃²⁻]. Buffering slows the pH change but does not stop carbonate being used up.
chem12a3-go-4
Which organisms are most directly threatened by ocean acidification?
Organisms that build calcium carbonate shells or skeletons, such as corals and molluscs
Large fish that breathe through gills
Seaweeds that photosynthesise
Seabirds that feed at the surface

Lower carbonate ion concentration makes it harder to form CaCO₃ and can dissolve existing structures, which threatens reef-building corals (e.g. on the Great Barrier Reef), molluscs and some plankton. The other groups are affected only indirectly.
chem12a3-go-5
The average surface ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 since pre-industrial times. By approximately what percentage has [H₃O⁺] increased?
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so the ratio is 10⁻⁸·¹ ÷ 10⁻⁸·² = 10⁰·¹ ≈ 1.26, an increase of about 26 %. pH is logarithmic, so a 0.1 drop is not a 1 % change.
chem12a3-go-6
Write a series of equations, with states, to show how carbon dioxide from the atmosphere lowers the pH of seawater. (3 marks)
CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq); CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq); H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), and the rise in [H₃O⁺] lowers the pH (some HCO₃⁻ also ionises further to CO₃²⁻ and H₃O⁺).
chem12a3-go-7
Explain how ocean acidification affects the ability of marine organisms to build and keep calcium carbonate shells. Include at least one equation. (3 marks)

Shells form by Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → CaCO₃(s), which needs a good supply of carbonate ions; extra H₃O⁺ from dissolved CO₂ converts carbonate to hydrogencarbonate (H₃O⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)), so less CO₃²⁻ is available and shell building costs organisms more energy; at lower pH existing shells can dissolve: CaCO₃(s) + H₃O⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l).
chem12a3-go-8

Distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect, and explain why methane is a significant contributor despite its much lower atmospheric concentration than CO₂. (3 marks)

The natural greenhouse effect is warming from naturally occurring greenhouse gases that keeps Earth's average temperature about 33 °C warmer than it would be otherwise; the enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming caused by human activities (fossil fuel combustion, land clearing, agriculture) raising greenhouse gas concentrations; methane absorbs infrared radiation far more effectively per molecule than CO₂ (a global warming potential of roughly 25–30 times CO₂ over 100 years), so emissions from livestock, landfill and gas leaks have a large effect.
chem12a3-go-9
Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be closest to:
Greenhouse gases raise the average from about −18 °C to about 15 °C. 15 °C is the actual present average, not the value without the effect.
chem12a3-go-10
The main reason atmospheric CO₂ concentration has risen since the Industrial Revolution is:
increased volcanic eruptions
a decrease in the Sun's output
combustion of fossil fuels and land clearing
increased photosynthesis in the oceans
Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests release CO₂ faster than natural sinks remove it. Photosynthesis removes CO₂, so more of it would lower, not raise, the concentration.
chem12a3-go-11
Methane burns according to CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). What mass of CO₂ is produced by the complete combustion of 16.0 g of methane? (M(CH₄) = 16.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n(CH₄) = 16.0 ÷ 16.0 = 1.00 mol, the mole ratio is 1 : 1, so n(CO₂) = 1.00 mol and m = 1.00 × 44.0 = 44.0 g. Giving 16.0 g wrongly assumes mass is conserved between methane and CO₂.
chem12a3-go-12
Octane burns completely: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l). What mass of CO₂ forms from 57.0 g of octane? (M(C₈H₁₈) = 114.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n(C₈H₁₈) = 57.0 ÷ 114.0 = 0.500 mol; the ratio is 2 : 16, so n(CO₂) = 4.00 mol and m = 4.00 × 44.0 = 176 g. Forgetting the 8 : 1 ratio gives only 0.500 mol of CO₂ (22.0 g).
chem12a3-go-13
The surface ocean has a pH of 8.1. What is [H₃O⁺] in this seawater?
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁸·¹ = 7.9 × 10⁻⁹ M. The pH value is a negative logarithm, so it cannot be written directly as the exponent coefficient.
chem12a3-go-14
Scientists describe the ocean as undergoing 'acidification' even though its pH is about 8.1. This is because:
the ocean's pH is below 7 and it is already acidic
pH is falling, so seawater is becoming less basic (moving towards neutral)
the ocean contains no bases
CO₂ is converted into strong acids in the water
Seawater is still slightly basic (pH above 7), but its pH is decreasing as [H₃O⁺] rises. Dissolved CO₂ forms only a weak acid, and the ocean has not become acidic.
chem12a3-go-15
An increase in atmospheric CO₂ partial pressure shifts the equilibrium CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) so that:
more CO₂ dissolves in seawater, because the system partly opposes the increase in CO₂(g)
less CO₂ dissolves in seawater
the equilibrium constant increases
there is no change, because the ocean is very large
By Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts right to consume some added CO₂(g). K depends only on temperature, so it does not change.
chem12a3-go-16
Compared with cold polar water, warm tropical surface water can hold less dissolved CO₂. This is because the solubility of a gas in water generally:
increases as temperature rises
decreases as temperature rises
is independent of temperature
depends only on the salt content
Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, so warming oceans can absorb less CO₂. Saying it is independent of temperature ignores the endothermic loss of gas from solution on heating.
chem12a3-go-17
Which human activity is a major source of nitrous oxide, N₂O?
Rice paddies and livestock digestion
Burning of coal for electricity
Use of nitrogen-based fertilisers on farmland
Refrigerant leaks from air conditioners
Microbial processes in soil acting on nitrogen fertilisers release N₂O. Livestock and rice paddies are mainly methane sources, and coal combustion mainly releases CO₂.
chem12a3-go-18
As CO₂ dissolves in seawater, the concentration of hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO₃⁻:
decreases, because it is converted to CO₃²⁻
stays constant
decreases, because it is converted to CO₂ gas
increases, because carbonic acid ionises and carbonate reacts with H₃O⁺
Both H₂CO₃ ionising and CO₃²⁻ reacting with H₃O⁺ produce HCO₃⁻, so [HCO₃⁻] rises while [CO₃²⁻] falls. The shift is in the opposite direction to the carbonate change.
chem12a3-go-19
What volume does 22.0 g of CO₂ occupy at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa, molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹)? (M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n = 22.0 ÷ 44.0 = 0.500 mol, so V = 0.500 × 24.8 = 12.4 L. Using 22.0 as the number of litres confuses mass with moles.
chem12a3-go-20
Earth's surface radiates mainly infrared rather than visible light because:
greenhouse gases convert visible light to infrared
infrared is the only radiation that reaches Earth
the surface is much cooler than the Sun
the atmosphere absorbs all visible light

The wavelengths emitted by an object depend on its temperature, so the cool Earth emits infrared while the hot Sun emits mostly visible light. Greenhouse gases absorb that infrared rather than creating it.
chem12a3-go-21
The global warming potential (GWP) of methane over 100 years is about 28. How many tonnes of CO₂-equivalent are represented by 2.0 tonnes of methane released?
CO₂-e = 2.0 × 28 = 56 t. Dividing by 28 reverses the relationship and gives 0.071 t.
chem12a3-go-22
The pH of surface seawater is predicted to fall from 8.2 to 7.9. By what factor does [H₃O⁺] change? (3 marks)
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so initial [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁸·² = 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ M [1]; final [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁷·⁹ = 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ M [1]; the ratio is 10⁰·³ ≈ 2.0, so [H₃O⁺] doubles [1].
chem12a3-go-23
Identify one human activity that releases each of the following greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O. (3 marks)
CO₂: burning fossil fuels (or land clearing) [1]; CH₄: livestock digestion, landfill or rice paddies (or gas leaks) [1]; N₂O: use of nitrogen-based fertilisers (or some industrial processes) [1].
chem12a3-go-24
Propane burns completely in air. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) when 5.00 g of propane, C₃H₈, is burned. (M(C₃H₈) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a3-go-25
Ethanol burns completely: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). What mass of CO₂ forms when 23.0 g of ethanol is burned? (M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n(C₂H₅OH) = 23.0 ÷ 46.0 = 0.500 mol, so n(CO₂) = 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol and m = 44.0 g. The tempting 22.0 g forgets the 1 : 2 mole ratio.
chem12a3-go-26
The pH of surface seawater falls by 0.2 units. By what factor does [H₃O⁺] change?
It increases by a factor of about 0.2
It increases by a factor of about 1.6
It increases by a factor of about 2.0
It increases by a factor of about 20
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so a fall of 0.2 in pH multiplies [H₃O⁺] by 10⁰·² ≈ 1.6. A factor of 2.0 is the result for a 0.3 unit change, not 0.2.
chem12a3-go-27
Shells of marine organisms are mainly CaCO₃(s), which is in equilibrium with its ions: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq). Why does ocean acidification tend to dissolve shells?
Extra H₃O⁺ reacts with Ca²⁺, which lowers the solubility product
Extra H₃O⁺ makes the water warmer, so more CaCO₃ dissolves
Dissolved CO₂ reacts directly with solid CaCO₃ to form a precipitate
Extra H₃O⁺ removes CO₃²⁻ by forming HCO₃⁻, so the equilibrium shifts right and CaCO₃(s) dissolves
H₃O⁺ reacts with CO₃²⁻ to form HCO₃⁻, lowering [CO₃²⁻], so the system shifts right to oppose this and CaCO₃(s) dissolves. H₃O⁺ does not react with Ca²⁺.
chem12a3-go-28
Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain why the ability of the oceans to absorb CO₂ decreases as sea temperature rises, and state the consequence for atmospheric CO₂. (3 marks)

The dissolving of CO₂ is exothermic: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq), ΔH < 0 [1]; a rise in temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) reaction, so the equilibrium shifts left and less CO₂ stays dissolved [1]; less CO₂ is absorbed by the oceans, so more remains in the atmosphere, strengthening the enhanced greenhouse effect [1].
chem12a3-go-29

A farm releases 150 t of methane and 4.0 t of nitrous oxide in a year. The 100-year global warming potentials are 28 for CH₄ and 265 for N₂O. Calculate the total emissions in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. (3 marks)
CO₂-e from methane = 150 × 28 = 4200 t [1]; CO₂-e from nitrous oxide = 4.0 × 265 = 1060 t [1]; total = 4200 + 1060 = 5260 t (5.3 × 10³ t) CO₂-equivalent [1].
chem12a3-go-30

A furnace burns 1.00 × 10³ kg of pure carbon completely to carbon dioxide. Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced and its volume at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹). (M(C) = 12.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
vce-chem12-gg-c1
How does increased atmospheric CO₂ make it harder for shellfish to build calcium carbonate shells?
CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid; the extra H⁺ reacts with carbonate ions, lowering [CO₃²⁻]
CO₂ reacts directly with calcium ions in seawater, so less calcium is left for building shells
CO₂ raises the pH of seawater, so calcium carbonate is less likely to precipitate
CO₂ dissolves and releases extra carbonate ions, which dissolve the existing shells
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, and H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻. Less carbonate is available to form CaCO₃.
vce-chem12-challenge: Copper is 69.2% ⁶³Cu and 30.8% ⁶⁵Cu. Its relative atomic mass is closest to:
2.4 g of magnesium burns to form 4.0 g of magnesium oxide. Find the empirical formula of the oxide.
CO₂ and H₂O both contain polar bonds. Which statement is correct?
Both are polar, because both contain polar bonds to oxygen
Both are non-polar, because both are symmetrical molecules
H₂O is linear, so it is non-polar; CO₂ is bent, so it is polar
CO₂ is linear, so its dipoles cancel; H₂O is bent, so it is polar
Polarity depends on bond polarity and shape. The two lone pairs on oxygen make water bent.
0.010 mol of AgNO₃ is mixed with 0.015 mol of NaCl in solution. What mass of AgCl (M = 143.4 g/mol) forms?
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl reacts 1 : 1, so Ag⁺ (0.010 mol) is limiting. Mass = 0.010 × 143.4 = 1.43 g.
50.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.0800 M NaOH. Find the pH of the mixture.
Using PV = nRT, the volume of 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 0 °C and 100 kPa is about:
In the reaction Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq), the reductant is:
Br⁻ loses electrons (oxidised from −1 to 0), so it is the reductant; Cl₂ is the oxidant.
A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with Ba²⁺(aq) but no precipitate with Ag⁺(aq). It most likely contains:
BaSO₄ is insoluble; chloride would precipitate with Ag⁺; nitrates are always soluble.
The average pH of surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1. The hydronium ion concentration has increased by about:
[H₃O⁺] changes by a factor of 10^0.1 ≈ 1.26, so about 26%. The pH scale is logarithmic.
Explain why butan-1-ol (M = 74) boils at a much higher temperature than pentane (M = 72).
Both have similar dispersion forces because their molar masses are similar, but butan-1-ol also forms hydrogen bonds between its O–H groups, which need more energy to overcome.
Compare the same type of force first, then identify the extra force.

X.title: Magnesium: atoms, bonds and reactions
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Magnesium, Mg, has atomic number 12. Use M(Mg) = 24.3 g mol⁻¹ and M(O) = 16.0 g mol⁻¹.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write the electronic configuration of a magnesium atom using subshell notation.

steps.working: Fill the 12 electrons in order of increasing energy: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s².

pieces.mistake: Writing the shell configuration 2, 8, 2. The question asks for subshell (s, p) notation.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. Explain, in terms of electrons, how the ions in MgO form, and why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point.
pieces.answer: Each Mg atom loses its two 3s electrons to form Mg²⁺, and each O atom gains two electrons to form O²⁻. The ions are held in a lattice by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, which takes a lot of energy to overcome.

steps.working: Electron transfer: a magnesium atom loses its two outer-shell electrons to become Mg²⁺, and an oxygen atom gains two electrons to become O²⁻.
In the ionic lattice, every ion is strongly attracted to the oppositely charged ions around it (ionic bonding), so a lot of energy is needed to separate them and the melting point is high.

pieces.mistake: Describing MgO as made of molecules with weak forces between them, or saying electrons are shared. Ionic compounds are lattices of ions, not molecules.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed when 4.86 g of magnesium burns completely: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).

steps.working: n(Mg) = 4.86 ÷ 24.3 = 0.200 mol. From the equation, n(MgO) = n(Mg) = 0.200 mol.

pieces.mistake: Using the 2 : 2 coefficients as a reason to double the amount. The mole ratio of Mg to MgO is 1 : 1.

pieces.text: Another 4.86 g sample of magnesium is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The magnesium dissolves and bubbles of hydrogen gas form.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Write a balanced equation, including states, for the reaction.

steps.working: A reactive metal and an acid give a salt and hydrogen: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

pieces.mistake: Writing H instead of H₂, or MgCl instead of MgCl₂. Hydrogen gas is diatomic, and Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Identify the species that is oxidised, and write the half-equation for its oxidation.

steps.working: Magnesium is oxidised: it loses electrons (its oxidation number rises from 0 to +2).
Oxidation half-equation: Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.

pieces.mistake: Saying the hydrochloric acid is oxidised. H⁺ gains electrons to form H₂, so it is reduced.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa). The molar volume of a gas at SLC is 24.8 L mol⁻¹.

steps.working: n(Mg) = 0.200 mol and the mole ratio Mg : H₂ is 1 : 1, so n(H₂) = 0.200 mol.

pieces.mistake: Using 22.4 L mol⁻¹, the molar volume at STP. At SLC the molar volume is 24.8 L mol⁻¹.

X.title: Water, acids and a titration
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: A student is investigating the chemistry of water samples.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Water (H₂O, molar mass 18.0 g mol⁻¹) boils at 100 °C, while hydrogen sulfide (H₂S, molar mass 34.1 g mol⁻¹) boils at −60 °C. Explain this difference in terms of intermolecular forces.
pieces.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds: H is bonded to the highly electronegative O atom and is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbouring molecule. H₂S cannot form hydrogen bonds (S is not electronegative enough); it has only weaker dipole–dipole and dispersion forces. More energy is needed to separate water molecules.

steps.working: Water forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, because H is bonded to the small, highly electronegative O atom.
H₂S has only weaker dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, so less energy is needed to separate its molecules, even though they are heavier.

pieces.mistake: Saying the O–H covalent bonds break when water boils. Boiling separates molecules; it breaks intermolecular forces, not the bonds inside molecules.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: A river water sample has a pH of 6.0 at 25 °C. Calculate the concentration of H₃O⁺ ions, and state whether the sample is acidic, neutral or basic.

steps.working: At 25 °C a pH below 7 means [H₃O⁺] is greater than 10⁻⁷ M, so the sample is (slightly) acidic.

pieces.mistake: Writing [H₃O⁺] = 6.0 M or 10⁶ M. pH is the negative logarithm of the concentration, so \([\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}\).

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: A 10.0 mL sample of 0.500 M hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to a total volume of 250.0 mL. Calculate the concentration and the pH of the diluted acid.

steps.working: HCl is a strong acid, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.0200 M and pH = −log₁₀(0.0200) = 1.70.

pieces.mistake: Using 240.0 mL (the volume of water added) as V₂. V₂ is the total volume after dilution.

pieces.text: To find the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution, the student titrated 20.00 mL aliquots of it with 0.0200 M hydrochloric acid. The average titre was 18.40 mL.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

steps.working: An acid and a hydroxide base react to form a salt and water: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l).

pieces.mistake: Leaving out the water. Neutralisation of a hydroxide always produces water.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution.

steps.working: n(HCl) = c × V = 0.0200 × 0.01840 = 3.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and the mole ratio is 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 3.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol.

pieces.mistake: Leaving the volumes in mL. Convert to litres before using n = cV.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: State what the burette should be rinsed with just before it is filled, and why.
pieces.answer: With the hydrochloric acid it will contain, so that any water left inside does not dilute the acid.

steps.working: Rinse the burette with the 0.0200 M HCl, because water left in it would dilute the acid and make the titre too large.

pieces.mistake: Saying the burette should be rinsed with water. That leaves water behind, which dilutes the solution.

X.title: Hydrocarbons and plastics
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Ethene, C₂H₄, is the starting material for polyethene, one of the most widely used plastics.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain why ethene can undergo addition polymerisation.
pieces.answer: It has a carbon–carbon double bond, which can open to form single bonds to other monomers.

steps.working: Ethene is unsaturated: its C=C double bond can break open so that monomers join in a chain.

pieces.mistake: Saying it is because ethene is small. The key feature is the double bond.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Name the type of polymerisation and give the repeating unit of polyethene.
pieces.answer: Addition polymerisation; the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–.

steps.working: Addition polymerisation (no small molecule is lost).
Repeating unit: –CH₂–CH₂–.

pieces.mistake: Calling it condensation polymerisation. No water or other small molecule is produced.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain the difference between a thermoplastic and a thermoset in terms of their structure and how they behave when heated.
pieces.answer: Thermoplastics have no cross-links; their chains are held by intermolecular forces, so they soften and can be remoulded. Thermosets have covalent cross-links, so they do not soften and char instead.

steps.working: Thermoplastic: chains held together only by weak intermolecular forces, so they soften and melt when heated and can be reshaped and recycled.
Thermoset: chains joined by strong covalent cross-links, so they do not melt when heated (they decompose instead).

pieces.mistake: Saying thermosets have stronger intermolecular forces. The difference is covalent cross-linking.

pieces.text: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Use M(C) = 12.0 g mol⁻¹ and M(H) = 1.0 g mol⁻¹.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Determine the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon.

steps.working: Ratio C : H = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂.

pieces.mistake: Using the percentages as the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: The molar mass of the hydrocarbon is 56.0 g mol⁻¹. Find its molecular formula and name one possible structural isomer.

steps.working: M(CH₂) = 14.0, and 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.
A possible isomer: but-1-ene (but-2-ene or methylpropene are also correct).

pieces.mistake: Naming butane. Butane is C₄H₁₀; C₄H₈ has a double bond (or a ring).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Describe one way the circular economy could reduce plastic waste.
pieces.answer: For example, designing products to be reused or recycled so that plastic stays in use instead of going to landfill.

steps.working: Keeping materials in use: design for reuse and recycling, collect and reprocess plastics, or use renewable feedstocks.

pieces.mistake: Describing burning plastic for energy. A circular economy aims to keep materials in use.

X.title: Sulfate in fertiliser and a displacement reaction
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: To find the sulfate content of a fertiliser, a student dissolved 2.50 g of it in water and added excess barium chloride solution. The barium sulfate precipitate was filtered, washed and dried; its mass was 1.86 g. Use M(BaSO₄) = 233.4 g mol⁻¹ and M(SO₄²⁻) = 96.1 g mol⁻¹.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write an ionic equation, with states, for the formation of the precipitate.

steps.working: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).

pieces.mistake: Including spectator ions such as Cl⁻ in an ionic equation.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the percentage by mass of sulfate in the fertiliser.

steps.working: n(BaSO₄) = 1.86 ÷ 233.4 = 7.97 × 10⁻³ mol, which equals n(SO₄²⁻).

pieces.mistake: Dividing the mass of precipitate by the mass of fertiliser (1.86 ÷ 2.50). The precipitate is BaSO₄, not sulfate alone.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain why the precipitate is washed and then dried to constant mass.
pieces.answer: Washing removes soluble impurities that would add mass; drying to constant mass makes sure all the water has gone, so the mass is BaSO₄ only.

steps.working: Washing removes soluble ions (impurities) from the surface of the precipitate.
Heating until the mass no longer changes ensures all water has been removed.

pieces.mistake: Saying it is dried only once. Without reaching constant mass you cannot be sure all the water is gone.

pieces.text: A strip of zinc is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Use M(Zn) = 65.4 g mol⁻¹ and M(Cu) = 63.5 g mol⁻¹.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Write the ionic equation for the reaction and describe two observations.
pieces.answer: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); a brown/pink solid forms on the zinc and the blue colour fades.

steps.working: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Observations: brown copper deposits on the zinc, and the blue solution becomes paler.

pieces.mistake: Writing Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) as the reactants. The more reactive metal, zinc, displaces copper.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why no reaction occurs when copper is placed in zinc sulfate solution.
pieces.answer: Copper is less reactive than zinc (a weaker reductant), so it cannot reduce Zn²⁺ ions.

steps.working: Copper is below zinc in the reactivity series, so it cannot give electrons to Zn²⁺.

pieces.mistake: Saying copper is too heavy. Reactivity, not mass, decides displacement.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Calculate the mass of copper formed when 0.654 g of zinc reacts completely.
pieces.mistake: Assuming the same mass of copper forms. Use moles: 1 mol Zn gives 1 mol Cu.

X.title: Challenge: testing a river sample
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: A student analyses water from a river near an old mine. Excess silver nitrate solution is added to a 100.0 mL sample, and 0.574 g of dry silver chloride (M = 143.4 g/mol) is collected.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write the ionic equation for the precipitation reaction.

steps.working: Correct ionic equation with states.

pieces.mistake: Including the spectator ions Na⁺ and NO₃⁻.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the chloride concentration of the river water in ppm (mg/L).
pieces.mistake: Using the mass of AgCl instead of the mass of chloride.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain why silver nitrate is added in excess, and why the precipitate is dried to constant mass.
pieces.answer: Excess Ag⁺ ensures all the chloride precipitates. Drying to constant mass ensures all water has gone, so the mass is not too high.

steps.working: Excess reagent makes the precipitation complete.
Constant mass shows that all the water has been removed.

pieces.mistake: Saying excess makes the reaction faster.

pieces.text: The water is also acidic. A 25.00 mL sample needs 12.50 mL of 0.0100 M NaOH to neutralise its acid.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Calculate the concentration of H₃O⁺ in the river water, and its pH.
pieces.mistake: Dividing by the NaOH volume instead of the sample volume.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Downstream, the river water is diluted tenfold by a clean creek. Predict the new pH, assuming the acid is strong.

steps.working: A tenfold dilution lowers [H₃O⁺] by a factor of 10, raising the pH by 1.

pieces.mistake: Dividing the pH by 10.

X.title: Challenge: a barbecue's carbon footprint
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: A gas barbecue burns propane, C₃H₈ (M = 44.0 g/mol). A full cylinder holds 2.20 kg of propane.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, with states.

steps.working: Correctly balanced equation with states.

pieces.mistake: Balancing oxygen before carbon and hydrogen.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when the whole cylinder burns.
pieces.mistake: Assuming the mass of CO₂ equals the mass of propane.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: What volume would this carbon dioxide occupy at SLC?
pieces.mistake: Using 22.4 L/mol, which is not SLC.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: On a hot day (30 °C) at 101.3 kPa, what volume of oxygen is used?
pieces.mistake: Using 30 instead of 303 K.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain, using equations, how some of this carbon dioxide can lower the pH of the ocean.
pieces.answer: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq); CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq); H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq). The extra H₃O⁺ lowers the pH.

steps.working: CO₂ dissolves and forms carbonic acid.
Carbonic acid donates H⁺ to water, increasing [H₃O⁺], so pH falls.

pieces.mistake: Saying CO₂ is a strong acid.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Explain why the water produced has a higher boiling point than propane, although its molar mass is lower.
pieces.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds (O–H with lone pairs on O), which are much stronger than the weak dispersion forces between non-polar propane molecules.

steps.working: Water: hydrogen bonding between molecules.
Propane: only dispersion forces, which are weaker, so less energy is needed to separate the molecules.

pieces.mistake: Saying the O–H covalent bonds break when water boils.
